.gitattributes.summary: `.gitattributes` defines path-specific rules for Git. Rules can control line endings, filters, diffs, merges, and archive behavior.
.gitattributes.explanation: Git reads attribute rules from files such as .gitattributes and applies matching rules to paths. A rule contains a pattern and one or more attributes. An attribute can be enabled, disabled, assigned a string value, or reset to unspecified. Later matching rules override earlier ones for each attribute.

example.title: Set path attributes
example.code:
*.txt text
*.sh text eol=lf
*.jpg -text

printf 'hello\n' > notes.txt
git add --renormalize .
git status
example.explanation: This marks text files for line-ending normalization, keeps shell files with LF endings, and excludes JPG files. The renormalize command updates the index using the new rules.

useCases.title: Normalize line endings
useCases.scenario: A project is edited on systems with different line-ending conventions.

useCases.title: Run content filters
useCases.scenario: A file needs a custom transformation when staged or checked out.

useCases.title: Mark special files
useCases.scenario: A binary or machine-generated file should not receive normal text handling.

useCases.title: Control archives
useCases.scenario: Generated files should be omitted from exported archives.

interview.question: How are attributes represented and overridden?
interview.answer: Git reads a pattern followed by attributes. A name enables an attribute, `-name` disables it, `name=value` assigns a value, and `!name` resets it to unspecified. Later matching lines override earlier lines per attribute.
interview.followUp: Where should shared rules go? Put them in a versioned `.gitattributes` file; use `$GIT_DIR/info/attributes` for rules limited to one repository and one user's workflow.

interview.question: What does the `text` attribute do?
interview.answer: The `text` attribute controls line-ending normalization. Git stores normalized text with LF in the repository, while `eol` can select the working-tree line-ending style for a path.
interview.followUp: How would you normalize an existing repository? Add the rule, run `git add --renormalize .`, inspect `git status`, and commit the result.

interview.question: When are clean and smudge filters used?
interview.answer: A filter attribute selects a configured clean and smudge process. The clean process runs when content is staged, and the smudge process runs when content is checked out.
interview.followUp: What property should a clean filter have? Running it twice should produce the same result as running it once, so repeated staging does not keep changing content.

keyPoints: `.gitattributes` assigns behavior to paths in a repository.
Each rule has a path pattern followed by one or more attributes.
Use `name=value` when an attribute needs a string value.
Rules later in the file take precedence for attributes they also set.
Repository-local rules in `$GIT_DIR/info/attributes` have the highest precedence.
The `text` attribute enables Git's line-ending conversion for a path.
gotchas: Attribute files cannot use negative patterns.
A directory pattern does not automatically apply to files below it; use `path/**` when needed.
After changing a clean filter, run `git add --renormalize .`.

.gitconfig.summary: git config reads and changes Git settings. Settings can apply to the system, one user, one repository, or one worktree.
.gitconfig.explanation: Git reads configuration from system, global, repository, and sometimes worktree files. Later files override earlier single values. Use a scope option to choose where Git reads or writes a setting.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Configuration key, usually written as section.name, such as core.editor.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: New value when setting a key. Some commands also accept a value pattern for matching.

parameters.name: scope
parameters.description: Configuration source selector, such as --global, --local, --system, --worktree, or --file.

.gitconfig.returns: Read operations return the requested value or an error if no value is found. Writing operations update the selected configuration file.

example.title: Set and read Git configuration
example.code:
git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace"
git config --global user.email ada@example.com

git config --local core.editor "code --wait"
git config --local --get core.editor
example.explanation: This sets user details in the global configuration, sets an editor in the repository configuration, and reads that local value.

useCases.title: Configure user identity
useCases.scenario: Set a name and email for all repositories on one machine.

useCases.title: Set repository behavior
useCases.scenario: Keep a setting limited to one repository.

useCases.title: Configure a worktree
useCases.scenario: Use different settings for linked worktrees.

useCases.title: Read or edit configuration
useCases.scenario: Inspect or change a setting in a chosen configuration file.

interview.question: How does Git choose between configuration files?
interview.answer: Git normally reads system, global, repository, and, when enabled, worktree configuration. For a single-valued setting, a later value takes precedence over an earlier one.
interview.followUp: How can a script provide temporary configuration without editing files? Use git -c key=value for a command, or the GIT_CONFIG_COUNT, GIT_CONFIG_KEY_n, and GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_n environment variables for runtime pairs.

interview.question: How do you select a configuration scope?
interview.answer: Use --global for the user configuration, --system for the system file, --local for the repository file, and --worktree for config.worktree when worktree configuration is enabled. --file selects a specific file.
interview.followUp: What happens with --global when both global paths exist? Git reads $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/config and ~/.gitconfig in that order.

interview.question: How are configuration names structured?
interview.answer: A Git configuration file contains sections and variables. A variable name is the final dot-separated part, and a subsection is written in quotes in a header such as [remote "origin"].
interview.followUp: What is special about repeated variables? They are multivalued, so commands can read all values rather than only the last one.

keyPoints: Git can read settings from system, global, repository, and optional worktree files.
For a single-valued setting, a value from a later source overrides an earlier value.
Without a scope option, writing targets the repository's .git/config file.
--global limits reads to the global configuration files and writes to the global location.
--worktree uses config.worktree only when worktree configuration is enabled; otherwise it acts like --local.
A variable may have several values, and Git can use all occurrences of that variable.
gotchas: A command changes only one configuration file. Choose the target with --system, --global, --local, --worktree, or --file.
A missing or unreadable repository configuration file causes an error, unlike missing global or system files, which Git ignores.
Section names and variable names are case-insensitive, but subsection names preserve case and have different allowed characters.

.gitignore.summary: A .gitignore file tells Git which untracked paths to ignore. Its patterns support directory-relative matching, wildcards, and exceptions with !.
.gitignore.explanation: Git reads patterns from .gitignore files and other exclude files. Patterns can match files or directories, use shell-style wildcards, and be reversed with a leading !. A tracked file is not affected by a matching pattern; remove it from the index first with git rm --cached.

example.title: A .gitignore file
example.code:
# Ignore editor backups everywhere in this repository
*.swp

# Ignore only the root build directory
/build/

# Ignore generated HTML under Documentation, except one kept file
Documentation/*.html
!Documentation/foo.html
example.explanation: Save these patterns in a repository .gitignore file. Git ignores matching untracked paths. The later exception keeps foo.html visible.

useCases.title: Share project ignore rules
useCases.scenario: A build creates files that should not be committed by any developer.

useCases.title: Keep repository-local files private
useCases.scenario: One repository needs local ignore rules that should not be committed.

useCases.title: Ignore user-wide temporary files
useCases.scenario: An editor creates backup files in many repositories.

interview.question: What is the purpose of .gitignore?
interview.answer: A .gitignore file contains patterns for intentionally untracked paths. Git checks patterns from the relevant directory and its parents, and a lower directory's file can override a higher one.
interview.followUp: What wins when several patterns match?

interview.question: How does a slash affect a pattern?
interview.answer: A pattern without a slash can match at any level below the .gitignore file. A slash at the start or middle makes the pattern relative to that file's directory.
interview.followUp: What does a trailing slash change?

interview.question: How do negation patterns work?
interview.answer: A leading ! reverses an earlier ignore rule. The exception works only when no parent directory of the target is excluded.
interview.followUp: How can a file inside an otherwise excluded tree be restored?

keyPoints: Use .gitignore to keep selected untracked files out of normal Git operations.
When rules at the same precedence match, the last matching rule wins.
Git can use a .gitignore beside the path, or one in a parent directory up to the worktree root.
Put shared project rules in .gitignore so cloned repositories receive them.
The * wildcard matches any sequence except a directory separator.
The ? wildcard matches exactly one non-separator character.
A pattern ending in /** matches all contents below that directory.
gotchas: Adding a tracked file to .gitignore does not stop tracking it. Use git rm --cached, then add its name to .gitignore.
An exception cannot restore a file inside an excluded parent directory. Keep the parent directory reachable, then exclude its contents.
Blank lines do not create ignore rules. They only separate groups of patterns.
Do not end a pattern with an unescaped backslash. Such a pattern never matches.

Commit graph.summary: A commit graph is a supplemental file that stores commit relationships and metadata. Git uses it to speed up history walks and merge-base calculations.
Commit graph.explanation: Git stores commit relationships and extra data in a commit-graph file. Git can use this data to speed up history walks and merge-base calculations. The file is stored in the object database, and Git can verify it against that database.

parameters.name: command
parameters.description: Selects a subcommand such as write or verify.

parameters.name: --reachable
parameters.description: Build from commits reachable from all references.

parameters.name: --append
parameters.description: Add commits already in the existing graph.

parameters.name: --split
parameters.description: Store the graph as a chain of files.

parameters.name: --shallow
parameters.description: Check the graph against the object database.

Commit graph.returns: The write command creates or updates a commit-graph file. The verify command checks its contents against the object database and exits successfully when the data is valid.

example.title: Create and check a commit graph
example.code:
git commit-graph write --reachable
git commit-graph verify
example.explanation: Writes a graph from commits reachable from all references, then checks the graph against the object database.

useCases.title: Speed up commit walks
useCases.scenario: A repository has a large commit history and history commands are slow.

useCases.title: Update a graph incrementally
useCases.scenario: A repository receives new commits regularly.

useCases.title: Check graph integrity
useCases.scenario: You suspect the graph cache is damaged.

useCases.title: Choose graph input
useCases.scenario: You need a graph from selected commits or references.

interview.question: What is a commit graph and why does Git use it?
interview.answer: A commit graph is a supplemental structure that stores commit relationships and metadata outside commit objects. It helps Git walk history and compute merge bases faster.
interview.followUp: What data does it store? It can provide each commit's object ID, parents, date, root tree, and generation number.

interview.question: How can git commit-graph write choose its input commits?
interview.answer: The write command creates a graph from packed commits by default. With --reachable, it starts from all references; with --stdin-commits or --stdin-packs, it uses the specified input instead.
interview.followUp: Which input modes cannot be combined? --reachable cannot be combined with either stdin mode, and the two stdin modes cannot be combined with each other.

interview.question: How do split commit graphs work?
interview.answer: A split graph stores multiple files in the commit-graphs directory. New commits go into a tip file, which Git may merge with the previous tip based on size and maximum-commit rules.
interview.followUp: When are old split files removed? Git removes unused files older than the expiration time, which defaults to the current time after writing.

keyPoints: It is an optional cache that makes commit-history walks faster.
Besides parent links, it stores metadata used during graph traversal.
A normal repository stores the file at .git/objects/info/commit-graph.
Git must have core.commitGraph enabled to read the graph.
The --reachable option builds the graph from commits reachable from every reference.
--append preserves commits already present in the current graph while adding new ones.
gotchas: Shallow clones disable commit-graph reading and writing when shallow commits are present.
The object database remains sufficient if commit-graph use is disabled or Git is downgraded.
A commit graph from another source should be trusted carefully because verification can cost as much as rebuilding it.

commit-msg hook.summary: Git hooks are scripts that Git runs during commands such as commit, merge, rebase, checkout, and patch application. Some hooks can reject an operation; others run afterward for notification.
commit-msg hook.explanation: Git calls hooks at defined points during commands. A hook can inspect or change some files, and a non-zero exit can stop operations for hooks that support rejection. Some hooks run after the operation and are for notifications only.
commit-msg hook.syntax: Executable scripts in .git/hooks/; each hook uses its documented command-specific arguments.

parameters.name: message-file
parameters.description: Path to the proposed commit-message file.

parameters.name: upstream
parameters.description: For pre-rebase, the upstream from which the series was forked.

parameters.name: branch
parameters.description: For pre-rebase, the branch being rebased; omitted for the current branch.

parameters.name: checkout-data
parameters.description: For post-checkout, the previous HEAD ref, new HEAD ref, and checkout type flag.

commit-msg hook.returns: A non-zero hook exit status aborts operations where the hook is allowed to reject them. Notification hooks such as post-commit cannot affect the completed operation.

example.title: Validate a commit message
example.code:
#!/bin/sh
# .git/hooks/commit-msg
message_file="$1"
if ! grep -q '^JIRA-[0-9][0-9]*: ' "$message_file"; then
  echo "Commit message must start with a JIRA key" >&2
  exit 1
fi
example.explanation: Save this executable script as .git/hooks/commit-msg. It checks the proposed message file and rejects messages without the required prefix.

useCases.title: Validate changes before commit
useCases.scenario: Run tests, lint, or whitespace checks before creating a commit.

useCases.title: Check commit messages
useCases.scenario: Require a project format or ticket prefix in commit messages.

useCases.title: Notify after Git actions
useCases.scenario: Send notifications after commits or patch application.

useCases.title: Control rebasing
useCases.scenario: Prevent selected branches from being rebased.

interview.question: How does pre-commit work?
interview.answer: pre-commit runs before Git creates the commit and receives no parameters. A non-zero exit stops the commit, and git commit --no-verify can bypass it.
interview.followUp: Which hook validates the message instead? commit-msg receives the message-file path and can reject the commit with a non-zero exit.

interview.question: What is the role of commit-msg?
interview.answer: commit-msg receives one parameter: the file containing the proposed commit message. It may edit that file or reject the operation by exiting non-zero.
interview.followUp: Can prepare-commit-msg replace it? No. The documentation says prepare-commit-msg edits the message before the editor and should not replace pre-commit.

interview.question: What arguments does pre-rebase receive?
interview.answer: pre-rebase can prevent a branch from being rebased. Its first parameter is the upstream; its optional second parameter is the branch being rebased when that is not the current branch.
interview.followUp: What happens when the current branch is rebased? The second parameter is omitted, so the hook must handle one-parameter calls.

keyPoints: pre-commit can inspect the worktree or run checks before a commit is created.
commit-msg can rewrite the proposed message before Git finishes the commit.
post-commit runs after success and cannot make the commit fail.
post-checkout receives the old ref, new ref, and a flag identifying branch or file checkout.
Git's sample pre-commit hook can reject non-ASCII filenames, depending on configuration.
gotchas: prepare-commit-msg cannot be skipped with --no-verify, unlike several other commit hooks.
post-checkout cannot change whether checkout or switch succeeds, although its exit status is returned.
pre-rebase has no second parameter when the current branch is being rebased.

Detached HEAD.summary: Git worktree lets one repository have several working directories. Each worktree can check out a different branch or commit while sharing the repository's data.
Detached HEAD.explanation: A worktree is another working directory connected to the same Git repository. Each worktree has its own checked-out commit, HEAD, index, and working files, while the repository data is shared. Use it to work on another branch without changing the files in the current directory.
Detached HEAD.syntax:
git worktree add <path> [<commit-ish>]
git worktree list
git worktree remove <worktree>

parameters.name: <path>
parameters.description: Directory where Git creates the additional working tree.

parameters.name: <commit-ish>
parameters.description: Commit, branch, or other commit-ish to check out. If omitted, Git uses the documented default behavior.

parameters.name: <new-branch>
parameters.description: New branch name used with -b or -B.

Detached HEAD.returns: The commands create, inspect, lock, move, repair, prune, or remove linked working trees. The documentation does not define a programming return value.

example.title: Use a second working tree
example.code:
git worktree add ../feature feature-branch
git -C ../feature status
git worktree list
example.explanation: This creates a second working tree for an existing branch, checks its status, and lists all worktrees.

useCases.title: Parallel branch work
useCases.scenario: Work on a second branch without stashing changes in the current directory.

useCases.title: Temporary experiment
useCases.scenario: Run tests or inspect files at a specific commit without changing the main worktree.

useCases.title: Long-running branches
useCases.scenario: Keep separate working directories for a main branch and a feature branch.

interview.question: What does git worktree add do?
interview.answer: git worktree add creates another working directory linked to the current repository. It shares repository data but has separate files such as HEAD and the index.
interview.followUp: How do you create a temporary worktree without a branch? Use git worktree add -d <path>, which creates a detached HEAD worktree.

interview.question: How do you inspect worktrees?
interview.answer: Use git worktree list to show the main and linked worktrees. The output includes their paths, checked-out revisions, and branches or detached HEAD states.
interview.followUp: How can a script parse the output safely? Use git worktree list --porcelain, optionally with -z for NUL-terminated records.

interview.question: When can a worktree be removed?
interview.answer: git worktree remove deletes a linked worktree when it is clean. A worktree with changes or untracked files requires --force, and a locked worktree requires --force twice.
interview.followUp: What should you do after manually deleting a worktree? Run git worktree prune to remove stale administrative information.

keyPoints: git worktree add creates a new directory and checks out the selected commit or branch there.
Worktrees share repository objects and configuration-related data, but each has its own HEAD and index.
Use -d when you want a temporary worktree for experiments without creating a branch.
git worktree list shows every worktree, including its current revision and branch state.
git worktree prune cleans up records for worktree directories that were deleted outside Git.
gotchas: By default, remove only a clean worktree. Use --force for an unclean worktree.
git worktree remove cannot remove the main working tree.
A locked worktree needs two --force options before it can be removed.

Fast-forward merge.summary: Git merge combines another commit or branch with the current branch. It either fast-forwards the current branch or creates a merge commit; conflicts require manual resolution.
Fast-forward merge.explanation: A fast-forward merge moves the current branch to the other commit when the current commit is its ancestor. Otherwise, Git creates a merge commit with both branch tips as parents. Conflicts leave HEAD unchanged, record multiple index stages, and add conflict markers to affected working-tree files.

parameters.name: <commit>
parameters.description: The branch or commit to merge into the current branch.

parameters.name: [options]
parameters.description: Optional options such as --no-ff or --abort.

Fast-forward merge.returns: A fast-forward updates the current branch without a new commit. A true merge creates a merge commit, or leaves conflict state for resolution when paths cannot be reconciled.

example.title: Merge a feature branch
example.code:
git switch main
git merge feature/login
# Resolve conflicts if Git reports them
git add <resolved-files>
git commit
example.explanation: This merges the feature branch into main. Git may fast-forward or create a merge commit. If files conflict, resolve them, stage the results, and commit the merge.

useCases.title: Integrate a feature branch
useCases.scenario: A feature branch is complete and its changes must enter the main branch.

useCases.title: Update by fast-forwarding
useCases.scenario: The current branch is behind a descendant commit.

useCases.title: Join diverged histories
useCases.scenario: Two branches changed independently and their histories must be joined.

interview.question: What is a fast-forward merge?
interview.answer: Git fast-forwards when the current branch tip is an ancestor of the commit being merged. It moves HEAD and the index without creating a merge commit.
interview.followUp: How can you force a merge commit in that case? Use git merge --no-ff.

interview.question: What happens during a true merge?
interview.answer: A true merge creates a commit with both branch tips as parents. Git updates HEAD, the index, and the working tree to the reconciled result.
interview.followUp: What happens when reconciliation fails? HEAD stays unchanged, MERGE_HEAD points to the other tip, and conflict stages are recorded.

interview.question: How does Git represent a merge conflict?
interview.answer: For a conflict, the index can contain stage 1 for the common ancestor, stage 2 for HEAD, and stage 3 for MERGE_HEAD. The working tree contains three-way results with conflict markers.
interview.followUp: Which command displays those unmerged index stages? Run git ls-files -u.

keyPoints: A fast-forward merge needs no new commit when the current tip already leads to the named commit.
Use --no-ff when you want Git to create a merge commit instead of fast-forwarding.
A non-fast-forward merge records both merged branch tips as parents of the new commit.
When conflicts stop a true merge, MERGE_HEAD identifies the other commit involved.
The unmerged index keeps the ancestor, current branch, and other branch versions in separate stages.
Conflicted files in the working tree contain the three-way result, including familiar conflict markers.
gotchas: The merge normally stops when the index contains staged changes that differ from HEAD.
Uncommitted working-tree changes can remain only when they do not overlap with files that the merge updates.
Use git merge --abort to return from a difficult conflicted merge.

git add.summary: git add copies the current content of new or changed files into the index (the staging area), which holds what the next commit will contain. A plain git commit records only what has been staged.
git add.explanation: The index sits between your working tree and your commit history. When you run git add, Git stores the file's content as it is at that moment and points the matching index entry at it. Later edits to the file are not staged until you run git add again. Pathspecs choose which files are affected. Naming a directory makes the index match that whole directory, including files added or deleted in it. Options control the details: -u updates only files Git already tracks, -A covers all files, -p lets you pick individual hunks, and -N records an empty placeholder entry.

parameters.name: <pathspec>...
parameters.description: The files to stage. Accepts file globs such as *.c and directory names. Naming a directory stages new, modified and deleted files inside it.

parameters.name: -n, --dry-run
parameters.description: Lists what would be added or ignored without changing the index.

parameters.name: -f, --force
parameters.description: Stages files that would otherwise be ignored. Also stages a submodule update when that submodule is set to ignore=all.

parameters.name: -p, --patch
parameters.description: Lets you choose, hunk by hunk, which changes between the index and the working tree to stage.

parameters.name: -i, --interactive
parameters.description: Opens the interactive menu (status, update, revert, add untracked, patch, diff).

parameters.name: -e, --edit
parameters.description: Opens the diff against the index in your editor and stages the patch you save.

parameters.name: -u, --update
parameters.description: Updates only paths the index already tracks, staging their modifications and deletions but never adding new files.

parameters.name: -A, --all
parameters.description: Makes the index match the working tree by staging additions, modifications and deletions.

parameters.name: --no-all, --ignore-removal
parameters.description: Stages new and modified files but leaves files deleted from the working tree alone.

parameters.name: -N, --intent-to-add
parameters.description: Records that the path will be added later by placing an entry with no content in the index.

parameters.name: --renormalize
parameters.description: Runs the clean filter again on all tracked files, for example to fix line endings. Implies -u.

parameters.name: --resolved
parameters.description: Marks unmerged paths as resolved when no conflict markers remain in them. Cannot be combined with -u or -A.

example.title: Stage selectively, then commit
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Preview what would be staged
git add --dry-run src/

# Stage one file completely
git add README.md

# Pick individual hunks from a file you edited
git add -p src/app.py

# Stage edits and deletions of tracked files only (no new files)
git add -u

# Mark a script as executable in the repository only
git add --chmod=+x scripts/deploy.sh

# Quote the glob so Git also matches files in subdirectories
git add 'docs/*.md'

# Review the staged changes, then commit them
git diff --cached --stat
git commit -m "Update docs and app logic"
example.explanation: The script previews what would be staged, stages files in several different ways, checks the staged result with git diff --cached, and then commits it.

useCases.title: Split work into focused commits
useCases.scenario: One file has a bug fix mixed with unrelated refactoring. Use git add -p to stage only the fix hunks and commit them first.

useCases.title: Finish a merge after resolving conflicts
useCases.scenario: After removing the conflict markers by hand, run git add (or git add --resolved) on those paths to mark them resolved before you commit the merge.

useCases.title: Fix line endings in the repository
useCases.scenario: After changing core.autocrlf or .gitattributes, run git add --renormalize . so every tracked file is stored with the corrected line endings.

useCases.title: Stage a large or generated list of paths
useCases.scenario: Write the paths to a file, or pipe them in with --pathspec-from-file=- and --pathspec-file-nul, so the command line does not get too long.

interview.question: How do git add ., git add -u and git add -A differ?
interview.answer: git add . stages new, modified and deleted files under the current directory, because a directory pathspec makes the index match that directory. -u touches only files already in the index, so it stages edits and deletions but never new files. -A stages additions, edits and deletions, and with no pathspec it applies to the entire working tree.
interview.followUp: What does --no-all do? It stages new and modified files but skips deletions, which is how older Git versions behaved, and it does nothing if you give no pathspec.

interview.question: You run git add on a file, edit it again, and then commit. What gets committed?
interview.answer: The version you staged, not the later edit. git add copies the file's content at the moment you run it, and a plain git commit records only the index. git status will list the file as both staged and modified.
interview.followUp: How do you include the newer edit? Run git add on the file again before committing, or use git commit -a, which updates the index with all changes to tracked files before committing.

interview.question: What does git add -N do, and why use it?
interview.answer: It records only an intent to add the file: an index entry with no content. The file then counts as tracked, so git diff shows its contents as unstaged changes and git commit -a will include it.
interview.followUp: How is that different from git add -p on a brand-new file? -p offers hunks only for differences between the index and the working tree, so add the new file with -N first, and then -p can stage parts of it.

keyPoints: Staging records a snapshot. If you edit a file after adding it, the staged version stays the old one until you run git add on it again.
-u works only on files Git already tracks. It stages their edits and deletions, but untracked files stay untracked.
-A brings the index fully in line with the working tree, covering new, changed and deleted files.
-p lets you stage only some of the changes in a file, hunk by hunk, so one file's edits can go into separate commits.
-N adds a placeholder entry for a new file. This makes the file show up in git diff and lets git commit -a include it.
--chmod=+x marks a file as executable in the repository without touching its permissions on disk. This is handy on file systems that cannot store the executable bit.
--renormalize stages tracked files again through the clean filter. Use it after changing core.autocrlf or the text attribute.
gotchas: Ignored files behave differently depending on how you name them. If you name an ignored file exactly, git add fails with an error. If it only matches a glob or sits inside a directory you added, it is skipped without any message.
Whether you quote a glob matters. If the shell expands it, only matching files in the current directory are staged. If Git expands it, matching files in subdirectories are included too.
--ignore-errors keeps adding the other files when some fail, but the command still exits with an error code, which scripts should check.
When editing patches by hand with -e, it is easy to make a patch that cannot be applied to the index.

git am.summary: git am takes patches that arrive as email, in a mailbox file or a Maildir, and turns each one into a commit on the current branch. It keeps the original author, date and message, so it does the reverse of git format-patch.
git am.explanation: git am splits a mailbox into separate messages. For each message, it pulls the author and date from the headers and uses the Subject line, minus any [PATCH ...] prefix, as the commit title. The body becomes the rest of the commit message, up to the first line that looks like the start of a diff. The diff part is applied with git apply, and the result is committed. If a patch fails, the session stops partway through and saves its state. You then fix the problem and run --continue, or use --skip, --abort, --quit or --retry. Hooks can check each message and the applied tree before the commit is made.

parameters.name: <mbox> | <Maildir>
parameters.description: Mailbox files to read patches from. Directories are treated as Maildirs. If you give none, standard input is used.

parameters.name: -s, --signoff
parameters.description: Adds a Signed-off-by trailer using your own committer identity.

parameters.name: -3, --3way / --no-3way
parameters.description: If a patch does not apply cleanly, falls back to a 3-way merge when the needed blobs exist locally. --no-3way overrides the am.threeWay setting.

parameters.name: -k, --keep
parameters.description: Passes -k to git-mailinfo, which keeps the subject line as it is.

parameters.name: --empty=(drop|keep|stop)
parameters.description: Decides what happens to a message that has no patch: skip it, record an empty commit, or stop (the default).

parameters.name: --whitespace=<action>, -p<n>, -C<n>, --directory, --exclude, --include, --reject
parameters.description: Passed straight to git apply. Valid --whitespace actions are nowarn, warn, fix, error and error-all.

parameters.name: --patch-format=<format>
parameters.description: Skips automatic format detection. Accepts mbox, mboxrd, stgit, stgit-series or hg.

parameters.name: --continue / --skip / --abort / --quit / --retry
parameters.description: Controls a session that stopped on a failed patch: commit your manual fix, drop the patch, roll back, leave without resetting, or try the patch again.

parameters.name: --show-current-patch[=(diff|raw)]
parameters.description: Shows the message the session stopped on, either the whole email (raw, the default) or just the diff.

git am.returns: One new commit on the current branch for each patch that applies. If a patch fails, the session stops partway and waits for --continue, --skip, --abort, --quit or --retry.

example.title: Round-trip a branch through format-patch and am
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Export commits on 'feature' that are not on 'main' as mbox patches
git format-patch main..feature -o /tmp/series

# Apply them on a fresh branch, adding a sign-off and allowing a 3-way fallback
git switch -c integrate main
git am -3 --signoff /tmp/series/*.patch

# If it stops on a conflict:
#   git am --show-current-patch=diff   # inspect the failing patch
#   # ...edit files, then:
#   git add -A && git am --continue
#   # or give up entirely:
#   git am --abort

git log --oneline main..integrate
example.explanation: This exports a branch as email-style patches with format-patch, then replays them onto a new branch with git am, using a 3-way fallback and sign-offs, and shows the commands for handling a conflict.

useCases.title: Mailing-list maintainers
useCases.scenario: A maintainer saves a contributor's emailed patch series to an mbox, creates a topic branch, and runs git am -3 -s to turn it into signed-off commits that keep the contributor as author.

useCases.title: Moving commits between unrelated repositories
useCases.scenario: Pipe git format-patch --stdout from one repo into git am in another. This carries commits over with their messages and authors, even when the two repos share no history.

useCases.title: Editing a patch series by hand
useCases.scenario: Export commits as .patch files, reset the branch, then edit, reorder or delete the files. Running git am *.patch rebuilds the series.

useCases.title: Enforcing message rules on incoming patches
useCases.scenario: Use the applypatch-msg and pre-applypatch hooks to reject or rewrite messages, or to run checks on the tree, before each emailed patch is committed.

interview.question: How is git am different from git apply?
interview.answer: git apply only changes the working tree (and the index, if asked) and never creates a commit. git am reads email messages, takes the author, date, subject and body from each one, applies the diff through git apply, and makes one commit per patch. It also adds a resumable session (--continue/--skip/--abort), hooks and sign-off support.
interview.followUp: Which git am options are just passed on to git apply? Options such as --whitespace, -p<n>, -C<n>, --directory, --exclude, --include, --reject and the ignore-whitespace flags are all passed directly to git apply.

interview.question: git am stops partway through a series because a patch doesn't apply. What can you do?
interview.answer: You can drop that patch with git am --skip. Or you can fix the files by hand, stage the result with git add, and run git am --continue, which commits using the email's author and message. You can also try git am --retry --3way, or end the session with --abort (restores everything) or --quit (leaves HEAD and the index as they are).
interview.followUp: How do you see which patch failed? Run git am --show-current-patch=diff to see only the diff, or use the default raw mode to see the whole email.

interview.question: What does --3way do, and when does it fail to help?
interview.answer: When a patch doesn't apply cleanly, --3way falls back to a 3-way merge. It uses the blob IDs recorded in the patch's index lines to rebuild the base version. This only works if those blobs exist in your repository; otherwise it can't help. You can make it the default with am.threeWay=true.
interview.followUp: How do you turn off a configured 3-way default for one run? Pass --no-3way, which overrides am.threeWay for that run.

keyPoints: Authorship is preserved: the email's From: header becomes the commit author and its Date: header becomes the author date. You can override these with matching lines at the very start of the body.
The Subject: line becomes the commit title, with a leading [PATCH ...] tag removed first. This way, series numbering from format-patch does not end up in the history.
If you give no mailbox arguments, git am reads from stdin. This lets you pipe output straight in, for example git format-patch --stdout A..B | git am.
The commit message ends at the first line that is exactly '---', starts with 'diff -', or starts with 'Index: '. Everything after that point is treated as the patch.
Before applying anything, git am saves the current branch tip as ORIG_HEAD. If you applied a series to the wrong branch, you can reset back to that point.
A message with no diff, such as a cover letter, stops the session by default. Use --empty=drop to skip such messages or --empty=keep to record them as empty commits.

--abort and --quit both end the session but leave the repo differently. --abort puts the branch and files back as they were before git am started, while --quit leaves HEAD and the index exactly as they are.
gotchas: --committer-date-is-author-date can make committer dates go backwards in history, which can confuse tools that walk history. Only use it when the base commit is older than every patch you are applying.

A diff that is not indented inside a commit message (for example, in a Markdown code block) can be taken for the real patch. It may then be applied wrongly or cause the patch to fail. Indent such text to avoid this.
You can't start a new mailbox while an earlier session is still stopped. Finish it, or run git am --abort first.
Running --retry with the same options just fails the same way again. It only helps if you add something new, such as --3way.

git apply.summary: git apply reads a diff (a patch) and applies it to files in the working tree, the index, or both. It does not create a commit. Use git am when you want commits made from mailed or format-patch patches.
git apply.explanation: You give git apply one or more patch files, or - to read from stdin. It finds the target paths, strips leading path components (one by default), and checks that the context lines match. Then it changes the files. With no flags it only edits working-tree files and works even outside a repository. --index patches both the files and the index, while --cached patches only the index. Some options, like --stat, --numstat, --summary and --check, only report on the patch and change nothing, unless you add --apply after them.

parameters.name: <patch>...
parameters.description: The patch files to read. Use - to read from standard input.

parameters.name: --check
parameters.description: Only tests whether the patch would apply and reports errors. Nothing is changed.

parameters.name: --index / --cached
parameters.description: --index patches the index and the working tree. --cached patches only the index.

parameters.name: -3, --3way
parameters.description: Falls back to a 3-way merge using the blob IDs recorded in the patch, and may leave conflict markers.

parameters.name: -R, --reverse
parameters.description: Applies the patch in reverse, which undoes it.

parameters.name: --reject
parameters.description: Applies the hunks that fit and saves the failed ones to *.rej files.

parameters.name: -p<n>
parameters.description: How many leading path components to remove from the paths in the diff. Default is 1.

parameters.name: --directory=<root>
parameters.description: Adds <root> in front of every filename, after any -p stripping.

parameters.name: --whitespace=<action>
parameters.description: What to do with whitespace errors: nowarn, warn (the default), fix, error, or error-all.

parameters.name: --exclude / --include=<path-pattern>
parameters.description: Skip, or limit the patch to, files that match the pattern.

git apply.returns: Changes the working tree and/or the index, but makes no commit. Report-only options such as --stat, --numstat, --summary and --check print information and change nothing. --allow-empty stops it from failing on a patch with no diff.

example.title: Preview, check, apply, and undo a patch
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Make a patch from uncommitted changes, then reset the tree
git diff > fix.patch
git restore .

# See what the patch touches
git apply --stat fix.patch

# Check that it applies cleanly
git apply --check fix.patch

# Apply to the working tree and stage it as well
git apply --index fix.patch
git status --short

# Undo it again
git apply -R --index fix.patch
example.explanation: The script saves local changes as a patch, previews it with --stat, checks it with --check, applies and stages it with --index, then undoes it with -R.

useCases.title: Applying a contributor's diff
useCases.scenario: Someone sends you a plain diff, not a format-patch email. You apply it with git apply, review the result, and commit it under your own message.

useCases.title: Moving a change to a vendored copy
useCases.scenario: A fix written for an upstream repo is applied to a copy kept in a subfolder, using --directory=vendor/lib and, if needed, -p to adjust the paths.

useCases.title: Staging an edited patch
useCases.scenario: You edit a saved hunk by hand and then put it straight into the index with --cached --recount, leaving the working tree untouched.

useCases.title: Checking patches in CI
useCases.scenario: A pipeline runs git apply --check --whitespace=error so that patches that don't apply or have whitespace errors are rejected before merging.

interview.question: What is the difference between git apply and git am?
interview.answer: git apply only changes files and/or the index and never makes a commit. git am reads patches from a mailbox, such as git format-patch output, and creates a commit for each one, keeping the author and message. Use git apply for plain diffs, and git am when you want the history kept.
interview.followUp: Can git am pass options through to git apply? Yes. Options like -p, -C, --directory, --exclude, --include, --reject and the whitespace flags are handed on to git apply.

interview.question: How do --index and --cached change what git apply does?
interview.answer: With neither flag, only working-tree files are patched, and you don't even need a repository. --index patches both the index and the working tree, and needs them to match for the affected paths. --cached updates only the index and leaves the files alone.
interview.followUp: Which option turns on --index without you asking? --3way does, unless you also pass --cached. In that case any conflicts are stored as higher stages in the index.

interview.question: A patch fails because a few hunks don't match. What can you do?
interview.answer: Use --3way to merge using the blob IDs in the patch, which may leave conflict markers for you to resolve. Or use --reject to apply the good hunks and save the failed ones as .rej files. If the patch had only small whitespace changes, --ignore-whitespace or -C<n> can make it apply.
interview.followUp: Can --3way and --reject be used together? No, the docs say they are incompatible. Choose merging with conflict markers or partial application with .rej files.

keyPoints: git apply never records a commit. You stage and commit the result yourself, or use git am to keep the authorship and message.
Run --check first, for example in CI or a script, to see whether a patch will apply without touching any files.
-p<n> sets how many leading directory parts to drop from the diff paths. The default of 1 removes the a/ and b/ prefixes that git diff adds.
With --3way, Git can merge a patch whose context no longer matches exactly, provided you have the original blobs locally. Conflicts can then be settled with --ours, --theirs or --union.
If you run it inside a subdirectory of a repository, changes to files outside that subdirectory are quietly skipped.
When you combine --include and --exclude, each path is tested against them in the order given on the command line, and the first pattern that matches wins.
Whitespace problems such as trailing spaces only produce warnings by default and the patch still applies. Use --whitespace=fix or error to be stricter.
gotchas: By default it is all or nothing: if one hunk fails, no file is changed. Add --reject to apply what fits and get .rej files for the rest.
--index fails if a file's staged copy and working copy differ, even when the patch would apply to each of them separately.
Patches made with --unified=0 have no context lines, so they need --unidiff-zero, and the docs advise against using them.
A patch that touches paths outside the working area is refused unless you pass --unsafe-paths, and that option does nothing when --index or --cached is used.

git archive.summary: git archive packs the files of one commit, tag or tree into a tar or zip archive. It works straight from repository objects and does not need a checkout, so it is the usual way to build source release tarballs.
git archive.explanation: You give it a tree-ish (a branch, tag, commit, tree, or rev:path). Git walks that tree and streams an archive to stdout, or to a file if you pass -o. Built in, it can write tar, zip, tar.gz and tgz. Other formats work by piping tar output through a shell command set in tar.<format>.command. Optional paths cut the archive down to parts of the tree, and --prefix adds a leading directory to every entry. Before writing, Git checks the export-ignore and export-subst attributes. With --remote, the archive is built on the server by git-upload-archive and sent back to you.

parameters.name: --format=<fmt>
parameters.description: Archive format: tar, zip, tar.gz, tgz, or a custom format set up with tar.<format>.command. Defaults to tar unless the output filename suggests something else.

parameters.name: -l, --list
parameters.description: Lists every format you can use.

parameters.name: -v, --verbose
parameters.description: Prints progress to stderr.

parameters.name: --prefix=<prefix>/
parameters.description: Adds <prefix>/ to the start of each path in the archive. You can repeat it; tracked files get the last value given.

parameters.name: -o <file>, --output=<file>
parameters.description: Writes the archive to a file instead of stdout.

parameters.name: --add-file=<file>
parameters.description: Puts an untracked file in the archive, named with the last preceding --prefix plus the file's basename. Can be repeated.

parameters.name: --add-virtual-file=<path>:<content>
parameters.description: Adds a regular file with the given path and inline content. Can be repeated.

parameters.name: --worktree-attributes
parameters.description: Also reads .gitattributes files from the working tree.

parameters.name: --mtime=<time>
parameters.description: Sets the modification time stored on every archive entry.

parameters.name: <extra>
parameters.description: Options for the archiver backend, such as compression level (-0 to -9 for zip, default -6).

parameters.name: --remote=<repo>
parameters.description: Gets the archive from a remote repository instead of building it locally.

parameters.name: --exec=<git-upload-archive>
parameters.description: Used with --remote: the path to git-upload-archive on the remote side.

git archive.returns: Writes the archive bytes to stdout, or to the file given with -o/--output.

example.title: Build a release tarball and a docs zip from a tag
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

TAG=v1.4.0
NAME=myproj-${TAG#v}

# Keep dev-only files out of release archives
printf '.github/ export-ignore\ntests/ export-ignore\n' >> .gitattributes

# Gzipped tarball; format inferred from extension
git archive --prefix="$NAME/" -o "$NAME.tar.gz" "$TAG"

# Only the docs/ subtree, as zip at max compression
git archive --format=zip -9 --prefix=docs/ -o "$NAME-docs.zip" "$TAG:docs/"

# Read back the embedded commit ID
gzip -dc "$NAME.tar.gz" | git get-tar-commit-id

# List available formats
git archive --list
example.explanation: The script builds a prefixed .tar.gz of a tag and a zip of just its docs subtree, then reads back the commit ID stored in the tarball. Note that export-ignore only takes effect once .gitattributes is committed in the tagged tree, or if you pass --worktree-attributes.

useCases.title: Source release tarballs
useCases.scenario: Make myproj-1.2.0.tar.gz from tag v1.2.0, with every file under myproj-1.2.0/, to attach to a release.

useCases.title: Lightweight deploy artifacts
useCases.scenario: Send a clean snapshot of a commit, with no .git directory, to a server or into a Docker build context.

useCases.title: Shipping a subdirectory
useCases.scenario: Package only HEAD:Documentation/ as a zip for publishing docs separately.

useCases.title: Fetching a snapshot from a server
useCases.scenario: Use --remote to pull a tag's tree as a tarball without cloning the whole repository.

interview.question: How is git archive different from cloning a repo and zipping the folder?
interview.answer: git archive reads the tree straight from the object database, so there's no .git directory, no untracked files and no local edits in the output. It applies export-ignore and export-subst, can add a top-level prefix directory, and when given a commit it stamps every entry with the commit time.
interview.followUp: Why are two archives of the same commit usually byte-identical, but archives of the same tree ID aren't? Because a commit or tag gives every entry its commit timestamp, while a bare tree ID has no commit, so the current time is used.

interview.question: How would you keep CI configuration and tests out of release tarballs?
interview.answer: Mark those paths with export-ignore in .gitattributes and commit the change, because attributes come from the tree being archived. For a commit that is already tagged, edit the working-tree .gitattributes and run git archive with --worktree-attributes, or put the rules in $GIT_DIR/info/attributes.
interview.followUp: How can you embed the commit hash in a file inside the archive? Set export-subst on that file, and Git replaces its placeholders (as described in gitattributes) when it writes the file into the archive.

interview.question: What happens when you run git archive --remote=origin master^?
interview.answer: The remote's git-upload-archive will usually refuse it. To protect unreachable objects, it only accepts refs and ref:path forms, not relative expressions or raw SHAs. Use a ref such as a tag or branch name instead.
interview.followUp: How can a server admin relax that rule? Set uploadArchive.allowUnreachable=true on the server, which lets clients use any SHA-1 expression.

keyPoints: If you skip --format but give -o, Git picks the format from the file extension, so -o latest.zip produces a zip. With neither, you get tar.
Entry timestamps depend on what you pass. A commit or tag gives every file the commit time, so the timestamps are the same on every run. A bare tree ID gives the current time instead.
When you archive a commit as tar, Git records the commit ID in a pax header, and git get-tar-commit-id can read it back. In zip files the ID is stored as the file comment.
Mark files with the export-ignore attribute in .gitattributes to keep them out of archives. Typical examples are CI configs and test fixtures.
The export-subst attribute tells Git to fill in placeholders inside a file as it is archived, for example to stamp a version or commit hash into it.
You can add build outputs that aren't committed, such as a generated configure script, with --add-file. Its archive path comes from the last --prefix given before it.
For zip, a single-digit option sets the compression level. Higher numbers take longer but make smaller files.
tar.umask sets the permission bits stored in tar entries. The default 0002 removes the world-write bit.
gotchas: Git does not clean up --prefix. Values containing ../ or a leading slash go into the archive exactly as typed, and some extractors will warn about them or rewrite them.
With --remote, the server may reject some revision expressions, such as a raw SHA or master^. Refs and ref:path usually work.
Attributes are read from the commit being archived, not from your working tree. To fix a missing export-ignore after the fact, edit .gitattributes in the working tree and pass --worktree-attributes.
--add-virtual-file ignores --prefix, so you must write the full path inside the archive yourself.

git bisect.summary: git bisect does a binary search through commit history to find the commit that introduced a bug. More generally, it finds the commit where any testable property of the project changed.
git bisect.explanation: You start a session and mark one commit as bad (it has the bug) and at least one as good (it does not). Git then checks out a commit about halfway between them. You test it and mark it good or bad, and each answer cuts the remaining range roughly in half. When no candidates are left, Git reports the first bad commit and points refs/bisect/bad at it. You can do the testing by hand or hand it to a script with `git bisect run`, which reads the script's exit code. When you finish, `git bisect reset` clears the bisect state and puts you back where you started.
git bisect.syntax:
git bisect start [--term-(bad|new)=<term-new> --term-(good|old)=<term-old>] [--no-checkout] [--first-parent] [--reset-when-found[=<where>]] [<bad> [<good>...]] [--] [<pathspec>...]
git bisect (bad|new|<term-new>) [<rev>]
git bisect (good|old|<term-old>) [<rev>...]
git bisect skip [(<rev>|<range>)...]
git bisect reset [<commit>]
git bisect run [--reset-when-found[=<where>]] <cmd> [<arg>...]

parameters.name: <bad> [<good>...]
parameters.description: Optional arguments to start: one known-bad commit followed by any number of known-good commits. Giving them here saves running separate bad/good commands.

parameters.name: <pathspec>
parameters.description: Limits the search to commits that touch these paths, so fewer steps are needed.

parameters.name: --term-old / --term-new
parameters.description: Your own names for the before and after states, such as fast/slow or broken/fixed.

parameters.name: --no-checkout
parameters.description: Does not check out each candidate. It only moves BISECT_HEAD to the commit being tested. This is assumed in bare repositories.

parameters.name: --first-parent
parameters.description: Follows only the first parent of merge commits, so a merge is reported as the culprit and the commits on the merged branch are ignored.

parameters.name: --reset-when-found[=<where>]
parameters.description: After the culprit is found, report it and clean up the bisect state. The default, original, returns to the commit you started from; found leaves the culprit checked out.

parameters.name: <cmd> [<arg>...]
parameters.description: For bisect run: a script or command whose exit code marks each commit as good, bad, or skipped.

git bisect.returns: Prints a description of the first bad (or new) commit and leaves refs/bisect/bad pointing at it.

example.title: Automated bisect that skips broken builds
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Save as ~/bisect-test.sh (keep it outside the repo) and chmod +x it
set -u
make >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 125   # can't build: skip this commit
./run_regression_test.sh            # exit 0 = good, 1 = bad

# --- Then, in the repository: ---
# git bisect start HEAD v1.2 --      # HEAD is bad, v1.2 is good
# git bisect run ~/bisect-test.sh
# git show refs/bisect/bad           # inspect the culprit
# git bisect reset                   # return to the original HEAD
example.explanation: The script skips commits that won't build by exiting 125 and otherwise reports the test's exit code, so bisect run can find the first bad commit without any manual steps.

useCases.title: Finding a regression after a release
useCases.scenario: A feature worked in the last tagged release and is broken on main. Start bisect with main as bad and the tag as good, then test each commit Git checks out until it names the culprit.

useCases.title: Finding which commit fixed a bug
useCases.scenario: Start with --term-old broken --term-new fixed to find the commit that fixed a problem, for example to decide whether that fix should be backported.

useCases.title: Finding a performance regression in CI
useCases.scenario: Use bisect run with a benchmark script that exits non-zero when timings go over a threshold, and use the terms fast/slow so the output is easy to read.

interview.question: How does git bisect find a bad commit, and how many steps should it take?
interview.answer: It does a binary search over the commits that are reachable from the bad commit but not from any good commit. Each commit you test as good or bad removes about half of the remaining candidates, so the number of steps grows with the logarithm of the range. In the docs' example, about 675 candidate revisions need roughly 10 steps.
interview.followUp: Does this work when history contains merges? Yes. Bisect works on the commit graph, not just a straight line of commits. If you want a broken merge reported as one culprit instead of commits on the merged branch, use --first-parent.

interview.question: How do you automate a bisect, and what does the script's exit code mean?
interview.answer: Run git bisect run <cmd> after setting good and bad bounds. Exit 0 marks the commit good. Exit 1 to 127, except 125, marks it bad. Exit 125 skips the commit, and any other code stops the bisect.
interview.followUp: Why is 125 the skip code instead of 126 or 127? POSIX shells already use 126 and 127 for 'command found but not executable' and 'command not found', so 125 is the highest value that doesn't clash with them.

interview.question: What do you do if you marked a commit as good when it was actually bad?
interview.answer: Save the output of git bisect log to a file and delete the wrong entry. Then run git bisect reset followed by git bisect replay <file>. This rebuilds the session with only the correct marks.
interview.followUp: How do you leave the session but stay on the culprit commit? Run git bisect reset bisect/bad. Alternatively, start with --reset-when-found=found, which leaves the first bad commit checked out once the search ends.

keyPoints: The search ends when there are no candidates left. Git then prints details of the culprit commit.
To automate the search with bisect run, your script should exit 0 for a good commit and with a code from 1 to 127, except 125, for a bad one.
Exit code 125 tells bisect run that a commit can't be tested, for example because it doesn't build. Bisect then skips that commit instead of marking it good or bad.
If you pass paths after -- to bisect start, Git only considers commits that touch those paths, which reduces the number of steps.
If you already know several good commits, list them all after the bad commit when you start. This narrows the search range from the beginning.
If you marked a commit wrongly, save the output of git bisect log to a file, delete the wrong lines, then run reset followed by replay to rebuild the corrected session.
Use --no-checkout when your test doesn't need the files on disk. Git then only updates BISECT_HEAD at each step, which is faster.
Use --first-parent to avoid blaming individual commits on a merged branch that were broken or didn't build, when the merge result itself was fine.
gotchas: If you skip a commit right next to the culprit, bisect may only be able to name a group of possible first-bad commits instead of a single one.
With bisect run, any exit code outside the accepted ranges stops the whole session. A script that calls exit(-1) actually returns 255, which also stops it.
Within one session you must use either good/bad or old/new. You can't mix the two pairs of terms.

git blame.summary: git blame shows, for every line of a file, which commit last changed that line, along with its author and date. Use it to find out where a specific piece of code came from.
git blame.explanation: Git starts from a revision (HEAD by default, or the <rev> you pass) and walks back through history. At each step it compares a commit's version of the file with its parent's version. Lines that are the same in both are passed on to the parent. Lines that differ are credited to that commit. This continues until every line has a commit or reaches a boundary, such as a range limit or the root commit. The default output puts the short commit hash, author, date and line number in front of each line. Options can limit the line range, detect moved or copied code, or skip commits you choose.

parameters.name: <file>
parameters.description: The file to annotate (required).

parameters.name: <rev>
parameters.description: The revision to start annotating from (HEAD if omitted). A range such as v2.6.18.. limits how far back blame looks.

parameters.name: -L <start>,<end> | -L :<funcname>
parameters.description: Annotates only the given lines. Each end can be a line number, a /regex/ or a +/-offset. A function-name regex can be used instead of a range.

parameters.name: -M[<num>] / -C[<num>]
parameters.description: Detect lines moved or copied within the file (-M, default threshold 20 alphanumeric characters) or from other files (-C, default threshold 40). -C can be repeated to search more widely.

parameters.name: --ignore-rev <rev> / --ignore-revs-file <file>
parameters.description: Skip the given commits when assigning blame.

parameters.name: -p, --porcelain / --line-porcelain / --incremental
parameters.description: Machine-readable output formats.

parameters.name: --contents <file>
parameters.description: Annotate the given contents (use - for stdin) instead of the version stored in the repository.

git blame.returns: Writes to stdout one annotation per line of the file. By default each line has the abbreviated commit hash, the author ident and the line number, followed by the line's content. Porcelain and incremental modes print structured headers instead.

example.title: Blame a function while skipping formatting commits
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Commit hashes of bulk reformatting commits to ignore (one per line)
cat > .git-blame-ignore-revs <<'EOF'
# example: prettier reformat
# 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567
EOF

# Make every git blame in this repository use the ignore list
git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs

# Blame only the body of main(); ignore whitespace; detect moved/copied code
git blame -w -C -L ':main' -- src/app.c

# Count how many lines each author is credited with
git blame --line-porcelain -- src/app.c \
  | sed -n 's/^author //p' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
example.explanation: The script adds an ignore-revs file to the repository config, blames a single function with whitespace changes ignored and copy detection on, then counts lines per author from the line-porcelain output.

useCases.title: Finding who to ask about a line
useCases.scenario: While fixing a bug, find the commit and author behind a suspicious line, then read that commit's message to understand why it was written.

useCases.title: Skipping reformatting commits
useCases.scenario: After a project-wide formatter run, add that commit to an ignore file so blame keeps crediting the real authors.

useCases.title: Spotting copy-paste in a new file
useCases.scenario: Run git blame -C -C -f $commit^! -- file to see which lines of a newly added file were copied from existing files.

useCases.title: Seeing when a line was removed
useCases.scenario: Use --reverse <start>..HEAD to find the last commit in which a line still existed.

interview.question: A team ran a formatter across the whole codebase, and now git blame credits that one commit for most lines. How do you fix this?
interview.answer: Pass the commit with --ignore-rev, or list its hash in a file and point blame.ignoreRevsFile or --ignore-revs-file at that file. Blame then treats that commit as if it never happened and credits the earlier commit that changed each line. Adding -w also helps when the changes were whitespace-only.
interview.followUp: How can you see which lines were affected by the ignored commit? Set blame.markIgnoredLines to mark lines that were re-credited with '?', and blame.markUnblamableLines to mark lines that couldn't be credited to any other commit with '*'.

interview.question: What is the difference between -M and -C?
interview.answer: -M finds blocks of lines that were moved or copied within the same file. -C does that too, and also finds lines that came from other files changed in the same commit. Each takes an optional minimum number of alphanumeric characters that must match: 20 by default for -M and 40 for -C.
interview.followUp: What do -C -C and -C -C -C add? Given twice, blame also looks at other files in the commit that created the file. Given three times, it looks at other files in every commit, which is the most thorough but the slowest.

interview.question: How would you use git blame output in a script?
interview.answer: Use --porcelain or --line-porcelain. Each line gets a header with the full 40-character hash, the line number in the original and final file, and fields such as author and summary, and then the line's content after a tab. --line-porcelain repeats the commit details on every line, so the script doesn't need to remember them.
interview.followUp: Why might an interactive viewer use --incremental instead? It prints results while blame is still running, newest commits first, and every entry ends with a filename line, so a viewer can display results gradually.

keyPoints: Renamed files are followed automatically, and this can't be turned off. To follow code that was moved or copied between different files, you have to use -C.
-L can be given more than once, and the ranges may overlap. This lets you annotate several separate parts of a file in one run.
-C looks for lines that came from other files changed in the same commit. Giving it twice also checks the commit that created the file, and three times checks every commit.
Commits you ignore (for example, bulk reformatting commits) don't hide history. Their lines are credited to the commit that changed them before.
--first-parent shows when a line arrived on an integration branch, not when it was first written on a side branch.
--line-porcelain repeats the full commit details on every line. This makes it easy to process with tools like sed or sort, for example to count lines per author.
-w ignores whitespace changes, so commits that only re-indent lines don't take the credit for them.
gotchas: Blame only covers lines that still exist. To find deleted or replaced code, use git diff or git log -S (the 'pickaxe' search).
When you limit the history with a revision range or --since, lines older than the limit are credited to the boundary commit, not to the commit that actually wrote them.
Plain --porcelain prints a commit's details only the first time that commit appears. A parser that expects details on every line will miss them.
--incremental output does not come in line order, so tools reading it must reorder the results themselves.

git branch.summary: git branch manages branches. It can list, create, rename, copy and delete them, and it can set or change the upstream branch each one follows.
git branch.explanation: In Git, a branch is a named ref under refs/heads that points to a commit. With no name argument, git branch lists refs and accepts filters such as --merged, --contains, --sort and --format. Given a name, it creates a new ref at HEAD or at a start point you choose. A start point can be a branch, tag or commit ID, and A...B uses the merge base of A and B. If the start point is a remote-tracking branch, branch.<name>.remote and branch.<name>.merge are written by default, which lets pull and status know the upstream. Other flags rename, copy or delete refs, and renames and copies carry the branch's config and reflog with them.
git branch.syntax:
git branch [--list] [-r|-a] [<pattern>...]
git branch [--track[=(direct|inherit)] | --no-track] [-f] <branch-name> [<start-point>]
git branch (--set-upstream-to=<upstream>|-u <upstream>) [<branch-name>]
git branch (-m|-M) [<old-branch>] <new-branch>
git branch (-c|-C) [<old-branch>] <new-branch>
git branch (-d|-D) [-r] <branch-name>...

parameters.name: <branch-name>
parameters.description: Name of the branch to create or delete. It must pass the checks in git check-ref-format.

parameters.name: <start-point>
parameters.description: The commit the new branch will point to, given as a branch name, commit ID or tag. If left out, HEAD is used.

parameters.name: <old-branch>
parameters.description: An existing branch to rename or copy. If left out, the current branch is used.

parameters.name: <new-branch>
parameters.description: The new name used by a rename or copy. It has the same naming rules as <branch-name>.

parameters.name: <pattern>
parameters.description: Used with --list to show only matching branches. A branch is shown if it matches any of the patterns.

parameters.name: <commit>
parameters.description: The commit used by --merged, --no-merged, --contains and --no-contains. Defaults to HEAD.

parameters.name: <upstream>
parameters.description: The branch to set as upstream with -u or --set-upstream-to.

example.title: Feature-branch lifecycle with git branch
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Create a branch from the remote main, tracking it
git fetch origin
git branch --track feature/login origin/main
git switch feature/login

# Inspect: current branch, verbose list with upstreams
git branch --show-current
git branch -vv

# List only matching branches, newest first
git branch --list 'feature/*' --sort=-committerdate

# Rename the branch and point it at a new upstream
git branch -m feature/login feature/auth-login
git branch -u origin/main feature/auth-login

# After merging into main, clean up
git switch main
git branch --merged main
git branch -d feature/auth-login

useCases.title: Start work from a release tag
useCases.scenario: Create a branch at a tag such as v2.6.14 to fix something in that release without touching your current branch.

useCases.title: Prune merged topic branches
useCases.scenario: After a release, run git branch --merged main to list local branches that are already merged into main, then remove them with -d.

useCases.title: Find branches affected by a bad commit
useCases.scenario: Before rebasing or amending a commit, run git branch --contains <sha> to find every branch that includes it and will need attention.

useCases.title: Fix tracking after a remote rename
useCases.scenario: Use git branch -u <remote>/<branch> to point an existing local branch at a new upstream so pull and status work again.

interview.question: If you create a local branch from origin/main, how does Git know where git pull should pull from?
interview.answer: When the start point is a remote-tracking branch, git branch records branch.<name>.remote and branch.<name>.merge in the config. This happens because branch.autoSetupMerge defaults to true. You can change this per command with --track or --no-track, or later with --set-upstream-to.
interview.followUp: What is the difference between --track=direct and --track=inherit? With direct, the start-point branch itself becomes the upstream. With inherit, the new branch copies the start point's own upstream configuration.

interview.question: How do --merged and --contains differ?
interview.answer: --merged <commit> lists branches whose tips can be reached from that commit, meaning their work is already included in it. --contains <commit> lists branches whose tips descend from that commit, meaning the branch includes it. Both default to HEAD when no commit is given, and both turn on list mode.
interview.followUp: How are several --merged and --no-merged filters combined? A ref is shown only if it can be reached from at least one --merged commit and from none of the --no-merged commits.

interview.question: Does git branch -d -r origin/foo delete foo on the server?
interview.answer: No. It only deletes your local remote-tracking ref. The manual says this is only worth doing if the branch no longer exists on the remote, or if fetch has been set up not to fetch it.
interview.followUp: How do you clean up all stale remote-tracking branches at once? Use the prune subcommand of git remote, as the git-branch manual suggests.

keyPoints: With no arguments, git branch lists local branches and marks the one you are on. Add -r to list only remote-tracking branches, or -a to list local and remote-tracking branches together.
-d deletes a branch only if its work is already in its upstream, or in HEAD when it has no upstream. -D (--delete --force) deletes it whether or not it has been merged.
-m renames a branch and -c copies one. Both bring the branch's configuration and reflog along. Use the uppercase forms -M or -C to overwrite a branch that already has the new name.
Upstream tracking set with --track or -u is what lets git status and git branch -v show how far ahead or behind a branch is, and it gives a plain git pull its default source.
--merged lists branches whose tips can be reached from the given commit, so it is the usual way to find branches that are safe to clean up.

You can pass --sort more than once, and the last key you give is the primary one. Keys use git for-each-ref field names, for example --sort=-committerdate to show the most recently changed branches first.
-vv adds each branch's upstream name and linked worktree path to the verbose listing. --show-current prints only the current branch name, which is handy in scripts.
gotchas: If you run git branch 'feat-*' without --list, Git can treat the glob as the name of a new branch to create instead of a filter.
Creating a branch does not move you onto it, so your next commit still goes to the old branch. Use git switch, or git switch -c to create and switch in one step.
git branch -f cannot reset a branch that is checked out in another linked worktree, even though -f is meant to force the change.
The old --set-upstream option no longer works. Use --track when creating a branch, or -u / --set-upstream-to for an existing one.

git bundle.summary: git bundle packs Git objects and refs into a single file. You can move that file by USB, email or any other channel and clone or fetch from it later, with no network connection between the two repositories.
git bundle.explanation: `git bundle create` takes rev-list style arguments, such as branch names, `--all` or ranges like `old..new`. It writes a pack file with a header that lists the refs in the bundle. If you give exclusions such as `^old` or `old..new`, those commits become prerequisites, and the receiving repository must already have them. On the receiving side the bundle works like a read-only remote: you can clone from it, fetch from it, or list its refs. `verify` checks that the file is valid and that the prerequisites are present, `list-heads` prints the refs, and `unbundle` stores the objects through `index-pack`.
git bundle.syntax:
git bundle create [-q | --quiet | --progress] [--version=<version>] <file> <git-rev-list-args>
git bundle verify [-q | --quiet] <file>
git bundle list-heads <file> [<refname>…]
git bundle unbundle [--progress] <file> [<refname>…]

parameters.name: <file>
parameters.description: The bundle file to write or read. Use - to write to stdout (create) or read from stdin (verify, list-heads, unbundle).

parameters.name: <git-rev-list-args>
parameters.description: Arguments that git rev-parse and git rev-list accept, including at least one named ref. They choose which refs and objects go into the bundle, for example master, --all or master~10..master.

parameters.name: [<refname>…]
parameters.description: Limits which refs list-heads and unbundle report. This is mainly used by git fetch.

parameters.name: --progress
parameters.description: Shows progress on stderr even when stderr is not a terminal.

parameters.name: --version=<version>
parameters.description: Sets the bundle format version. Version 2 works only with SHA-1 repositories. Version 3 supports capabilities. The default is the oldest format that works with the repository's hash algorithm.

parameters.name: -q, --quiet
parameters.description: Turns off progress reporting on stderr.

git bundle.returns: create writes a bundle file. verify exits with 0 if the bundle is valid and can be applied, and prints any missing prerequisite commits. list-heads and unbundle print the refs defined in the bundle.

example.title: Full bundle, then an incremental update via a tag marker
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
