cd "$(mktemp -d)"

# Source repository
git init -q -b main src && cd src
git commit -q --allow-empty -m "first"

# Full, self-contained bundle + remember what was sent
git bundle create ../full.bundle main
git tag -f lastSent main
cd ..

# Offline side: clone straight from the file
git bundle verify full.bundle
git clone -q -b main full.bundle dst

# More work on the source, then an incremental bundle
cd src
git commit -q --allow-empty -m "second"
git bundle create ../full.bundle lastSent..main
git tag -f lastSent main
cd ..

# Receiver checks prerequisites, then pulls from the replaced file
cd dst
git bundle verify ../full.bundle
git bundle list-heads ../full.bundle
git pull -q
git log --oneline
example.explanation: The script sends a self-contained bundle first, then sends only the new commits in a replacement bundle, which the clone picks up with git pull because its origin remote points at the bundle file.

useCases.title: Air-gapped transfer
useCases.scenario: Move the history of a branch from a machine on a restricted network to an isolated one by carrying bundle files on removable media, and update with incremental ranges.

useCases.title: Consistent repository backup
useCases.scenario: Run `git bundle create backup.bundle --all` from a scheduled job, then restore later with `git clone backup.bundle <dir>`.

useCases.title: Sharing commits without a shared server
useCases.scenario: Email a colleague a bundle of a few local commits (for example `main ^origin/main`), which they can verify and fetch into a separate branch.

useCases.title: Streaming through pipes
useCases.scenario: Use `-` as the file name to write a bundle to stdout or read one from stdin, so you can chain it with compression, encryption or ssh.

interview.question: What is a Git bundle, and how does someone use one?
interview.answer: A bundle is a pack file with a header that lists the refs it contains, created with `git bundle create <file> <rev-list-args>`. The receiver treats the file as a remote: they can `git clone` it, `git fetch` from it, or run `git ls-remote` against it. This lets you move history between repositories with no network connection or server.
interview.followUp: Can you push into a bundle? No. Bundles support only reading, so to send newer history you create a new bundle file and replace the old one.

interview.question: How do you create an incremental bundle, and what risk does it bring?
interview.answer: Exclude commits the receiver already has, either with a range like `lastSent..main` or with options like `^old`, `--since` or `-10`. Those excluded commits become prerequisites that must already be in the receiving repository. To check for them, the receiver runs `git bundle verify`, which lists any missing commits and exits with a nonzero code if the bundle cannot be applied.
interview.followUp: How can you keep track of the cut-off point between bundles? Move a tag (for example `git tag -f lastR2bundle master`) after each bundle and use it as the left side of the next range.

interview.question: Why does `git bundle create x.bundle $(git rev-parse HEAD)` fail?
interview.answer: The bundle has to record refs. A raw commit ID does not resolve to a ref name, so Git refuses with 'Refusing to create empty bundle'. Give a branch or tag name, or use `--all`. The same error happens if the right side of a range is not a ref.
interview.followUp: Which arguments give a bundle the same refs a normal clone would get? Use `--branches --tags` as the rev-list arguments.

keyPoints: After you have the bundle file, the receiving repository treats it like any other read-only remote. You can map refs while fetching, for example `git fetch mybundle master:localRef`, or run `git ls-remote` on it.
A bare commit ID is not enough. The arguments must name at least one ref, or you can use `--all` to include every ref.
Run `verify` before applying a bundle that has prerequisites. It checks the file format and confirms that the commits the bundle depends on are already present in the receiving repository.
The exit status tells you whether the bundle is valid, so `git bundle verify` works well as a check in scripts or CI before an import.
Incremental bundles built with exclusions are stored as thin packs, which makes them smaller than full bundles. You cannot choose a thick pack in this case, and you don't need to.
The v2 format works only with SHA-1. Repositories that use another hash algorithm need v3, which supports capabilities such as an object filter.
You don't need to know exactly which objects the receiver is missing. Including too much is safe, because objects the destination already has are skipped when the bundle is unpacked.
You rarely need `git bundle unbundle` yourself. Use `git fetch` or `git clone`, which call it for you.
gotchas: A bundle is read-only. You can fetch and clone from it, but you cannot push into it. To send updates, create a new bundle.
A backup made with `--all` contains only refs and the commits reachable from them. Local configuration, hooks, stashes, the index and uncommitted work are not included.
If you pass a raw SHA, or a range whose right side is not a ref (such as master~10..master~5), the command fails with 'Refusing to create empty bundle'.
Don't back up a live repository with `cp -r`. Git might write to it during the copy and leave a corrupted copy. A bundle is the safer option.

git checkout.summary: git checkout either moves you to another branch or commit, or overwrites chosen files with the version stored in the index or in a given commit. It is the older all-in-one command whose two jobs are now also covered separately by git switch and git restore.
git checkout.explanation: Git looks at the arguments to decide which job to do. Given a branch name and no paths, it points HEAD at that branch and updates the index and working tree to match. Uncommitted edits come along unless the switch would overwrite them. Given a commit that is not a branch, HEAD points straight at that commit, which is called a detached HEAD. Given pathspecs, HEAD stays where it is. Git copies those files from the index, or from a tree-ish if you name one. With a tree-ish, the restored files are also staged. If an argument could be either a ref or a file, Git treats it as a ref unless you put -- in front of the paths.
git checkout.syntax:
git checkout [-q] [-f] [-m] [[-b|-B|--orphan] <new-branch>] [<start-point>]
git checkout [-q] [-f] [-m] [--detach] <commit>
git checkout <tree-ish> [--] <pathspec>...
git checkout [-f|--ours|--theirs|-m|--conflict=<style>] [--] <pathspec>...
git checkout (-p|--patch) [<tree-ish>] [--] [<pathspec>...]

parameters.name: <branch>
parameters.description: The branch to switch to. If the name is not a local branch but is a valid commit, HEAD becomes detached. @{-N} and - (the previous checkout) are accepted.

parameters.name: <new-branch>
parameters.description: Name of the branch created by -b, -B or --orphan.

parameters.name: <start-point>
parameters.description: The commit a new branch starts from. Defaults to HEAD. A...B means their merge base.

parameters.name: <tree-ish>
parameters.description: Where file contents are taken from when paths are given. If omitted, the index is used.

parameters.name: <pathspec>...
parameters.description: Limits the operation to these files or directories.

parameters.name: -b / -B
parameters.description: Create a branch and switch to it. -B resets the branch if it already exists.

parameters.name: --detach
parameters.description: Check out a commit with HEAD detached, even when you give a branch name.

parameters.name: -f / --force
parameters.description: Throw away local changes when switching. When restoring paths, skip unmerged entries instead of failing.

parameters.name: -m / --merge
parameters.description: Carry conflicting local changes across the switch by stashing and reapplying them. When restoring paths, recreate the conflicted merge result.

parameters.name: --ours / --theirs
parameters.description: For unmerged paths, take stage #2 (ours) or stage #3 (theirs) from the index.

parameters.name: -p / --patch
parameters.description: Choose hunks interactively and revert them in the working tree.

parameters.name: --orphan
parameters.description: Create an unborn branch whose first commit will have no parent.

example.title: Branching, restoring files and leaving a detached HEAD
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e

# Create a feature branch from main and switch to it
git checkout -b feature/login main

# Throw away unstaged edits to one file (restore it from the index)
git checkout -- src/app.js

# Take a file from two commits back on main (it is staged too)
git checkout main~2 -- Makefile

# Look at an old release without moving any branch
git checkout --detach v2.0

# Keep experimental work made there by putting it on a new branch
git checkout -b spike/v2-fix

# Go back to the branch you were on before
git checkout feature/login
example.explanation: The script runs through the common checkout jobs: creating a branch, restoring files from the index or from a commit, detaching HEAD, saving work made while detached, and switching back with a branch name.

useCases.title: Starting a topic branch
useCases.scenario: Create a branch from main or a remote branch with 'git checkout -b feat origin/main' and start working on it right away.

useCases.title: Undoing a bad edit to one file
useCases.scenario: Restore a file from the index, or pull the version from an earlier commit after a broken change.

useCases.title: Inspecting an old release
useCases.scenario: Check out a tag with HEAD detached to reproduce a bug, then make a branch only if you need to keep fixes.

useCases.title: Resolving merge conflicts per file
useCases.scenario: Use --ours or --theirs on conflicted paths to keep one side in full, or -m to bring the conflict markers back.

interview.question: What is a detached HEAD, and how do you end up in one with git checkout?
interview.answer: Normally HEAD points to a branch name. With a detached HEAD it points straight at a commit. This happens when you check out a tag, a commit hash or an expression like master^^, or when you use --detach. New commits made in this state are referenced only by HEAD.
interview.followUp: You already switched away and the detached commits seem gone. How do you get them back? Find their IDs with git reflog (or git log -g), then create a branch or tag on them before garbage collection removes them.

interview.question: What is the difference between 'git checkout file.txt' and 'git checkout HEAD file.txt'?
interview.answer: Without a tree-ish, the file is copied from the index into the working tree, so only unstaged edits are thrown away. With HEAD (or any commit), the file is replaced with the committed version in both the index and the working tree, which also drops staged changes.
interview.followUp: How do you get the same result with the newer commands? 'git restore file.txt' restores from the index, and 'git restore --source=HEAD --staged --worktree file.txt' matches the HEAD form.

interview.question: Your edits block a branch switch with 'You have local changes; not switching branches'. What are your options with checkout?
interview.answer: Use 'git checkout -m <branch>' to stash the conflicting edits, switch, and reapply them. Use -f to switch and throw the edits away. You can also commit or stash the edits yourself first.
interview.followUp: What happens if reapplying with -m causes conflicts? The stash entry is kept. Resolve the conflicts and run git stash drop, or run git reset --hard and apply the changes later with git stash pop.

keyPoints: -B works like -b, but if the branch already exists it moves that branch to the start point instead of stopping with an error.
--detach, or naming a commit that is not a branch, gives you a commit to look at or experiment with without moving any branch.
Use @{-N} for the Nth branch or commit you checked out before. A plain - means the previous one, so 'git checkout -' switches back.

If the branch name only exists as a remote-tracking branch on exactly one remote, Git creates a local branch that tracks it. --no-guess turns this off, and checkout.defaultRemote decides which remote wins when several match.
Git normally refuses to switch if your edits would be overwritten. With -m, it stashes the conflicting edits, switches, and then reapplies them.
When you name a commit and paths, the files are staged as well as written to the working tree, not just written to disk.
--orphan starts a branch with a separate history. Its first commit has no parent, which helps when publishing a tree without its old history.
-p shows the differences hunk by hunk so you can pick which edits to throw away, using the same interface as git add -p.
gotchas: Commits made on a detached HEAD are lost once you switch away, unless a branch or tag points to them. If that happens, find them with git reflog.
If a file has the same name as a branch, Git treats the argument as the branch. Put -- before file names so they are read as paths.
During a rebase, --ours and --theirs seem reversed: --ours is the branch you are rebasing onto, and --theirs is your own work.
-f does not keep your work safe. It throws away local edits and any untracked files that are in the way.

git cherry-pick.summary: git cherry-pick takes the changes made by one or more existing commits and replays them on your current branch, making a new commit for each one. It is the usual way to copy specific fixes between branches without merging the whole branch.
git cherry-pick.explanation: For each commit you name, Git works out what changed between that commit and its parent. It then applies that change on top of HEAD using the merge machinery and records the result as a new commit. The new commit has a different ID, but by default it keeps the original message and author. If a change does not apply cleanly, HEAD stays at the last commit that succeeded. Git sets CHERRY_PICK_HEAD to the commit causing trouble, stages the paths that applied cleanly and puts conflict markers in the paths that clashed. You then resolve the conflicts and use the sequencer subcommands to continue.

parameters.name: <commit>…
parameters.description: The commits to apply. Any revision syntax works. Ranges are walked, but listing several commits does not trigger a walk.

parameters.name: -e, --edit
parameters.description: Lets you edit the commit message before the commit is made.

parameters.name: -x
parameters.description: Adds a '(cherry picked from commit …)' line to the message so you can trace where the change came from.

parameters.name: -m, --mainline <parent-number>
parameters.description: For a merge commit, picks which parent (counting from 1) the change is measured against.

parameters.name: -n, --no-commit
parameters.description: Applies the changes to the index and working tree without making a commit.

parameters.name: -s, --signoff
parameters.description: Adds a Signed-off-by trailer to the commit message.

parameters.name: -S[<keyid>], --gpg-sign[=<keyid>], --no-gpg-sign
parameters.description: GPG-signs the new commits, or turns signing off.

parameters.name: --ff
parameters.description: Fast-forwards instead of making a new commit when HEAD is already the parent of the picked commit.

parameters.name: --allow-empty / --allow-empty-message
parameters.description: Keeps commits that were empty to begin with, or commits whose message is empty.

parameters.name: --empty=(drop|keep|stop)
parameters.description: Decides what happens to commits that become redundant because their changes are already in history. The default is stop.

parameters.name: --strategy=<strategy>, -X<option>
parameters.description: Chooses the merge strategy, or passes an option to that strategy.

parameters.name: --continue | --skip | --abort | --quit
parameters.description: Controls a cherry-pick that is in progress. --continue resumes it, --skip drops the current commit, --abort returns to where you started and --quit clears the sequencer state.

git cherry-pick.returns: One new commit per picked commit on the current branch. With -n, no commit is made and the changes are left staged.

example.title: Backport a fix to a maintenance branch
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Switch to the release branch that needs the fix
git switch maint-1.4

# Replay the fix from main, recording where it came from
if ! git cherry-pick -x a1b2c3d; then
  echo "Conflict: resolve the files, git add them, then run:"
  echo "  git cherry-pick --continue   # or --skip / --abort"
  exit 1
fi

# Squash two commits into the working tree for review instead of committing
# git cherry-pick -n main~3 main~1 && git commit -m "Backport fixes"

git log --oneline -1
example.explanation: The script copies one commit from main onto a release branch with -x so it can be traced, and tells the user what to do if there is a conflict.

useCases.title: Hotfix backport
useCases.scenario: A bug fixed on main also needs to go into an older release branch, but the rest of main must not ship there.

useCases.title: Rescuing a commit from an abandoned branch
useCases.scenario: A useful commit sits on a feature branch that will never be merged. You copy just that commit onto your current branch.

useCases.title: Combining scattered changes
useCases.scenario: You pipe rev-list output that touches one file into cherry-pick -n --stdin to stage all of those edits, then review them and commit them together.

useCases.title: Moving a commit made on the wrong branch
useCases.scenario: You committed on main by mistake. You pick the commit onto the correct topic branch, then remove it from main.

interview.question: How is cherry-picking different from merging a branch?
interview.answer: A merge works on whole branches and brings in everything from the other side, while recording that the histories joined. A cherry-pick works on single commits: it copies the diff of each chosen commit onto HEAD as a brand-new commit with a new ID, and it does not record any ancestry link. The gitworkflows guide recommends merges in general and keeps cherry-picks for cases like moving fixes downward to a maintenance branch.
interview.followUp: Why can picking the same fix to many branches cause trouble later? Each copy is a separate commit with no shared ancestry, so later merges can conflict or duplicate the change. Use -x, or git cherry, to find commits that are equivalent.

interview.question: What happens when you cherry-pick a merge commit, and how do you make it work?
interview.answer: By default it fails, because a merge has several parents and Git cannot tell which side the change should be measured against. Pass -m with a parent number, counting from 1. Git then replays the difference between that parent and the merge commit. Usually you pass -m 1, which brings in everything the merged branch added.
interview.followUp: What does -m 2 give you instead? The diff is measured against the second parent, so you get what the mainline brought in relative to the merged branch. That is rarely what you want.

interview.question: A multi-commit cherry-pick stops with conflicts. What are your options?
interview.answer: HEAD stays at the last commit that succeeded, CHERRY_PICK_HEAD points to the commit that failed, and the conflicting files contain markers. You can fix the files, stage them and run --continue. You can run --skip to drop this commit and move on. You can run --abort to go back to the state before the sequence started, or --quit to forget the sequencer state but keep what has already been done.
interview.followUp: How does --quit differ from --abort? --abort rewinds to where you started. --quit only clears .git/sequencer, so the commits that were already picked stay on the branch.

keyPoints: You can pass a range, or a negated ref, to replay every commit that one branch has and HEAD lacks, with one new commit for each.
A merge commit has no single diff, so you have to tell cherry-pick which parent to treat as the mainline. You do that with -m.
-n stages the combined effect of several commits without committing, so you can fold them into a single commit of your own.
-x records where the commit came from. It is worth using when you backport between branches that other people can see.
--ff avoids creating a duplicate commit when HEAD already sits on the picked commit's parent.
After you fix conflicts and stage the files, --continue resumes the rest of the multi-commit sequence.
--empty controls what happens to commits whose changes are already in your branch: drop them, keep them, or stop (the default).
You can pass merge strategy options with -X, for example -Xpatience, to cut down on bad context matches when the code has drifted.
gotchas: A normal cherry-pick refuses to start if you have uncommitted changes to tracked files.
With -n, a later git commit lists you as the author, not the original author.
--allow-empty only keeps commits that were empty to begin with. A commit that becomes empty because of an earlier pick still fails unless you use --empty=keep.
The -x provenance line is not added when the pick had conflicts.

git clean.summary: git clean deletes untracked files from your working tree. It can also delete untracked directories and files that Git ignores, so you can get back to a pristine checkout.
git clean.explanation: Starting from the current directory, git clean works through the working tree and finds paths that are not tracked. By default it only picks unknown files that are not ignored, and it does not go into untracked directories. Flags change what it targets: -d includes untracked directories, -x includes ignored files, -X targets only ignored files, and pathspecs limit the paths it touches. Because deletions can't be undone, it refuses to run without -f unless clean.requireForce is false. You can also use -n to preview or -i to choose items interactively.

parameters.name: -d
parameters.description: Go into untracked directories and remove them too when no pathspec is given.

parameters.name: -f, --force
parameters.description: Required to delete anything unless clean.requireForce is false. Give it twice to also remove untracked nested Git repositories.

parameters.name: -i, --interactive
parameters.description: List the candidates and let you choose what to delete in an interactive menu.

parameters.name: -n, --dry-run
parameters.description: Only report what would be removed, without deleting anything.

parameters.name: -q, --quiet
parameters.description: Print errors only, not the files that were removed.

parameters.name: -e <pattern>, --exclude=<pattern>
parameters.description: Add an exclude pattern on top of the standard ignore rules, so matching files are kept.

parameters.name: -x
parameters.description: Ignore the standard ignore rules so that ignored files are removed as well. Patterns given with -e still apply.

parameters.name: -X
parameters.description: Remove only the files that Git ignores.

parameters.name: <pathspec>…
parameters.description: Restrict the cleanup to paths that match these patterns.

example.title: Preview, then reset the working tree to a pristine state
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# 1. See what would be deleted (untracked dirs + ignored files), keeping .env
git clean -n -d -x -e .env

# 2. Discard changes to tracked files
git restore --staged --worktree .

# 3. Actually delete untracked and ignored files/dirs, still keeping .env
git clean -f -d -x -e .env

# Alternative: wipe only ignored build output, keep hand-made files
# git clean -f -d -X
example.explanation: The script previews the cleanup with -n, resets tracked files with git restore, then deletes untracked and ignored files and directories while -e keeps .env.

useCases.title: Clean build verification
useCases.scenario: Before a release build, combine git restore with git clean -fdx so the build starts from exactly what is committed, with no leftover artifacts.

useCases.title: Clearing merge leftovers
useCases.scenario: After a messy merge or rebase, remove stray .orig files and scratch files with git clean -i, picking only the ones you no longer need.

useCases.title: Rebuild from scratch, keep notes
useCases.scenario: Run git clean -fX to delete ignored outputs such as compiled objects while keeping untracked notes or drafts you haven't committed yet.

interview.question: Why does running plain `git clean` often do nothing except print an error?
interview.answer: The clean.requireForce setting defaults to true, so git clean refuses to delete files unless you pass -f. This guards against accidental data loss, because the files it removes are untracked and Git cannot recover them. The -n and -i modes don't need -f, since one deletes nothing and the other asks before deleting.
interview.followUp: Does `git clean -f` remove an untracked directory that contains a cloned repo? No. Untracked nested repositories, meaning directories with a .git subdirectory, are only removed if you give -f twice.

interview.question: What is the difference between -x and -X?
interview.answer: -x stops applying the standard ignore rules, so it removes both ignored files and ordinary untracked files. -X removes only files Git ignores and keeps untracked files you created yourself. Use -x when you want everything gone, and -X when you only want to rebuild artifacts.
interview.followUp: Can you protect a file while using -x? Yes. Patterns passed with -e still apply when -x is used, so `git clean -fdx -e .env` keeps .env.

interview.question: How does -d interact with a pathspec?
interview.answer: Without a pathspec, git clean skips untracked directories unless you pass -d. Once you give a pathspec, -d makes no difference: every untracked file that matches is removed, except for nested Git repositories.
interview.followUp: Where does git clean start when you run it from a subdirectory? It starts in the current directory and works downward, so files above or beside it are left alone.

keyPoints: The cleanup starts at your current directory and works down from there, not from the repository root, so running it in a subfolder only affects that subtree.
Without a pathspec, untracked directories are left alone on purpose. You have to add -d to remove them as well.
-X is the opposite of the default: it removes only ignored files, such as build output, and keeps untracked files you created by hand.
-e adds your own patterns to protect files from deletion, and those patterns still apply when -x turns off the standard ignore rules.
The clean.requireForce setting is true by default, which is why a plain `git clean` with no flags refuses to delete anything.
Interactive mode doesn't need -f because it asks for confirmation itself. Its menu lets you filter by pattern, select items by number or range, or confirm each item one at a time.
Use -q in scripts to hide the list of removed files so that only errors are printed.
gotchas: Once you give a pathspec, every matching untracked file goes, including files inside untracked directories, whether or not you passed -d.
Even with -f, untracked directories that contain their own .git (for example, nested clones) are kept. You need -ff to delete them, and that also deletes their history.
-x also deletes ignored local files such as .env files or editor settings, not just build artifacts. Preview with -n first, or protect those files with -e.

git clone.summary: git clone copies an existing repository into a new directory. It sets up remote-tracking branches for every branch in the source and checks out a starting branch based on the source's active branch.
git clone.explanation: Clone sets up a new repository, records the source as a remote (called origin by default) and downloads its objects and refs. Each remote branch head gets a ref under refs/remotes/origin. Clone also writes remote.origin.url and remote.origin.fetch into the config, which is why a later plain git fetch or git pull with no arguments knows where to go. Options change how much gets copied: history depth, single branch, object filters, bare or mirror layout and submodules. Other options control how objects are stored, such as hardlinks, alternates or a separate git dir.

parameters.name: <repository>
parameters.description: The repository to copy, which may be remote. Accepts ssh, git, http(s), scp-like or local path/file:// forms, plus bundle files.

parameters.name: <directory>
parameters.description: Target directory to create. If you leave it out, Git derives the name from the source.

parameters.name: -b, --branch=<name>
parameters.description: Branch (or tag) for the new HEAD to point at, instead of the remote's HEAD.

parameters.name: --depth=<depth>
parameters.description: Makes a shallow clone that keeps only this many recent commits.

parameters.name: --single-branch / --no-single-branch
parameters.description: Fetches only the history leading to one branch tip.

parameters.name: --filter=<filter-spec>
parameters.description: Makes a partial clone, e.g. blob:none or blob:limit=<size>.

parameters.name: --bare
parameters.description: Makes the target directory the repository itself, with no working tree.

parameters.name: --mirror
parameters.description: A bare clone that copies every ref and is set up to stay in sync with the source.

parameters.name: -o, --origin=<name>
parameters.description: Name to use for the remote instead of origin.

parameters.name: --recurse-submodules[=<pathspec>]
parameters.description: Initializes and clones submodules once the clone finishes.

parameters.name: -c, --config=<key>=<value>
parameters.description: Writes a config variable into the new repository before the fetch.

example.title: Fast, lightweight clones for CI and day-to-day work
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Standard clone into a custom directory name
git clone https://github.com/git/git.git my-git

# CI: newest commit of one branch only, with submodules also shallow
git clone --depth 1 --branch main --recurse-submodules --shallow-submodules \
  https://github.com/git/git.git ci-build

# Blobless partial clone: full history, file contents fetched on demand
git clone --filter=blob:none https://github.com/git/git.git git-blobless

# Bare mirror for a backup or a server copy
git clone --mirror https://github.com/git/git.git git-backup.git

# Later, refresh the mirror
git -C git-backup.git remote update
example.explanation: Shows a regular clone, a shallow CI clone with submodules, a blobless partial clone, and a mirror that you keep up to date with git remote update.

useCases.title: Starting work on a project
useCases.scenario: A new team member clones the team repo over SSH. They can then branch, commit and push right away, because origin is already set up.

useCases.title: Fast CI checkouts
useCases.scenario: A build pipeline uses --depth 1 --single-branch, so it downloads only the commit it is building and not years of history.

useCases.title: Backup or migration mirror
useCases.scenario: An admin runs clone --mirror to copy every ref, notes included, into a bare repository before moving to a new hosting provider.

useCases.title: Working in a huge monorepo
useCases.scenario: A developer combines --filter=blob:none with --sparse, so the first checkout has only top-level files. They then add the directories they need with git sparse-checkout.

interview.question: What is the difference between git clone --bare and git clone --mirror?
interview.answer: Both make a repository with no working tree. --bare copies the remote's branch heads straight into local branches and creates no remote-tracking branches or remote config. --mirror goes further: it copies every ref, including remote-tracking branches and notes. It also sets up a refspec so that git remote update overwrites all of them to match the source.
interview.followUp: Which one would you use for a backup that has to stay in sync? --mirror, because a plain git remote update then copies every ref from the source, deletions included. A bare clone has no fetch refspec set up to do that.

interview.question: How do you clone a repository that has submodules and get the submodule contents too?
interview.answer: Pass --recurse-submodules, with an optional pathspec. After the main clone finishes, it does the same as running git submodule update --init --recursive. It also sets submodule.active to that pathspec, or to "." (all submodules) if you didn't give one. --jobs sets how many submodules download at once.
interview.followUp: Why might the submodules still be empty after a clone with --recurse-submodules? Because the option is ignored when there is no working tree, i.e. with --no-checkout, --bare or --mirror.

interview.question: How is cloning a local path different from cloning a file:// URL?
interview.answer: With a plain path, Git uses --local by default: it skips the normal transport, copies HEAD, objects and refs directly, and hardlinks object files when it can. A file:// URL goes through the regular Git transport instead. You can force that for a path with --no-local, and you must do so if another user owns the source repository.
interview.followUp: When would you use --no-hardlinks? When the clone is a backup. Hardlinked object files share storage with the source, so damage to the source's disk would hit both copies.

keyPoints: If you don't give a target directory, Git takes the name from the source path. For example, /path/to/repo.git becomes repo.
--depth makes a shallow clone that keeps only the last N commits. It also turns on --single-branch unless you pass --no-single-branch.
With --single-branch, later fetches keep updating only the one branch you cloned. Other remote branches don't show up unless you change the fetch refspec.
--filter makes a partial clone. For example, blob:none skips file contents until Git actually needs them, which keeps the first download small.
--branch also accepts a tag name. In that case the new repository starts with a detached HEAD on that tag's commit.
--revision fetches only the history behind one ref or commit hash and detaches HEAD there. It creates no branches, and you can't combine it with --branch or --mirror.
--no-tags is permanent: it saves a tagOpt setting so later fetches and pulls skip tags too. Pair it with --single-branch for the smallest possible clone.
gotchas: Cloning into a directory that already exists only works if that directory is empty.
--shared borrows objects from the source repository. If the source later deletes branches and garbage collection prunes those objects, the clone can become corrupt.
git:// URLs have no authentication, so be careful using them on untrusted networks.
Some settings passed with -c only take effect after the first fetch, for example remote.<name>.mirror and tagOpt. Use --mirror and --no-tags for those instead.

git commit.summary: git commit records a new snapshot in the repository from the current contents of the index, together with a log message. The new commit becomes a child of HEAD, and the current branch moves forward to point at it.
git commit.explanation: Git builds a tree from the index (the staging area) and writes a commit object whose parent is HEAD. It then moves the current branch to the new commit. If no branch is checked out, HEAD is detached and moves on its own. You choose what goes into the commit by staging with git add or git rm beforehand, by using -a to stage all tracked changes automatically, by naming paths on the command line, or by picking hunks with --patch. The message comes from -m, -F, -C or -c, or from an editor. A cleanup mode trims the message, and hooks such as pre-commit and commit-msg can check or reject the commit.

parameters.name: -a, --all
parameters.description: Stages modified and deleted tracked files before committing. Untracked files are left out.

parameters.name: -m <msg>, --message=<msg>
parameters.description: Sets the commit message. If you repeat it, each value becomes its own paragraph. It cannot be combined with -c, -C or -F.

parameters.name: -F <file>, --file=<file>
parameters.description: Reads the message from a file. Use - to read it from standard input.

parameters.name: --amend
parameters.description: Replaces the tip of the current branch with a new commit that keeps the same parents and author.

parameters.name: --fixup=[(amend|reword):]<commit>
parameters.description: Creates a fixup! or amend! commit for git rebase --autosquash to fold into <commit> later.

parameters.name: -p, --patch
parameters.description: Lets you choose the hunks to commit interactively.

parameters.name: -s, --signoff
parameters.description: Adds a Signed-off-by trailer for the committer.

parameters.name: -S[<key-id>], --gpg-sign
parameters.description: GPG-signs the commit. Without a key ID it uses the committer identity.

parameters.name: -n, --no-verify
parameters.description: Skips the pre-commit and commit-msg hooks.

parameters.name: --dry-run
parameters.description: Shows what would be committed without creating a commit.

parameters.name: <pathspec>...
parameters.description: Commits the current working-tree contents of the matching files and leaves other staged changes out of this commit.

git commit.returns: Creates a new commit object and moves the current branch (or a detached HEAD) to it. Unless -q is given, it prints a summary of the commit.

example.title: Stage, commit, then fix up the last commit
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

git init -q demo && cd demo
git config user.name "Ada Lovelace"
git config user.email "ada@example.com"

echo "hello" > hello.txt
git add hello.txt

# Preview, then commit with a title and a body paragraph
git commit --dry-run --short
git commit -m "Add greeting file" -m "Initial content for the demo."

# Edit a tracked file and commit it without git add
echo "hello, world" > hello.txt
git commit -a -m "Expand greeting"

# Forgot a file? Stage it and fold it into the last commit
echo "notes" > NOTES.md
git add NOTES.md
git commit --amend --no-edit

git log --oneline
example.explanation: The script stages and previews a first commit, commits a tracked-file change with -a, and then folds a forgotten file into the latest commit with --amend --no-edit, which keeps the original message.

useCases.title: Everyday snapshot
useCases.scenario: After staging related edits with git add, record them as one focused commit with a clear title line.

useCases.title: Correcting the latest local commit
useCases.scenario: You spot a typo or a missing file just after committing and haven't pushed yet. Use --amend to replace the commit.

useCases.title: Preparing autosquash cleanups
useCases.scenario: During code review, use --fixup=<sha> to make commits that git rebase -i --autosquash will merge into the right earlier commits.

useCases.title: Concluding a merge
useCases.scenario: Once the conflicts are resolved and staged, run git commit to record the merge commit using the message Git has pre-filled.

interview.question: What exactly does git commit put into the new commit, and how does -a change that?
interview.answer: By default it records the contents of the index, not the working tree, so unstaged edits are left out. With -a, Git first stages every change to tracked files, including deletions, and then commits. Untracked files are never added by -a.
interview.followUp: What happens with `git commit file.c` when other files are already staged? Only file.c's current working-tree contents are committed. The other staged changes are held back and still staged for the next commit.

interview.question: How does git commit --amend work, and when should you avoid it?
interview.answer: It replaces the tip of the current branch with a new commit. The tree is rebuilt as usual, the old message is the starting point, and the parents and author stay the same. Because the commit ID changes, it rewrites history, so avoid it on commits others may already have.
interview.followUp: How do you amend only the message while ignoring what is currently staged? Use `git commit --amend --only`, which needs no paths and leaves the staged changes out. To change authorship too, add --reset-author.

interview.question: How can a team enforce checks or metadata on commits?
interview.answer: git commit runs the pre-commit, prepare-commit-msg, commit-msg and post-commit hooks, and any of them can validate or reject a commit. Policy metadata can be added with --signoff, --trailer and -S for GPG signing. A commit.template file can guide contributors on how to write messages.
interview.followUp: Can a developer skip those hooks? Yes. -n or --no-verify skips the pre-commit and commit-msg hooks, so important checks also need to run on the server side or in CI.

keyPoints: The -a shortcut only covers files Git already tracks. A brand-new file still needs git add before any commit will include it.
If you name paths on the command line, Git commits only those files as they are in your working tree. Changes staged for other files stay staged for a later commit.
You can pass -m more than once to build a message with several paragraphs, for example a short title followed by a longer body.
--dry-run lets you check what a commit would contain, given the same options and paths, before you actually make it.
Author and committer identity comes from GIT_AUTHOR_* and GIT_COMMITTER_* environment variables first. If those are not set, Git falls back to user.name and user.email in config.
With -v, the editor shows the diff being committed so you can write an accurate message. The diff is stripped out when the commit is saved.
--fixup=<commit> creates a follow-up commit that changes another commit's content but keeps its message. git rebase --autosquash squashes it into that commit later.
--signoff adds a Signed-off-by trailer. What that trailer means, such as agreeing to a DCO, is up to each project.
gotchas: --amend rewrites history. If you amend a commit that has already been pushed, collaborators who built on the old commit will have to recover.
While you are finishing a conflicted merge, git commit refuses to run if you give it pathnames.
If you use a message template and close the editor without changing anything, Git aborts the commit instead of saving the template as the message.
If a commit fails, the message you typed is saved in .git/COMMIT_EDITMSG. Copy it out before running git commit again, because the next run overwrites it.

git config.summary: git config reads, writes, and removes Git settings. These settings live in system, global (per-user), repository, and worktree config files, and they change how other Git commands behave.
git config.explanation: Each setting has a dotted name. The last dot-separated part is the variable, and everything before it is the section, optionally with a quoted subsection, for example remote.origin.url. When you read a setting without naming a scope, Git merges the system, global, local and worktree files in that order, and the last value it finds wins. When you write a setting, Git uses the repository's .git/config unless you pass --global, --system, --worktree or --file. Modern Git splits the work into subcommands: list, get, set, unset, rename-section, remove-section and edit. Flags such as --type, --value, --all and --show-origin refine how values are matched and printed.
git config.syntax:
git config get [<file-option>] [<display-option>] [--includes] [--all] [--regexp] [--value=<pattern>] [--fixed-value] [--default=<default>] [--url=<url>] <name>
git config set [<file-option>] [--type=<type>] [--all] [--value=<pattern>] [--fixed-value] <name> <value>
git config unset [<file-option>] [--all] [--value=<pattern>] [--fixed-value] <name>
git config list [<file-option>] [<display-option>] [--includes]

parameters.name: <name>
parameters.description: The setting's key, written as the section name and the variable name joined by a dot, with an optional subsection, for example core.filemode or http.<url>.sslVerify.

parameters.name: <value>
parameters.description: The value to store with set. Git escapes it when writing it to the file.

parameters.name: --global / --system / --local / --worktree / --file <config-file>
parameters.description: Picks which config file to read from or write to. Writes go to the local repository file unless you choose another one.

parameters.name: --value=<pattern>
parameters.description: Limits get, set and unset to entries whose current value matches the pattern. With --fixed-value the pattern must match the value exactly.

parameters.name: --all
parameters.description: With get, prints every value of a multi-valued key. With set or unset, replaces or removes all of them.

parameters.name: --type=<type>
parameters.type: bool | int | bool-or-int | path | expiry-date | color
parameters.description: Checks values against the given type and converts them to its standard form, for example normalizing yes/on/1 to true.

parameters.name: --default=<value>
parameters.description: With get, prints this value when the key is not set anywhere.

parameters.name: --show-origin / --show-scope
parameters.description: Shows the file (or other source) and the scope that each printed value came from.

git config.returns: Exit code 0 on success. Failures return a non-zero code: 1 for an invalid or missing key, 2 when no section or name is given, 3 for an invalid config file, 4 when the file cannot be written, 5 when unsetting a key that does not exist or when several lines match, and 6 for an invalid regexp. get prints the value (or values) to stdout.

example.title: Set identity, inspect overrides, and work with a multi-valued key
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Per-user defaults (written to ~/.gitconfig or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/config)
git config set --global user.name "Ada Lovelace"
git config set --global user.email ada@example.com
git config set --global init.defaultBranch main

# Repo-specific override (written to .git/config by default)
git config set user.email ada@work.example.com

# Which value wins, and from where?
git config list --show-origin --show-scope | grep user.email
git config get user.email

# Typed read with a fallback when unset
git config get --type=bool --default=false commit.gpgSign

# Multi-valued key: append, read all, remove one by exact value
git config set --append remote.origin.fetch '+refs/tags/*:refs/tags/*'
git config get --all remote.origin.fetch
git config unset --fixed-value --value='+refs/tags/*:refs/tags/*' remote.origin.fetch

# Script-safe existence check (exit code 1 = not set)
if ! git config get core.editor >/dev/null; then
  echo "core.editor not set"
fi
example.explanation: Run inside a repository that has an origin remote: the script sets global and local values, shows which one wins and where it is stored, reads a typed value with a fallback, works with a multi-valued key, and checks whether a key exists using get's exit code.

useCases.title: First-time machine setup
useCases.scenario: Set your name, email, editor and default branch once with --global so every repository on the machine uses them.

useCases.title: Per-repository identity
useCases.scenario: Use a work email in one client repository by setting user.email locally, which overrides your personal global address.

useCases.title: Debugging surprising behavior
useCases.scenario: Run list --show-origin --show-scope to find out which config file is setting an unexpected pull, editor or credential option.

useCases.title: CI and automation scripts
useCases.scenario: Read settings with get --type and --default, or supply them through GIT_CONFIG_COUNT environment variables, so pipelines don't depend on a user's config files.

interview.question: If user.email is set in /etc/gitconfig, ~/.gitconfig and .git/config, which value does a commit use, and why?
interview.answer: It uses the value in .git/config. Git reads the system file first, then the global (per-user) files, then the repository's file, and the last value it reads wins. A worktree's config.worktree is read after .git/config when worktree config is enabled, and settings passed with -c on the command line or through GIT_CONFIG_* variables override all of these files.
interview.followUp: How would you prove which file supplied the value? Run git config get --show-origin --show-scope user.email (or list with the same flags). The output shows the file path and the scope for each value.

interview.question: What is a multi-valued variable, and how do you safely change just one of its values?
interview.answer: It is a key that appears on several lines, such as remote.origin.fetch or core.gitproxy. set and unset refuse to touch such a key by default. To target one line, pass --value=<pattern> (an extended regex), or add --fixed-value to match the value exactly. --append adds a new line without changing the existing ones.
interview.followUp: How do you replace every line except one specific value? Put ! at the start of the --value pattern to match lines that do not match it, as in --value='! for '. This only works when --fixed-value is not used.

interview.question: Why might a setting in a cloned repository's .git/config be ignored even though git config get shows it?
interview.answer: Some options are only honored when they come from protected configuration, meaning the system, global or command scope. Git treats those scopes as controlled by the user or a trusted administrator, while a repository's own config may come from somewhere less trustworthy. To make such an option take effect, set it with --global or --system, or pass it with -c.
interview.followUp: How can a script inject config without touching any file? Set GIT_CONFIG_COUNT and the zero-indexed GIT_CONFIG_KEY_<n>/GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_<n> pairs. A missing key or value causes an error, and settings passed with git -c still take priority.

keyPoints: A key named in several files, or several times in one file, normally resolves to the occurrence Git reads last. This ordering is why a repository setting overrides your personal default.
get exits with status 1 when the key is missing, so a shell script can check whether a setting exists just by testing the exit code.
--show-origin labels each value with where it came from (a file path, standard input, a blob or the command line). This is the quickest way to find out which file is overriding a setting.
Some security-sensitive options are only honored when they come from the system, global or command scope. If such an option is set in a repository's own .git/config, Git ignores it.
GIT_CONFIG_COUNT together with GIT_CONFIG_KEY_<n>/GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_<n> injects settings for a single process without editing any file. Settings passed with git -c still take priority over them.
-z ends each value with a NUL character instead of a newline. Use it when a script parses the output and some values may contain line breaks.
Section and variable names ignore case, but subsection names (such as a remote's name or a URL) are case-sensitive.
gotchas: set and unset refuse to work on a key that has several values unless you add --all or narrow it down with --value. Commands that ran fine on a single-value key can therefore fail on a multivar.
Each run edits exactly one file. Unsetting a key locally does not remove a global or system copy of it, so the key can still have a value afterwards.
The old forms, such as git config <name>, --get, --add, --unset and --list, are deprecated. Prefer the get, set, unset and list subcommands in new scripts.
--type=path only expands ~ when reading. Setting a value with that type does not expand the path, so you have to let the shell expand it.

git describe.summary: git describe gives a commit a readable name based on the nearest tag it can reach, such as v1.0.4-14-g2414721. Release scripts and build tools often use it to create version strings.
git describe.explanation: Git starts at the commit you name, or HEAD if you name none. If a tag points straight at that commit, Git prints only the tag name. If not, it walks back through the commit's ancestors to find a tagged commit. It then prints that tag, the number of commits added since it, and a hash suffix made of 'g' plus a short, unique form of the commit's ID. When several tags are reachable, it picks the one with the fewest commits between the tag and the input. You can pass the result to other git commands as a revision.
git describe.syntax:
git describe [--all] [--tags] [--contains] [--abbrev=<n>] [<commit-ish>…]
git describe [--all] [--tags] [--contains] [--abbrev=<n>] --dirty[=<mark>]
git describe <blob>

parameters.name: <commit-ish>…
parameters.description: One or more commits to describe. If you leave this out, Git uses HEAD.

parameters.name: --dirty[=<mark>]
parameters.description: Describes the working tree. If it has local changes, Git adds the suffix -dirty, or the <mark> you give.

parameters.name: --broken[=<mark>]
parameters.description: Like --dirty, but if the repository is corrupt, Git adds a -broken suffix (or <mark>) instead of failing.

parameters.name: --all
parameters.description: Considers any ref under refs/, including branches, remote-tracking branches and lightweight tags.

parameters.name: --tags
parameters.description: Considers every tag under refs/tags, including lightweight tags.

parameters.name: --contains
parameters.description: Finds a tag that comes after the commit, so it contains the commit. This also turns on --tags.

parameters.name: --abbrev=<n>
parameters.description: Uses at least n hex digits for the hash, or more if needed to keep it unique. A value of 0 prints only the closest tag.

parameters.name: --candidates=<n>
parameters.description: Considers up to n candidate tags instead of the default 10. A value of 0 allows only exact matches.

parameters.name: --exact-match
parameters.description: Prints a result only if a tag points directly at the commit. It is the same as --candidates=0.

parameters.name: --debug
parameters.description: Prints details of the tag search to standard error.

parameters.name: --long
parameters.description: Always prints the full tag-count-hash form, even when the commit is tagged.

parameters.name: --match <pattern>
parameters.description: Considers only tags that match the glob pattern. You can repeat it, and --no-match clears the list.

git describe.returns: Prints a name to standard output. It is either just the tag name (exact match) or <tag>-<count>-g<abbrev>, with an optional -dirty or -broken suffix. For a blob, it prints <commit-ish>:<path>.

example.title: Build a version string from tags
example.code:
git init -q demo && cd demo
git config user.name dev && git config user.email dev@example.com

git commit -q --allow-empty -m "initial"
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "release 1.0.0"

git describe                 # v1.0.0 (exact match)
git describe --long          # v1.0.0-0-g<hash>

git commit -q --allow-empty -m "feature"
git commit -q --allow-empty -m "fix"
git describe                 # v1.0.0-2-g<hash>
git describe --abbrev=0      # v1.0.0

echo change > file.txt && git add file.txt
git describe --dirty         # v1.0.0-2-g<hash>-dirty

# Version string for CI: only v* tags, fall back to the hash if none
VERSION=$(git describe --tags --match 'v*' --dirty --always)
echo "Building $VERSION"
example.explanation: The script creates an annotated release tag, then shows how the output changes for an exact match, for later commits, with --abbrev=0, with uncommitted changes and in a typical CI version string.

useCases.title: Build version stamping
useCases.scenario: A Makefile or CI job adds git describe --tags --dirty --always output to the binary, so every build can be traced to an exact commit and you can see if it had local edits.

useCases.title: Finding the previous release
useCases.scenario: A changelog script runs git describe --abbrev=0 to find the last release tag, then lists the commits made since that tag.

useCases.title: Checking that a deploy uses a tagged release
useCases.scenario: A deploy script runs git describe --exact-match and stops if HEAD is not exactly on a release tag.

useCases.title: Finding the first release with a fix
useCases.scenario: A support engineer runs git describe --contains <sha> to find the first tag that includes a bug-fix commit.

interview.question: What does each part of the output v1.0.4-14-g2414721 mean?
interview.answer: v1.0.4 is the nearest tag that can be reached from the commit. 14 is the number of commits added since that tag, which is the number git log v1.0.4..<commit> would show. g2414721 is 'g' (for git) plus a short, unique form of the described commit's ID.
interview.followUp: Can you pass that string straight to other git commands? Yes. Git treats describe output as a valid revision, and it uses the short hash after the 'g' to find the commit.

interview.question: Why might git describe fail or skip a tag you just made with 'git tag v2.0'?
interview.answer: 'git tag v2.0' without -a or -s makes a lightweight tag, and by default describe only looks at annotated tags. Add --tags so lightweight tags count, or --all to also include branches and remote refs.
interview.followUp: How do you avoid failures in a fresh clone that has no usable tags? Add --always, so Git prints the short commit ID when it cannot find a tag.

interview.question: How is --contains different from the default behavior?
interview.answer: By default, describe looks backwards for a tag the commit is based on. --contains looks forwards for a tag that comes after the commit and therefore includes it, and it turns on --tags automatically. It answers 'which release first shipped this commit?'
interview.followUp: When several ancestor tags can be reached, which one does the default mode pick? The one with the fewest commits between the tag and the input. With --first-parent, Git only walks first parents at merge commits.

keyPoints: Lightweight tags are ignored unless you add --tags. Use --tags when your project marks releases with plain tags made by 'git tag v1.2'.
--all extends the search to every ref under refs/, so the output may be a branch path such as heads/topic-7-g975b instead of a tag.
With --dirty, Git also checks the working tree, so builds made from uncommitted changes get a -dirty marker in their version string.
Setting --abbrev=0 removes the count and hash, leaving only the nearest tag name. This is handy for finding the previous release.
--long keeps the output format the same even on a tagged commit (for example v1.2-0-gdeadbee), which helps scripts that split the output into fields.
If more than one tag points at the same commit, Git chooses annotated tags over lightweight ones, and newer tags over older ones.
--match and --exclude take glob patterns, so you can pick one tag family, such as v* release tags, and skip others like rc tags.
--first-parent ignores tags that only exist on side branches merged into the history, so the name stays tied to the mainline.
gotchas: By default Git looks at only 10 candidate tags. In repositories with many tags, this can give a less accurate result unless you raise --candidates.
The hash suffix can get longer as the repository grows, because it must stay unique. Do not assume it is always 7 characters.
Trees, and tags that do not point at commits, cannot be described.
On a corrupt repository, --dirty makes the command fail unless you use --broken.

git diff.summary: git diff shows line-level differences between two snapshots in a repository: the working tree, the index (staging area), commits, trees, or blobs. Outside a repository, or with --no-index, it compares two paths on disk.
git diff.explanation: git diff always compares two endpoints and prints a unified patch by default. Which endpoints it uses depends on the arguments. With no revision, it compares the index with the working tree. With --cached, it compares a commit (HEAD by default) with the index. With one commit, it compares that commit with the working tree. With two commits, it compares the two trees. Path arguments after -- narrow the comparison to those files or directories. Other options change the output (stat, names only, raw, word diff), the diff algorithm, how whitespace is treated, and rename detection.
git diff.syntax:
git diff [<options>] [<commit>] [--] [<path>…]
git diff [<options>] --cached [--merge-base] [<commit>] [--] [<path>…]
git diff [<options>] [--merge-base] <commit> [<commit>…] <commit> [--] [<path>…]
git diff [<options>] <commit>...<commit> [--] [<path>…]
git diff [<options>] <blob> <blob>
git diff [<options>] --no-index [--] <path> <path> [<pathspec>…]

parameters.name: <commit>
parameters.description: The snapshot to compare against. Give one to compare it with the working tree, or two to compare them with each other. A..B means the same as A B, and A...B starts from the merge base of A and B.

parameters.name: --cached / --staged
parameters.description: Compares the index with a commit, which is HEAD if you don't name one. It shows what the next commit would contain.

parameters.name: --merge-base
parameters.description: Uses the merge base of the given commit and HEAD (or of the two given commits) as the 'before' side, instead of the commit itself.

parameters.name: --no-index
parameters.description: Compares two paths on the filesystem, even if they are not tracked by Git.

parameters.name: <path>…
parameters.description: Restricts the diff to the named files, or to every file under the named directories.

parameters.name: <blob> <blob>
parameters.description: Compares the raw contents of two blob objects.

git diff.returns: Prints a patch (or a stat, name list, or raw output, depending on the options) to stdout. With --exit-code or --quiet, the exit status is 1 if there are differences and 0 if there are none. --no-index implies --exit-code.

example.title: Review unstaged, staged and branch changes
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Unstaged edits (working tree vs index)
git diff

# What the next commit will contain (index vs HEAD)
git diff --staged --stat

# Everything since the last commit, ignoring whitespace
git diff -w HEAD

# Files changed on this branch since it forked from main
git diff --name-status main...HEAD

# Fail a CI step if the working tree is dirty
if ! git diff --quiet; then
  echo "Uncommitted changes found" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Block whitespace errors / conflict markers in staged changes
git diff --cached --check
example.explanation: The script shows the main comparison modes and then uses --quiet and --check as automated checks.

useCases.title: Pre-commit review
useCases.scenario: Before committing, run git diff --staged to make sure only the intended hunks are staged.

useCases.title: Pull request scope
useCases.scenario: Run git diff --stat main...feature to see which files a feature branch changed relative to where it forked from main.

useCases.title: CI cleanliness check
useCases.scenario: After code generation or formatting, a CI job runs git diff --exit-code and fails if any files changed.

useCases.title: Comparing untracked files
useCases.scenario: Use git diff --no-index old.json new.json to get Git's diff output for two arbitrary files.

interview.question: What is the difference between git diff, git diff --cached, and git diff HEAD?
interview.answer: Plain git diff compares the working tree with the index, so it shows edits that are not yet staged. git diff --cached (or --staged) compares the index with HEAD, which is what the next commit will contain. git diff HEAD compares the working tree with HEAD, so it covers both staged and unstaged changes.
interview.followUp: What does git diff --cached show on a brand-new repository with no commits? HEAD doesn't exist yet, so it shows all staged changes.

interview.question: How do git diff A..B and git diff A...B differ?
interview.answer: A..B means the same as git diff A B: it compares the two tips directly. A...B compares B with the merge base of A and B, so you see only the changes made on B's side since the branches diverged. For git diff these are endpoint comparisons, not the commit ranges they mean in git log.
interview.followUp: How else can you get the A...B result? Use git diff --merge-base A B, which is equivalent to git diff $(git merge-base A B) B.

interview.question: How would you use git diff in a script to detect changes?
interview.answer: Use --exit-code, which returns 1 when there are differences and 0 when there are none. Use --quiet to get the same exit status without any output. For hooks, --check reports whitespace errors or conflict markers and exits non-zero when it finds them.
interview.followUp: Can you combine --check with --exit-code? No. The docs say --check is not compatible with --exit-code, so run them as separate commands.

keyPoints: Run with no arguments, git diff shows only the edits that are not yet staged. Changes you have already staged with git add do not appear.
git diff --cached (also spelled --staged) compares the index with HEAD by default. This is how you check exactly what git commit is about to record.
The three-dot form A...B diffs B against the common ancestor of A and B. It shows only the work done on B's side since the two branches diverged.
--exit-code makes git diff behave like diff(1) for scripts: it exits with 1 if there are differences and 0 if there are none. --quiet does the same without printing anything.
--check looks for leftover conflict markers and whitespace problems in the changes. This makes it useful in pre-commit hooks.
--name-only and --name-status print only file names, with or without a status letter, and no patch. They are handy for piping into other tools.
You can switch the diff algorithm with --diff-algorithm (myers, minimal, patience, histogram). Myers is the default.
gotchas: In git diff, A..B and A...B do not mean the commit ranges they mean in git log. git diff only ever compares two endpoint snapshots.
--check exits with a non-zero status when it finds problems, and it cannot be combined with --exit-code.
When you use --no-index on two directories, any extra pathspecs must be relative paths.
A diff produced through a textconv filter is meant for people to read. You cannot apply it as a patch.

git fetch.summary: git fetch downloads commits, trees, blobs and refs (branches and tags) from one or more other repositories and updates your remote-tracking branches. It does not merge anything into your own branches or change your working tree.
git fetch.explanation: Fetch first contacts the remote and works out which commits you already have. It then downloads only the objects you are missing. Next, it uses a refspec (+src:dst) to decide which remote refs to fetch and where to store them locally. If you give no refspec on the command line, Git uses the remote.<name>.fetch config values, which normally map refs/heads/* to refs/remotes/<name>/*. Updates that are not fast-forwards are refused unless the refspec starts with + or you pass --force. Fetch also writes the refs it got to FETCH_HEAD, which git pull and scripts can read.
git fetch.syntax:
git fetch [<options>] [<repository> [<refspec>…]]
git fetch [<options>] <group>
git fetch --multiple [<options>] [(<repository>|<group>)…]
git fetch --all [<options>]

parameters.name: <repository>
parameters.description: The repository to fetch from. This can be a URL or the name of a configured remote.

parameters.name: <group>
parameters.description: A name defined by remotes.<group> in your config that stands for a list of repositories.

parameters.name: <refspec>
parameters.description: Says which remote refs to fetch and which local refs to update. A leading + allows non-fast-forward updates, a ^ prefix makes it a negative (exclusion) refspec, and * acts as a pattern.

parameters.name: --prune / -p
parameters.description: Before fetching, deletes remote-tracking refs whose branches no longer exist on the remote.

parameters.name: --tags / --no-tags
parameters.description: --tags fetches every tag. --no-tags turns off automatic tag following.

parameters.name: --depth=<depth> / --unshallow
parameters.description: --depth limits or changes how much history a shallow repository has. --unshallow turns a shallow repository into a complete one.

parameters.name: --all / --multiple
parameters.description: --all fetches from every remote. --multiple lets you name several repositories or groups.

parameters.name: --dry-run
parameters.description: Shows what would happen without changing anything.

git fetch.returns: For each ref, fetch prints a status line of the form '<flag> <summary> <from> -> <to> [<reason>]' to stderr. The flags are: space = fast-forward, + = forced update, - = pruned, t = tag update, * = new ref, ! = rejected, = = up to date. With --porcelain it prints a machine-readable format to stdout instead.

example.title: Safely inspect upstream changes before integrating
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Update all remote-tracking branches for origin, dropping deleted ones
git fetch --prune origin

# See what arrived on main that you don't have yet
git log --oneline main..origin/main

# Fetch one branch into a local branch of your choice
git fetch origin feature/login:review-login

# Peek at a branch from an unconfigured repo via FETCH_HEAD
git fetch https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/git/git.git maint
git log -3 --oneline FETCH_HEAD

# Integrate only when ready
git merge --ff-only origin/main
example.explanation: The script updates and prunes origin's remote-tracking branches, shows the new upstream commits, fetches one branch under a local name, peeks at another repository through FETCH_HEAD, and fast-forwards main only at the end.

useCases.title: Review before merging
useCases.scenario: Fetch and compare main with origin/main (or run git log HEAD..origin/main) so you can see incoming commits before you merge or rebase them.

useCases.title: Cleaning up deleted branches
useCases.scenario: Run git fetch --prune, or set fetch.prune=true, so remote-tracking branches deleted on the server stop showing up in git branch -a.

useCases.title: Deepening a CI shallow clone
useCases.scenario: A CI job cloned with --depth=1 and now needs more history for git describe or a merge-base. Run git fetch --deepen=N or git fetch --unshallow.

useCases.title: Keeping several remotes in sync
useCases.scenario: Use git fetch --all -j 4 to update origin, upstream and the remotes of forks in parallel.

interview.question: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
interview.answer: git fetch only downloads objects and updates refs: remote-tracking branches and FETCH_HEAD. Your local branches and working tree stay as they were. git pull runs a fetch and then merges or rebases the fetched branch into your current branch, using the information fetch wrote. That makes fetch the safe choice when you only want to look at upstream changes.
interview.followUp: Why won't fetch update the branch you have checked out, even with a matching refspec? By default fetch refuses to update the ref for your current branch, because that would leave your working tree out of step with it. The --update-head-ok flag turns this check off, but it is meant only for git pull's internal use.

interview.question: Explain the refspec +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*.
interview.answer: The left side picks the source refs on the remote, here every branch. The right side is where each one is stored locally, with * replaced by the matched name. The leading + allows non-fast-forward updates, so the remote-tracking branches still update after someone force-pushes or rebases. This is the default remote.origin.fetch value that git clone sets up.
interview.followUp: How do you leave out some branches that a pattern matches? Add a negative refspec with a ^ prefix, for example ^refs/heads/tmp/*. A ref is fetched only if it matches at least one positive refspec and no negative one.

interview.question: What are stale remote-tracking branches and how do you deal with them?
interview.answer: They are refs/remotes/<name>/* entries whose branches have been deleted on the server. Git keeps them because it holds on to data until you explicitly remove it. Over time they clutter commands like git branch -a and can slow down busy repositories. You can remove them with git fetch --prune <name>, or with git remote prune <name> if you don't want to fetch, or set fetch.prune / remote.<name>.prune to prune on every fetch.
interview.followUp: Does --prune delete local tags? Usually not. Tags fetched through auto-following or --tags are never pruned. They are pruned only when an explicit tag refspec is in effect, which is what --prune-tags adds.

keyPoints: If you don't name a remote, fetch uses the current branch's upstream remote when one is set, and origin otherwise.
By default, fetch also downloads tags that point into the history it is fetching. Use --tags to get all tags, or --no-tags to get none automatically.
When you list refspecs on the command line, only those refs are fetched. The configured remote.<name>.fetch values then just act as a map that decides which remote-tracking ref gets updated.
--atomic updates all local refs in one transaction, so you never end up with only some refs updated after a failure.
--unshallow downloads the missing history so a shallow clone becomes a complete repository.
Fetching from several remotes or submodules happens one at a time unless you use -j/--jobs or the fetch.parallel setting.
If a remote has several url entries, fetch only uses the first one. Push, by contrast, goes to all of them.
gotchas: --prune-tags also deletes tags you created locally that don't exist on the remote, so it is much more destructive than --prune.
If you combine --prune with a refspec like refs/tags/*:refs/tags/*, Git can delete tags you got from other remotes.
Since Git 2.20, an existing local tag that changed on the remote is not updated unless you use + in the refspec or --force.
--recurse-submodules can't fetch a submodule that upstream just added. You have to clone it first, for example with git submodule update.

git format-patch.summary: git format-patch turns a range of commits into email-ready patch files, one per non-merge commit, in UNIX mbox style. It keeps the author, date and commit message, so the recipient can rebuild the same commits with git am or send them with git send-email.
git format-patch.explanation: You pick the commits in one of two ways. A single commit <since> means every commit on the current branch that is not reachable from it, and a revision range means exactly the commits in that range. Each patch has three parts: a header (a From <sha> line with a fixed fake date, plus author, date and a Subject taken from the commit title), the rest of the commit message, and a --- separator followed by the diffstat and diff against the parent. Files are named NNNN-title.patch and go in the current directory, or in the directory given by -o. With --stdout everything is written to standard output as one mbox stream.

parameters.name: <since> | <revision-range>
parameters.description: Which commits to format. A single commit means everything on the current branch since that commit. A range such as A..B means the commits in that range.

parameters.name: -<n>
parameters.description: Format only the topmost n commits. For example, -1 <commit> formats just that one commit.

parameters.name: -o, --output-directory=<dir>
parameters.description: Directory to write the patch files to. It overrides format.outputDirectory, and missing directories are created.

parameters.name: --stdout
parameters.description: Write all patches to standard output in mbox format instead of one file per commit.

parameters.name: --cover-letter
parameters.description: Also write a 0000 cover-letter file with the branch description, the commit list and the overall diffstat.

parameters.name: -v, --reroll-count=<n>
parameters.description: Marks the series as iteration n. It adds vN- to the filenames and appends vN to the subject prefix.

parameters.name: --subject-prefix=<prefix> / --rfc[=<rfc>]
parameters.description: Use your own subject prefix instead of [PATCH], or put RFC (or another word) in front of it.

parameters.name: --thread[=shallow|deep]
parameters.description: Adds Message-ID, In-Reply-To and References headers so the mails form a thread. Off by default.

parameters.name: --base[=<commit>|auto]
parameters.description: Records which base tree the series applies on top of.

parameters.name: -s, --signoff
parameters.description: Adds a Signed-off-by trailer using your committer identity.

git format-patch.returns: Writes one .patch file per selected non-merge commit, plus an optional cover letter, and prints the generated filenames to standard output. With --stdout it writes one mbox stream to standard output instead.

example.title: Prepare a patch series, reroll it, and round-trip a single patch
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# v1: every commit on the current branch that is not in origin/main
git format-patch -o outgoing/ --cover-letter --base=origin/main origin/main
# -> outgoing/0000-cover-letter.patch, 0001-....patch, ...

# v2 after review: compare with the old tip, kept as branch topic-v1
git format-patch -v2 -o outgoing/ --cover-letter \
  --range-diff=topic-v1 --base=origin/main origin/main
# -> outgoing/v2-0000-cover-letter.patch, v2-0001-....patch, ...

# Only the latest commit, as an mbox stream
git format-patch -1 --stdout HEAD > latest.patch

# On another clone: recreate the commit with author and message intact
git am latest.patch
example.explanation: The script makes a first and a second version of a series (the second includes a range-diff), then exports one commit and rebuilds it elsewhere with git am.

useCases.title: Mailing-list contributions
useCases.scenario: Projects such as Git or the Linux kernel take changes by email. You format your topic branch with a cover letter, -s for sign-off and --to/--cc, then send it with git send-email.

useCases.title: Moving commits without a shared remote
useCases.scenario: Two repositories can't reach each other over the network. You copy patch files across, and git am recreates the commits with their original authors and messages.

useCases.title: Reviewing a reworked series
useCases.scenario: After review feedback you rebase and send v3 with -v3 and --range-diff=<old-tip>, so reviewers only need to look at what changed.

useCases.title: Archiving or auditing a change set
useCases.scenario: You export a release branch's commits to numbered .patch files, for example with --numbered-files or --suffix=.txt, to attach to a ticket or keep for compliance.

interview.question: Why use git format-patch instead of git diff > change.patch to share commits?
interview.answer: git diff gives you only the code changes. format-patch writes one mail-style file per commit that also holds the author, the author date and the full commit message, with the diff after a --- line. git am can then rebuild the exact commits, keeping authorship and history, instead of leaving uncommitted changes.
interview.followUp: What happens to merge commits in the range? They are skipped, because format-patch only handles non-merge commits. A history that contains merges has to be made linear, or shared another way such as git bundle or a pull request.

interview.question: How would you send version 3 of a patch series so reviewers can follow what changed?
interview.answer: Run format-patch with -v3, which puts v3- in front of the filenames and gives subjects like [PATCH v3 n/m].
