Add --cover-letter and --range-diff=<v2-tip> or --interdiff=<v2-tip> so the comparison with v2 is included. You can also use --in-reply-to=<message-id> so v3 stays in the earlier thread.
interview.followUp: Why does --creation-factor default to 999 here and not 60 as in git range-diff? Because rerolls are expected to resemble the old series, the higher value makes the tool more willing to pair old and new commits.

interview.question: Every patch starts with 'From <sha> Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001'. What is that date for?
interview.answer: It is a fixed, made-up mbox separator date. It makes the file look like a UNIX mailbox while letting tools such as file(1) tell that it came from format-patch and is not a real mailbox. The real author date is in the Date: header.
interview.followUp: How can you hide the commit hash on that line, for example to get reproducible output? Pass --zero-commit, which writes an all-zero hash in place of the real one.

keyPoints: Patch numbers in the subject are automatic: a single patch gets plain [PATCH], while a series gets [PATCH n/m]. Use -n to force numbering on a single patch, or -N to turn it off.
--cover-letter gives you a 0000 introduction mail to edit before sending. It is already filled in with a summary of the series.
When you send a new version of a series, --range-diff or --interdiff adds a comparison with the old version to the cover letter (or to the single patch), which helps reviewers.
--base adds base-commit information so the recipient knows which commit the series should be applied on. --base=auto picks that commit automatically.
--ignore-if-in-upstream drops commits whose change has already been applied upstream, by comparing patch content rather than commit IDs.
Commits that change nothing are skipped unless you pass --always.
--notes puts git notes after the --- line, so per-commit reviewer comments can be kept in notes and reused from one version of the series to the next.
gotchas: A single commit argument is read as <since>, not as 'just this commit'. git format-patch abc123 formats everything after abc123. To format only that commit use -1 abc123, and to format all history up to it use --root.
git send-email threads mails itself. If you also use --thread in format-patch, turn off threading in send-email, or the threads will be wrong.
Don't use --from when the output goes to git send-email, because send-email already does that sender rewriting for you.
--no-binary swaps binary diffs for a short notice, so the patches can be reviewed but not applied.

git fsck.summary: git fsck checks a repository's object database for integrity. It confirms that objects are valid and that everything they refer to is present, then reports corruption, missing objects and objects that nothing points to.
git fsck.explanation: fsck starts from a set of head objects and walks every commit, tree, tag and blob that can be reached from them. Unless you name objects, the heads are the index, every ref and every reflog. Along the way it checks each object's hash and format. It reports missing or bad objects, plus dangling ones: objects that exist but that no other object points to. By default it also checks the refs database. Message IDs such as missingEmail can be configured to change how severe a problem is treated, and a skip list can exempt known-bad objects. The fsck.* settings apply only to this command.

parameters.name: <object>
parameters.description: An object to use as a head (starting point) for the reachability check. If none is given, fsck uses the index, all refs and all reflogs.

parameters.name: --unreachable
parameters.description: List objects that exist but cannot be reached from any of the heads.

parameters.name: --[no-]dangling
parameters.description: Show (default) or hide objects that exist but that no other object points to directly.

parameters.name: --root
parameters.description: Report root nodes.

parameters.name: --tags
parameters.description: Report tags.

parameters.name: --cache
parameters.description: Also use every object recorded in the index as a head.

parameters.name: --no-reflogs
parameters.description: Do not count commits as reachable if only a reflog entry refers to them.

parameters.name: --[no-]full
parameters.description: Also check alternate object stores and packfiles. This is on by default.

parameters.name: --connectivity-only
parameters.description: Check only that reachable objects are present. Blob contents are never read, which makes the check faster.

parameters.name: --strict
parameters.description: Use stricter checks, for example flagging file modes with the group-write bit set, which older versions of Git created.

parameters.name: --verbose
parameters.description: Print more detailed output.

parameters.name: --lost-found
parameters.description: Save dangling objects under .git/lost-found/commit/ or .git/lost-found/other/.

example.title: Find and save a commit lost after a hard reset
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
repo=$(mktemp -d)
cd "$repo"
git init -q
git commit -q --allow-empty -m "first"
git commit -q --allow-empty -m "second"

# Drop "second" from the branch; only the reflog still refers to it
git reset -q --hard HEAD~1

# Ignore reflogs so the dropped commit is reported as dangling
git fsck --no-reflogs

# Save dangling objects under .git/lost-found
git fsck --no-reflogs --lost-found
ls .git/lost-found/commit/

# Fast health check without the dangling-object list
git fsck --connectivity-only --no-dangling && echo "connectivity OK"
example.explanation: The script drops a commit from its branch, runs fsck with --no-reflogs so the commit shows up as dangling, saves it with --lost-found, and then runs a quick connectivity check.

useCases.title: Recovering deleted work
useCases.scenario: A branch was deleted together with its reflog. Running fsck lists the dangling commits that still exist, so you can find the right one and point a new branch at it.

useCases.title: Diagnosing a suspect repository
useCases.scenario: After a disk failure or a crash during a write, run git fsck --full --no-dangling to list only real problems, such as missing or broken objects.

useCases.title: Accepting a legacy project
useCases.scenario: An old repository has early commits with bad committer emails. List those object IDs in fsck.skipList, and set receive.fsck.skipList and fetch.fsck.skipList too, so fsck checks pass without hiding new problems of the same kind.

interview.question: What is the difference between a dangling object and an unreachable object in git fsck output?
interview.answer: An unreachable object cannot be reached, directly or indirectly, from any head. A dangling object exists but no other object points to it directly. fsck lists dangling objects by default, while unreachable objects appear only with --unreachable.
interview.followUp: Why can't fsck see a commit that only the reflog points to? Because reflogs are included in the default heads, so that commit counts as reachable. Pass --no-reflogs to have it reported.

interview.question: How would you speed up fsck on a very large repository, and what do you give up?
interview.answer: Use --connectivity-only, which skips reading blobs and only checks that every referenced object exists. Add --no-dangling as well, so fsck doesn't have to walk unreachable history to find dangling tips. The cost is that corrupted blobs and format errors are not detected.
interview.followUp: Does it still catch a missing blob? Yes. It confirms that referenced blobs exist; it just doesn't read their contents.

interview.question: An old repository fails fsck with missingEmail errors in a few early commits. How do you handle that properly?
interview.answer: The best approach is to list the specific bad object IDs in fsck.skipList. Setting fsck.missingEmail=ignore would also let new commits with the same problem pass unnoticed.
interview.followUp: Why do pushes to the server still fail after that change? Because receive.fsck.skipList doesn't fall back to fsck.skipList, so it has to be set on the server separately.

keyPoints: With no object arguments, fsck starts its walk from the index, every ref and every reflog. This is why commits you can still reach through the reflog are not reported.
Alternate object stores and packfiles are checked by default. Use --no-full to check only the main object directory.
--lost-found saves dangling objects so you can get them back. Blobs are written out as file contents, and other objects are saved under their object IDs.
fsck also checks the refs database by running git refs verify. Use --no-references to skip this step.
If the commit-graph feature is turned on, fsck also verifies the commit-graph file.
Each message ID can be set to error, warn or ignore in config. For example, fsck.missingEmail=ignore hides that problem. Messages marked FATAL cannot be changed.
A hash mismatch means an object's contents do not match its ID. This is real corruption, not harmless leftover data.
fsck cannot repair a corrupt object. You have to get a good copy from a backup or from another clone.
gotchas: --connectivity-only is faster but only checks that blobs exist. It never reads their contents, so a damaged file in history goes unnoticed.
The receive.fsck.* and fetch.fsck.* settings do not fall back to fsck.*. To get the same behaviour everywhere, you must set all three.
fsck.skipList only silences objects with non-fatal problems. It cannot hide objects that are actually corrupt.
A misspelled fsck.<msg-id> setting stops fsck completely. The same mistake in receive or fetch settings only produces a warning.

git gc.summary: git gc does housekeeping on your local repository. It compresses objects into packfiles, throws away unreachable data once it has aged enough, and tidies refs, reflogs, rerere records and worktree metadata so the repository takes less disk space and runs faster.
git gc.explanation: When you run it, git gc triggers several maintenance steps one after another. It runs git repack to gather loose objects and small packs into packfiles, and by default it puts unreachable objects into a separate cruft pack. It prunes unreachable objects older than a grace period (2 weeks by default), runs pack-refs, expires old reflog entries, cleans up rerere data and stale worktrees, and can rewrite the commit-graph. Many everyday porcelain commands call `git gc --auto` for you. That version only does real work once the repository passes certain thresholds, so running it by hand is rarely needed.

parameters.name: --aggressive
parameters.description: Optimizes much harder at the cost of far more time. It throws away existing deltas and recomputes them with a larger window and depth.

parameters.name: --auto
parameters.description: Does nothing unless the configured thresholds show that housekeeping is needed.

parameters.name: --[no-]detach
parameters.description: Runs in the background (or not), overriding gc.autoDetach.

parameters.name: --[no-]cruft
parameters.description: Turns on or off storing expiring unreachable objects in a cruft pack instead of as loose objects. On by default.

parameters.name: --max-cruft-size=<n>
parameters.description: Upper size limit for new cruft packs. Overrides gc.maxCruftSize.

parameters.name: --expire-to=<dir>
parameters.description: Writes a cruft pack of the pruned objects into this directory. Only has an effect together with --cruft.

parameters.name: --prune=<date>
parameters.description: Prunes loose objects older than this date. The default is 2 weeks ago, set by gc.pruneExpire.

parameters.name: --no-prune
parameters.description: Prunes no loose objects at all.

parameters.name: --quiet
parameters.description: Hides all progress output.

parameters.name: --force
parameters.description: Runs even if another gc may already be running on the repository.

parameters.name: --keep-largest-pack
parameters.description: Merges every pack except the largest non-cruft pack, .keep packs and cruft packs into one pack. gc.bigPackThreshold is ignored when this is used.

example.title: Inspect, clean up and re-inspect a repository
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Before: count loose objects and packs
git count-objects -v

# Standard cleanup; unreachable objects younger than 2 weeks are kept
git gc

# Cheap check that only does work if thresholds are exceeded
git gc --auto --quiet

# Keep the big pack and only consolidate the smaller ones
git gc --keep-largest-pack

# Turn off automatic gc for this repository (e.g. during a bulk import)
git config gc.auto 0

# After: compare the numbers
git count-objects -v
example.explanation: This shows a normal gc, a threshold-gated auto run and a run that keeps the largest pack, plus how to disable auto-gc, with object counts printed before and after so you can see the effect.

useCases.title: After a bulk import
useCases.scenario: You loaded a large history with git fast-import or a migration tool. The packs it produced are not well optimized, so you run git gc once to rebuild them properly.

useCases.title: Reclaiming space after history rewrites
useCases.scenario: Large blobs were removed from history. Once the reflogs and backup refs that still point at them are gone and the grace period has passed, git gc deletes the objects and the repository shrinks.

useCases.title: Avoiding surprise background work
useCases.scenario: On a big repository, run git gc yourself at a convenient time so that auto-gc does not start in the middle of something important.

interview.question: What is the difference between `git gc` and `git gc --auto`, and who calls the second one?
interview.answer: Plain `git gc` always does the full set of housekeeping steps. `git gc --auto` checks gc.auto (loose object count) and gc.autoPackLimit (pack count) first and stops if neither is exceeded. Common porcelain commands that create objects run it automatically, and once it is triggered it also handles reflogs, rerere data and worktrees.
interview.followUp: How do you turn auto-gc off completely? Set gc.auto to 0. That disables the loose-object heuristic and every other --auto heuristic, including gc.autoPackLimit.

interview.question: Why doesn't git gc delete an unreachable object right away?
interview.answer: By default it only prunes unreachable objects older than 2 weeks (gc.pruneExpire). This protects against concurrent processes that have written an object but have not referenced it yet. Git also keeps anything newer than the prune date plus everything reachable from it, and it refreshes an object's mtime when a command re-adds it.
interview.followUp: Is this a complete guarantee? No. The docs say the protections fall short of a full solution, so running commands concurrently still carries a small risk of corruption.

interview.question: You deleted a branch containing a large file and ran git gc, but the disk usage didn't drop. Why?
interview.answer: gc keeps every object that is still referenced from anywhere: reflogs, the index, remote-tracking branches or any other ref under refs/*. The deleted branch's commits are probably still in reflogs, and unreachable objects also wait out the 2-week grace period, now inside a cruft pack.
interview.followUp: How would you reclaim the space right away on a repository nothing else is touching? Expire the reflogs (for example `git reflog expire --expire-unreachable=now --all`) and then run `git gc --prune=now`, accepting that this is only safe when no other process is writing.

keyPoints: The `--auto` flag is a cheap check. It quits right away unless thresholds such as gc.auto (about 6700 loose objects) or gc.autoPackLimit (50 packs) have been exceeded.
Unreachable objects that are waiting to expire go into a single cruft pack by default rather than being written out as many loose files.
gc is cautious about what it deletes. Anything reachable from branches, tags, the index, remote-tracking branches, reflogs or any other ref under refs/* survives.
Unreachable loose objects are only removed after a grace period. You can change it per run with --prune=<date> or permanently with gc.pruneExpire.
Reflog entries left behind by amends and rebases (no longer reachable from the tip) expire after 30 days by default. Ordinary entries expire after 90 days.
To avoid rewriting a huge pack every time, use --keep-largest-pack or set gc.bigPackThreshold. Only the smaller packs then get merged.
gotchas: `--prune=now` removes the safety grace period. If another Git process is writing to the repository at the same moment, its new objects can be deleted.
`--aggressive` is not a free upgrade. It is much slower, and the docs advise against it unless you have benchmarked it on your repository.
A note made with git notes does not count as a reference. Objects that only a note points to can still be pruned.
If an earlier background auto-gc left a gc.log file, later `--auto` runs just print that log and stop until it is more than gc.logExpiry old (1 day by default).

git grep.summary: git grep searches text for patterns inside a Git repository. It can search the tracked files in your working tree, the staged content in the index, or any commit or tree, without checking that tree out.
git grep.explanation: You give it one or more patterns and, optionally, trees and pathspecs. If you pass no tree, Git reads the tracked files in your working tree. --cached makes it read the index blobs instead, and naming a tree such as a tag or commit makes it read the blobs stored there. Several -e patterns are joined with OR by default, and you can build Boolean expressions with --and, --not and parentheses. Matches are printed as filename:line, and flags like -n, -c, -l or -p change the output. By default the patterns are POSIX basic regular expressions. Searches run on several threads, and the grep.* config keys can set your preferred defaults.

parameters.name: <pattern>
parameters.description: The search expression. Put -e in front of it if it starts with a dash, and use -f <file> to read several patterns from a file.

parameters.name: <tree>...
parameters.description: Search the blobs in these trees instead of the tracked files in the working tree.

parameters.name: <pathspec>...
parameters.description: Only search paths that match at least one of these patterns. Leading paths, globs and magic such as :^ for exclusion all work.

parameters.name: --cached / --untracked / --no-index
parameters.description: Choose what to search: the index, the working tree plus untracked files, or a plain directory that Git doesn't manage.

parameters.name: -i, -w, -v, -E, -F, -P
parameters.description: Control matching: ignore case, match whole words only, invert the match, or use extended, fixed-string or Perl regex syntax.

parameters.name: -n, -c, -l/-L, -o, -p, -W, -A/-B/-C
parameters.description: Control output: line numbers, match counts, file names only, only the matched text, the enclosing function, or context lines.

parameters.name: --threads <num>
parameters.description: How many worker threads to use. This overrides grep.threads.

git grep.returns: Prints the matches to stdout. With -q it prints nothing and returns exit status 0 if there was a match and a non-zero status if there wasn't.

example.title: Searching the working tree, the index and an old tag
example.code:
# Search tracked C files for a word, with line numbers
git grep -n -w 'time_t' -- '*.[ch]'

# Count matches per file in the staged (index) content
git grep --cached -c 'TODO'

# Lines with #define AND (MAX_PATH or PATH_MAX) in tag v1.0, grouped by file
git grep --heading --break -n \
  -e '#define' --and \( -e MAX_PATH -e PATH_MAX \) v1.0

# Exclude a directory via pathspec magic
git grep 'solution' -- ':^Documentation'

# Use in a script: fail if a debug marker is staged
if git grep -q --cached 'console.log'; then
  echo 'Remove debug logging before committing' >&2
  exit 1
fi
example.explanation: These commands search the working tree, the index and an old tag, combine patterns with Boolean operators, exclude a directory with a pathspec, and use -q as a check in a script.

useCases.title: Pre-commit guard
useCases.scenario: A hook runs git grep -q --cached to block commits whose staged files contain secrets or leftover debug calls.

useCases.title: Investigating an old release
useCases.scenario: While fixing a bug in a production tag, you search that tag's tree for a symbol without checking it out or touching your current work.

useCases.title: Refactoring impact check
useCases.scenario: Before renaming a function, git grep -l -w lists every tracked file that uses it, and -p shows which functions call it.

useCases.title: Searching a non-Git directory
useCases.scenario: git grep --no-index gives you Git's pathspec filtering and output formatting in a folder that is not a repository.

interview.question: How is git grep different from running plain grep -r in a repository?
interview.answer: By default git grep only reads tracked files, so it skips build output, ignored files and the .git directory. It can also search the index (--cached) or any commit or tree directly, without a checkout. It supports pathspec filtering and runs on several threads.
interview.followUp: How would you search ignored files too? Use git grep --untracked --no-index-free form: git grep --untracked --no-exclude-standard, because --no-exclude-standard only has an effect together with --untracked.

interview.question: How do you find lines that contain '#define' together with either MAX_PATH or PATH_MAX?
interview.answer: Run git grep -e '#define' --and \( -e MAX_PATH -e PATH_MAX \). Several -e patterns are joined with OR by default, and --and binds more tightly than --or, so the escaped parentheses are needed to group the two alternatives.
interview.followUp: What does --all-match do differently? It works at the file level: it only shows OR-matched lines from files that contain a match for every pattern, while --and requires all patterns on the same line.

interview.question: How would you use git grep in a CI script to fail the build if a forbidden string exists?
interview.answer: Use git grep -q pattern and check the exit status. -q prints nothing and returns 0 when something matches and a non-zero status when nothing does. Put -e before the pattern if it could start with a dash.
interview.followUp: How do you check only the staged content in a pre-commit hook? Add --cached, so the search reads the index blobs instead of the working-tree files, which may contain changes that aren't staged.

keyPoints: --cached searches what is staged rather than what is on disk, so you can check the exact content your next commit will contain.
If you pass a commit, tag or tree name, Git searches that snapshot directly, so you can search old releases without switching branches.
--untracked adds untracked files to the search. Ignored files are still skipped unless you also pass --no-exclude-standard.
You can combine patterns with --and, --or, --not and escaped parentheses. OR is the default, and AND binds more tightly than OR.
Pathspecs narrow the search to certain paths. They accept globs such as '*.[ch]' and exclusions such as ':^Documentation'.
-W prints the whole function that contains each match, and -p prints only the function's header line. Both find functions the same way git diff finds hunk headers.
Patterns are POSIX basic regular expressions unless you pass -E, -F or -P, or set a different grep.patternType in your config.
-q makes git grep usable as a check in scripts: it prints nothing and reports through its exit status whether anything matched.
gotchas: -P (Perl regex) only works if your Git build includes PCRE support. Without it, git grep exits with an error instead of searching.
A pattern that starts with a dash is read as an option. Put -e in front of it, and always use -e in scripts that pass in user input.
If you search the index or a tree with --textconv, multiple threads can be slower than one. In that case try --threads=1.
--no-index cannot be combined with --cached or --untracked.

git init.summary: git init creates a new, empty Git repository, or reinitializes one that already exists. It is usually the first command you run to put a project under version control.
git init.explanation: git init builds the repository skeleton, which is normally a .git directory. It holds the object store, refs/heads and refs/tags, plus files copied from a template directory. It also creates an initial branch with no commits yet. You can set GIT_DIR to put the repository somewhere other than ./.git, and GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY to choose where objects are stored. If you pass a directory, Git runs inside it and creates it if needed. Options also control the hash algorithm, the ref storage format, the initial branch name and group-sharing permissions.

parameters.name: -q, --quiet
parameters.description: Prints only errors and warnings; all other output is hidden.

parameters.name: --bare
parameters.description: Creates a bare repository, which has no working tree. If GIT_DIR is unset, the current directory is used.

parameters.name: --template=<template-directory>
parameters.description: The directory whose template files are copied into the new repository.

parameters.name: --separate-git-dir=<git-dir>
parameters.description: Stores the repository at <git-dir> and leaves a small text file pointing to it where .git would normally be.

parameters.name: --object-format=<format>
parameters.description: The hash algorithm for the repository. sha1 is the default; sha256 only works if enabled.

parameters.name: --ref-format=<format>
parameters.description: How refs are stored: files (loose files plus packed-refs, the default) or reftable.

parameters.name: -b, --initial-branch=<branch-name>
parameters.description: The name of the first branch in the new repository.

parameters.name: --shared[=<permissions>]
parameters.type: false | true | umask | group | all | world | everybody | 0xxx
parameters.description: Makes the repository shareable by several users by setting core.sharedRepository. With no value it means group.

parameters.name: <directory>
parameters.description: The directory to run in; it is created if it does not exist.

example.title: Start a repo with a chosen branch name, plus a bare remote
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Bare repository to act as a shared remote
git init --bare --initial-branch=main /tmp/demo-remote.git

# New working repository (directory is created automatically)
git init -b main /tmp/demo-app
cd /tmp/demo-app

echo "# Demo" > README.md
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"

git remote add origin /tmp/demo-remote.git
git push -u origin main

# Safe to rerun: existing data is left alone
git init
example.explanation: The script creates a bare remote and a working repository, both starting on main, makes a first commit, pushes it, and then runs git init again to show that rerunning is harmless.

useCases.title: Version an existing project
useCases.scenario: A folder of code that was never tracked gets a repository; then you run git add . and git commit to record its starting state.

useCases.title: Central push target
useCases.scenario: An admin creates a bare repository on a server, using --shared=group so team members can push to it.

useCases.title: Keep repository data outside the work tree
useCases.scenario: With --separate-git-dir, the project folder holds only a pointer file, and the actual repository lives on another disk or path.

useCases.title: Standard team setup
useCases.scenario: A company template directory and init.defaultBranch give every new repository the same hooks, exclude patterns and branch name.

interview.question: What is a bare repository, and when would you create one with git init --bare?
interview.answer: A bare repository has no working tree, so there are no checked-out files to edit. With --bare, the repository itself is created in the current directory, or in GIT_DIR if that is set, instead of inside a .git subfolder. It is the usual choice for a central or server repository that people push to and fetch from.
interview.followUp: Why add --shared to a server repository? It sets core.sharedRepository so new files get group-friendly permissions, which lets everyone in the Unix group push. It also turns on receive.denyNonFastForwards by default.

interview.question: What happens if you run git init in a directory that is already a Git repository?
interview.answer: It is safe: Git reinitializes the repository without overwriting anything already there. People mostly do this to pick up newly added template files. It is also how you move the repository elsewhere with --separate-git-dir.
interview.followUp: Does rerunning it turn on the sample hooks? No. Sample hooks stay disabled until you rename each file to drop its .sample suffix.

interview.question: How do you control the name of the first branch in a new repository?
interview.answer: Pass -b <name> or --initial-branch=<name> to git init. To set it for every new repository, use the init.defaultBranch config variable. If you do neither, Git currently uses master, and the docs say this will become main in Git 3.0.
interview.followUp: Which wins between the --object-format option, GIT_DEFAULT_HASH and init.defaultObjectFormat? Both the command-line option and the environment variable take precedence over the config setting.

keyPoints: You can safely run it again inside an existing repository: nothing already there is replaced.
Rerunning it is mainly useful to pick up new template files, or, together with --separate-git-dir, to move the repository to another location.
With --bare and no GIT_DIR set, the current directory itself becomes the repository. This is the usual setup for a central repository that others push to.
With --separate-git-dir, .git becomes a plain text file that points to where the repository data actually lives.
If you give a target directory that does not exist yet, git init creates it for you.
Only template entries whose names do not start with a dot are copied into the new repository directory.
With --shared, people in the same Unix group can push to the repository.
Unless you choose otherwise, refs are stored in the traditional files format; reftable is an opt-in alternative.
gotchas: If you don't pass -b, the first branch is named master. Git 3.0 will change this default to main, so set init.defaultBranch or -b if you need a predictable name.
Choosing sha256 is a lasting decision: SHA-256 and SHA-1 repositories cannot currently exchange data with each other.
Shared repositories reject force pushes that are not fast-forwards by default, which can surprise people used to rewriting history.
The sample hooks copied from the templates do nothing until you rename each one to drop its .sample suffix.

git log.summary: git log shows commit history. It lists the commits you can reach from the starting points you give, newest first, and you can filter, order and format that list.
git log.explanation: Git starts from the revisions you name, or HEAD if you name none, and follows parent links back through history. Anything reachable from a revision marked with ^ (or placed after --not) is taken out of the result. The A..B form means ^A B, and A...B returns commits on either side but not both. Limiting options such as path filters, dates, authors and message patterns narrow that set. Ordering and formatting options then control how it prints. git log accepts git rev-list options for choosing commits and git diff options for showing each commit's changes.

parameters.name: <options>
parameters.description: Options for limiting, simplifying, ordering and formatting commits, taken from rev-list, plus diff options that control how each commit's changes are shown.

parameters.name: <revision-range>
parameters.description: Shows only commits in this range, for example origin..HEAD. If you leave it out, it defaults to HEAD, which is all history leading to the current commit.

parameters.name: [--] <path>…
parameters.description: Keeps only the commits needed to explain how the matching files reached their current state. Put -- in front when a path could be confused with an option or a revision.

git log.returns: Prints the selected commits to standard output, newest first by default, in the chosen pretty format (medium by default). Diff output can be added with options such as -p or --stat.

example.title: Review what your branch has that upstream lacks
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Commits on my branch that are not on origin/main, compact view
git log --oneline --no-merges origin/main..HEAD

# Same range, with per-file stats, only commits by me in the last 2 weeks
git log --stat --author="$(git config user.name)" --since="2 weeks ago" origin/main..HEAD

# History of one file, following renames, custom format
git log --follow --format='%h %ad %an %s' --date=short -- src/app.ts

# How a function evolved over time
git log -L :handleRequest:src/server.ts

# Mainline-only overview as a graph
git log --first-parent --graph --oneline -20
example.explanation: The script uses ranges, author and date filters, rename-following path history, function tracing with -L and a first-parent graph to show the most common ways to filter and format git log output.

useCases.title: Pre-push review
useCases.scenario: Run git log origin/main..HEAD before pushing or opening a pull request to see exactly which local commits will go out.

useCases.title: Blame-style archaeology
useCases.scenario: Use --follow on one file, or -L on a function, to find when and why a piece of code changed, even if it was renamed.

useCases.title: Release notes
useCases.scenario: List the non-merge commits between two tags in a custom --format to draft a changelog.

useCases.title: Recovering lost work
useCases.scenario: Use git log -g to walk the reflog and find commits that no branch points to anymore after a reset or rebase.

interview.question: What is the difference between git log A..B and git log A...B?
interview.answer: A..B is shorthand for ^A B: it shows commits reachable from B but not from A, which is what B has that A doesn't. A...B is the symmetric difference: commits reachable from either side but not from both. That is the same as listing A and B and excluding their merge base(s).
interview.followUp: How can you tell which side each commit in A...B came from? Add --left-right to mark commits with < or >, or use --left-only/--right-only to show one side; --cherry-pick also hides commits whose patch already exists on the other side.

interview.question: Why might git log -- path miss a commit you know changed that file, and how do you fix it?
interview.answer: By default git log simplifies history. When a merge is TREESAME to one of its parents for that path, Git follows only that parent and never looks at the other side. Commits that only existed on that other side drop out. --full-history follows every parent, and --simplify-merges or --show-pulls cut that output down to the merges that actually matter.
interview.followUp: What does --simplify-merges cost? Before it can print a single result it must walk the entire commit history, which makes it slow on very large repositories.

interview.question: How would you list commits by a given author, from the last week, whose message mentions 'fix', in one line each?
interview.answer: Use git log --oneline --author=<pattern> --since='1 week ago' --grep=fix. Each extra limiting option narrows the result further. --author and --grep take regular expressions, and -i makes them case-insensitive.
interview.followUp: If you pass two --grep patterns, does a commit need to match both? No. A match on any one pattern is enough by default; add --all-match to require all of them, or --invert-grep to keep commits that do not match.

keyPoints: Treat the arguments as set math. Start with every commit reachable from the positive revisions, then remove every commit reachable from the ones marked with ^.
A...B (three dots) lists commits that are on one side or the other but not both. Combine it with --left-only or --right-only to see a single side.
--follow keeps tracing a file's history back past renames, but it only accepts one file.
If you pass --grep more than once, a commit is kept when any pattern matches. Add --all-match to keep only commits that match every pattern.
--first-parent follows only the first parent of each merge. On a mainline branch this hides the individual commits that came in through merged topic branches.
--topo-order shows children before their parents and keeps parallel lines of development from being mixed together in the output.
-L<start>,<end>:<file> or -L:<funcname>:<file> follows how a range of lines or a single function changed over time. It turns on patch output automatically.
gotchas: Filters such as -n are applied before ordering. So `git log -n 3 --reverse` reverses the 3 newest commits; it does not show the 3 oldest.
--since stops walking at the first commit older than the date, so commits with out-of-order timestamps can be missed. --since-as-filter checks every commit in the range instead.
With -g/--walk-reflogs, git log walks reflog entries instead of ancestry, and you cannot use ^, .. or ... to exclude commits.
The default history simplification for a path can hide commits that really changed the file. Use --full-history, --simplify-merges or --show-pulls to see them.

git ls-files.summary: git ls-files is a low-level (plumbing) command that lists files by comparing what's in Git's index with what's in your working directory. Flags pick which groups to show: tracked, modified, deleted, untracked, ignored or unmerged.
git ls-files.explanation: The command reads the index (the staging area) and can also walk the working tree, then prints the paths that match the selection flags you give. If you pass no selection flag it acts like --cached and lists every tracked path. Other modes compare the index with the filesystem to find deleted, modified, untracked or conflicting paths. By default the output is just paths, relative to the current directory. --stage adds mode, object ID and stage number, and --format lets you build each line yourself from fields. If you list paths after the options, only those paths are shown.

parameters.name: -c, --cached
parameters.description: List every tracked file in the index. This is the default when no other mode is chosen.

parameters.name: -d, --deleted / -m, --modified
parameters.description: List tracked files that have an unstaged deletion or an unstaged modification.

parameters.name: -o, --others
parameters.description: List untracked files.

parameters.name: -i, --ignored
parameters.description: Only list files that match exclude patterns. You must also give -c or -o.

parameters.name: -s, --stage
parameters.description: Add the mode bits, object name and stage number to each line.

parameters.name: -u, --unmerged
parameters.description: Only list unmerged (conflicted) entries. Turns on --stage.

parameters.name: -z
parameters.description: End each entry with a NUL byte and print filenames without quoting.

parameters.name: --exclude-standard
parameters.description: Use the normal ignore sources: .git/info/exclude, every .gitignore, and the user's global excludes file.

parameters.name: --error-unmatch
parameters.description: Fail with exit status 1 if any <file> given is not in the index.

parameters.name: --format=<format>
parameters.description: Build each line from %(fieldname) placeholders such as objectname, objectmode, stage and path.

parameters.name: --full-name
parameters.description: Print paths relative to the repository root instead of the current directory.

parameters.name: <file>
parameters.description: Only show these paths. If none are given, every matching file is shown.

git ls-files.returns: Writes the selected paths to stdout, one per line by default. With --stage each line is '[<tag> ]<mode> <object> <stage> <file>'. With --error-unmatch the exit status is 1 if any given path is missing from the index.

example.title: Inspecting the index and the working tree
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# All tracked files, with paths relative to the repo root
git ls-files --full-name

# Untracked files that are not ignored, one entry per untracked directory
git ls-files --others --exclude-standard --directory

# Ignored files currently in the working tree
git ls-files --others --ignored --exclude-standard

# Index entries with object id and stage number
git ls-files --format='%(objectmode) %(objectname) %(stage)	%(path)'

# Conflicted entries during a merge (stages 1-3)
git ls-files --unmerged

# Check whether a path is tracked (exit status 1 if not)
if git ls-files --error-unmatch README.md >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "README.md is tracked"
fi

# Pass filenames safely to another tool using NUL separators
git ls-files -z -- '*.py' | xargs -0 wc -l
example.explanation: The script lists tracked, untracked and ignored files, shows index entries and merge conflicts, checks whether a file is tracked, and passes tracked filenames safely to another tool.

useCases.title: Feeding linters and formatters
useCases.scenario: A CI job uses `git ls-files -z -- '*.ts'` to get only the tracked TypeScript files, so build output and other untracked files are skipped, and filenames with spaces still work.

useCases.title: Finding stray untracked files
useCases.scenario: Before cutting a release, run `git ls-files -o --exclude-standard` to spot new files nobody has added yet, while leaving out anything .gitignore covers.

useCases.title: Debugging a merge conflict
useCases.scenario: While resolving a conflict, use `git ls-files -u` to see the base, ours and theirs blob IDs for each conflicted path.

useCases.title: Auditing line endings
useCases.scenario: Run `git ls-files --eol` to find files saved with CRLF or mixed endings and see which text/eol attributes apply to them.

interview.question: What does git ls-files print when you give it no options, and how does that differ from git ls-tree?
interview.answer: With no mode flag it acts like --cached and prints every tracked path in the index, relative to the current directory. git ls-tree lists the contents of a tree object, such as a commit's tree. ls-files reflects the current index, including staged changes that are not committed yet.
interview.followUp: How would you print object IDs along with the paths? Use `git ls-files -s` (mode, object, stage, path) or `--format='%(objectname) %(path)'`.

interview.question: How do you list ignored files with git ls-files?
interview.answer: Combine -i with -o (or with -c to find tracked files that match ignore rules), and add an exclude source such as --exclude-standard. -i does not load ignore rules on its own, so leaving out the exclude option gives no useful result.
interview.followUp: Which files does --exclude-standard read? .git/info/exclude, the .gitignore in each directory, and the user's global excludes file (core.excludesfile or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/ignore).

interview.question: How can you check in a script whether a given path is tracked?
interview.answer: Run `git ls-files --error-unmatch <path>`. It exits with status 1 if the path is not in the index, so the exit code tells you the answer. Send its output to /dev/null if you only care about the status.
interview.followUp: Why use -z when you pipe ls-files output to other tools? Without -z, unusual filenames are quoted according to core.quotePath. With -z they are printed as-is and separated by NUL, which works with `xargs -0`.

keyPoints: The same path can appear more than once in the output, for example when a conflicted file has several index stages or when it fits more than one of the modes you asked for.
--deduplicate removes repeated names when only filenames are printed. It does nothing when -t, --unmerged or --stage is used.
For a conflicted path the index can hold up to three versions: stage 1 is the common ancestor, stage 2 is one side, and stage 3 is the other. --stage and --unmerged show all of them.

-t puts a one-letter status tag before each path, for example H (tracked), S (skip-worktree), M (unmerged), R (removed), C (changed) and ? (untracked). -v does the same but uses lowercase for files marked assume-unchanged.
--directory prints an untracked directory once, as its name with a trailing slash, instead of listing every file inside it. It only matters together with --others.
--eol shows the line-ending type of each file in the index (i/) and in the working tree (w/), plus the text/eol attribute that applies to it.
--recurse-submodules runs ls-files inside each active submodule as well, but this only works with the --cached and --stage modes.
gotchas: -i/--ignored does not read .gitignore by itself. Without an --exclude* option (usually --exclude-standard) nothing counts as ignored.
A file whose deletion is unstaged shows up under both -d and -m, because a deletion also counts as a modification.
--format cannot be combined with several other output options.

git merge.summary: git merge brings the changes from one or more named commits, usually branch tips, into the current branch. Depending on the history, it either moves the branch pointer forward (a fast-forward) or records a new merge commit with several parents.
git merge.explanation: Git finds the merge base, which is the point where the two histories split. If your branch tip is an ancestor of the target, Git simply moves HEAD forward to it. If not, the strategy (ort by default) runs a 3-way merge using the base and both tips, then commits the result with every merged tip as a parent. If some changes cannot be reconciled automatically, HEAD stays where it was, MERGE_HEAD records the other tip, and conflict markers are written into the files. You fix them, git add the files, and finish with git merge --continue or git commit. ORIG_HEAD is saved before the merge starts, so you can find your way back.

parameters.name: <commit>...
parameters.description: The commits to merge in, usually other branch heads. If you give more than one, you get an octopus merge. If you give none, Git merges the upstream that the current branch is configured to track.

parameters.name: --ff / --no-ff / --ff-only
parameters.description: Controls what happens when a fast-forward is possible: fast-forward (the default), always create a merge commit, or allow only a fast-forward and fail otherwise.

parameters.name: --no-commit
parameters.description: Does the merge but stops just before creating the merge commit, so you can inspect or adjust the result first.

parameters.name: --squash
parameters.description: Puts the merged result into the index and working tree but does not commit, move HEAD or record MERGE_HEAD.

parameters.name: -s, --strategy=<strategy>
parameters.description: The merge strategy to use: ort, resolve, octopus, ours or subtree (recursive is now an alias for ort).

parameters.name: -X, --strategy-option=<option>
parameters.description: An option passed to the strategy, e.g. ours, theirs, ignore-space-change, renormalize, find-renames or diff-algorithm.

parameters.name: -m <msg> / -F <file>
parameters.description: The message for the merge commit, given inline or read from a file (only used if a merge commit is created).

parameters.name: --allow-unrelated-histories
parameters.description: Lets Git merge histories that have no common ancestor.

parameters.name: --autostash
parameters.description: Stashes local changes before the merge and reapplies them afterwards.

parameters.name: --abort / --continue / --quit
parameters.description: For a merge that has stopped: undo it and restore the pre-merge state, finish it after resolving conflicts, or forget it while leaving the index and working tree as they are.

git merge.returns: Exit status 0 on success. A non-zero status when a conflict stops the merge, or when --ff-only cannot fast-forward. If all named commits are already in HEAD's history, it prints "Already up to date."

example.title: Merge a feature branch with --no-ff and handle a conflict
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(mktemp -d)" && git init -q -b main demo && cd demo
git config user.name dev && git config user.email dev@example.com

echo "greeting=hello" > app.conf
git add app.conf && git commit -qm "initial"

git switch -qc feature
echo "greeting=hi" > app.conf
git commit -qam "feature: change greeting"

git switch -q main
echo "greeting=hey" > app.conf
git commit -qam "main: change greeting"

# Try the merge; it stops on a conflict
if ! git merge --no-ff feature -m "Merge feature"; then
  git status --short            # shows: UU app.conf
  git show :1:app.conf          # common ancestor version
  echo "greeting=hi" > app.conf # resolve by hand
  git add app.conf
  GIT_EDITOR=true git merge --continue
fi

git log --oneline --graph --all
example.explanation: The script builds two branches that edit the same line, merges them with --no-ff, looks at the base version from index stage 1, resolves the conflict by hand, and finishes with git merge --continue.

useCases.title: Integrating a finished feature
useCases.scenario: After review, run git merge --no-ff feature on main so the feature appears as a single merge commit with its own commits kept beneath it.

useCases.title: Syncing with upstream without accidental merges
useCases.scenario: After git fetch, run git merge --ff-only origin/main to update a local branch that has no commits of its own. If it has diverged, the command fails instead of creating a merge commit.

useCases.title: Superseding an obsolete branch
useCases.scenario: Run git merge -s ours old-experiment to record the old branch as merged while keeping your tree exactly as it is.

useCases.title: Combining two independent repositories
useCases.scenario: Fetch the other project and run git merge --allow-unrelated-histories other/main to join two histories that share no ancestor.

interview.question: What is the difference between a fast-forward merge and a true merge, and how do you control which one happens?
interview.answer: If the current branch tip is an ancestor of the commit being merged, Git can fast-forward: it moves HEAD and the index to that commit without creating a new commit. Otherwise it does a true merge, which records a new commit whose parents are both tips. By default Git fast-forwards when it can. --no-ff forces a merge commit, and --ff-only refuses anything that is not a fast-forward. The merge.ff config setting chooses the default.
interview.followUp: Why can merging an annotated tag create a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible? Git always creates a merge commit for annotated tags so the tag message (and its signature check) goes into the commit. To avoid that, merge tag^0 or use --ff-only.

interview.question: What happens during a conflict, and what are your options for getting out of it?
interview.answer: HEAD stays where it was, and MERGE_HEAD points to the other tip. Files that merged cleanly are updated. Conflicted files get <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> markers, and the index keeps stages 1, 2 and 3 for the base, ours and theirs. You can edit the files, git add them and finish with git merge --continue or git commit. You can run git merge --abort to restore the pre-merge state, or git merge --quit to stop tracking the merge while leaving the files as they are.
interview.followUp: How can you see the original base text inside the conflict markers? Set merge.conflictStyle to diff3 or zdiff3; Git then adds a ||||||| section showing the common ancestor's text.

interview.question: How does git merge --squash differ from a normal merge?
interview.answer: --squash prepares the same working tree and index a real merge would, but it does not commit, does not move HEAD and does not write MERGE_HEAD. When you commit afterwards, you get a normal single-parent commit. Git therefore does not record the branch as merged, and the branch's commits are not part of the new commit's ancestry. You cannot combine --squash with --commit.
interview.followUp: Why might merging the same branch again after a squash cause conflicts? The squash commit is not linked to the branch's history, so the merge base is still the old split point and Git tries to apply those changes a second time.

keyPoints: --ff-only is a safe way to update a branch: Git moves the pointer forward only when it can, and fails instead of creating a merge commit.
--no-ff always creates a merge commit, so the history shows that the feature was developed on its own branch.
--squash lets you land a whole branch as one ordinary commit, which you then create yourself with git commit.
If you name several branches at once, Git creates an octopus merge. The octopus strategy handles this and refuses merges that would need manual conflict resolution.
When merging a single branch, the default strategy is ort. It handles renames and builds a virtual base when the branches have more than one common ancestor.
While a conflict is open, the index holds the base, ours and theirs versions of each conflicted file. You can view them with git show :1:file, :2:file and :3:file.
Git refuses to start a merge if your staged changes differ from HEAD, so unrelated work cannot slip into the merge commit.
Joining two projects that were started separately requires --allow-unrelated-histories. There is deliberately no config setting to make this the default.
gotchas: If you start a merge with uncommitted changes, --abort may not be able to restore them, so commit or stash first.
--no-commit cannot pause a fast-forward, because a fast-forward never creates a commit. Use --no-ff together with --no-commit.
A 3-way merge only looks at the two tips and the base. A change made on both branches and later reverted on only one of them will still appear in the merged result.
The ours strategy (-s ours) throws away everything the other branch did. The -X ours option only picks our side for conflicting hunks.

git mv.summary: git mv renames or moves a tracked file, directory or symlink in your working tree. In the same step it records that change in the index (staging area).
git mv.explanation: The command has two forms. If you give one source and one destination, Git renames the source to the destination path. If the last argument is a directory that already exists, Git moves every listed source into that directory. Each move happens on disk and in the index together, so you don't need a separate git add or git rm. Nothing goes into history until you commit. Options control how it behaves: -f overwrites an existing destination, -k skips moves that would fail, -n only shows what would happen, and -v prints each name as it is moved. For submodules, it also updates the gitfile, core.worktree and the path setting in .gitmodules.

parameters.name: <source>
parameters.description: The file, directory or symlink to rename or move. It must exist and be tracked by Git. The second form accepts several sources.

parameters.name: <destination>
parameters.description: The new name for a single source (first form).

parameters.name: <destination-directory>
parameters.description: An existing directory that all the listed sources are moved into (second form).

parameters.name: -f, --force
parameters.description: Rename or move even when the destination already exists, overwriting it.

parameters.name: -k
parameters.description: Skip any move or rename that would cause an error and carry on with the others.

parameters.name: -n, --dry-run
parameters.description: Change nothing; only show what would be done.

parameters.name: -v, --verbose
parameters.description: Print the name of each file as it is moved.

example.title: Rename a file and move several files into a folder
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Rename a single tracked file
git mv README.txt README.md

# Preview a bulk move first
mkdir -p docs
git mv -n -v guide.md faq.md docs/

# Perform it, skipping anything that would error
git mv -k -v guide.md faq.md docs/

# Changes are staged; inspect and commit
git status --short
git commit -m "Rename README and move docs into docs/"
example.explanation: The script renames one file, previews a bulk move into an existing directory, runs the move while skipping any failures, and then commits the staged result.

useCases.title: Restructuring a project
useCases.scenario: Move a group of source files into a new package directory in one command, so that the commit records the files as moved.

useCases.title: Fixing a file name
useCases.scenario: Rename a misnamed config or documentation file without having to delete it and add it again by hand.

useCases.title: Relocating a submodule
useCases.scenario: Move a vendored submodule to another path and have Git update its gitfile and the .gitmodules entry for you.

interview.question: What does git mv do that a plain shell mv doesn't?
interview.answer: A shell mv only changes files on disk. git mv also updates the index, so the old path is removed from staging and the new path is added. Without it, you would have to stage the deletion and the addition yourself before committing.
interview.followUp: Is the rename visible to other people right after git mv? No. Only the index has changed, so the rename stays local until you commit it and push.

interview.question: How do you move several files at once, and what does the destination have to be?
interview.answer: Use the second form: list the sources and put the target directory last. That directory must already exist, and every source is moved into it.
interview.followUp: What if some of the sources are untracked or missing? Without -k the command reports an error. With -k Git skips those entries and moves the rest.

interview.question: What happens when the destination path already exists?
interview.answer: git mv treats this as an error and refuses to overwrite the existing file. -f/--force makes it go ahead and replace the destination. Running with -n first lets you see what would happen.
interview.followUp: Can -k and -f be combined meaningfully? Yes. -f turns an existing destination into an allowed overwrite rather than an error, so -k then only skips the remaining problems, such as sources that don't exist or aren't tracked.

keyPoints: In the single-target form, the source has to exist already, and it can be a regular file, a symlink or a whole directory.
To move several items at once, the last argument must be a directory that already exists. git mv will not create it for you.
The change is staged when the command succeeds. You still need to run git commit to record the rename in history.
By default git mv refuses to overwrite a destination that already exists. Pass -f/--force to overwrite it.
In a bulk move, -k makes Git skip the moves that would fail (for example, untracked or missing sources) and perform the rest.
Use -n/--dry-run to preview a move without touching anything, and -v/--verbose to list each file as it is moved.
If a submodule uses a gitfile (cloned with Git 1.7.8 or newer), git mv fixes up its links so it still works after the move. It also tries to update and stage the path entry in .gitmodules.
gotchas: If you check out commits from before and after a populated submodule was moved, the old checkout is left behind and the new location is just an empty directory.
After that kind of checkout, the submodule at its new location stays empty until you populate it yourself.
Don't delete a leftover submodule directory unless it uses a gitfile, because otherwise you lose the submodule's history.

git notes.summary: git notes lets you attach, read, change and remove extra text (notes) on Git objects, usually commits, without touching the objects. The commit hash stays the same, so you can annotate history that has already been published.
git notes.explanation: Each note is a blob. Notes live in a separate notes ref, which is refs/notes/commits by default. That ref works like a branch whose tree holds files named after the object IDs they annotate, split into two-hex-digit directories for speed. Subcommands such as add, append, edit, show, copy, remove and prune change this tree. git log and git show then print matching notes under a "Notes:" heading after the commit message. You can pick a different notes ref with --ref, GIT_NOTES_REF or core.notesRef, which lets you keep separate groups of notes, such as review notes or build notes.
git notes.syntax: git notes [list [<object>]] | add [-f] [--allow-empty] [-F <file> | -m <msg> | (-c | -C) <object>] [-e] [<object>] | append ... | edit [<object>] | show [<object>] | copy [-f] (--stdin | <from-object> [<to-object>]) | merge [-s <strategy>] <notes-ref> | remove [--ignore-missing] [--stdin] [<object>...] | prune [-n] [-v] | get-ref

parameters.name: <object>
parameters.description: The object the note is attached to. Most subcommands default to HEAD.

parameters.name: -m <msg> / --message=<msg>
parameters.description: Sets the note text. If you give it more than once, each value becomes its own paragraph.

parameters.name: -F <file> / --file=<file>
parameters.description: Reads the note text from a file. Use '-' to read from standard input.

parameters.name: -C / -c <object>
parameters.description: Uses an existing blob as the note text. -C copies it word for word; -c opens it in an editor first.

parameters.name: -f / --force
parameters.description: Replaces an existing note instead of stopping with an error.

parameters.name: --allow-empty
parameters.description: Keeps an empty note. Without it, empty notes are removed automatically.

parameters.name: --separator[=<paragraph-break>] / --no-separator
parameters.description: Sets the text placed between paragraphs. The default is a blank line.

parameters.name: --[no-]stripspace
parameters.description: Turns whitespace cleanup on or off. It is on by default, except with -C.

parameters.name: --ref=<ref>
parameters.description: Works on this notes ref instead of the default one. Overrides GIT_NOTES_REF and core.notesRef.

parameters.name: -s <strategy> / --strategy=<strategy>
parameters.description: Sets how merge resolves conflicting notes.

parameters.name: --stdin
parameters.description: Reads object names (for remove) or object pairs (for copy) from standard input.

parameters.name: -n / --dry-run
parameters.description: For prune: lists the notes that would be removed without removing them.

example.title: Annotate a commit, append to the note, and use a separate notes ref
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Attach a note to HEAD without changing its hash
git notes add -m 'Tested-by: CI pipeline #482'

# Add another paragraph to the same note
git notes append -m 'Perf: p95 latency 120ms'

# Print the note, and see it in the log
git notes show HEAD
git log -1

# Keep review notes in their own ref (refs/notes/review)
git notes --ref=review add -m 'LGTM - alice' HEAD
git log -1 --notes=review

# Show which notes ref is currently in use
git notes get-ref

# Keep notes when amending/rebasing
git config notes.rewriteRef refs/notes/commits

# Preview removal of notes on objects that no longer exist
git notes prune -n -v
example.explanation: This script adds a note to a commit and appends to it, keeps review notes in a separate ref, turns on note copying for amend and rebase, and previews a prune.

useCases.title: After-the-fact sign-offs
useCases.scenario: Add Tested-by or Reviewed-by lines to commits that are already published, without rewriting history or changing hashes.

useCases.title: CI and build metadata
useCases.scenario: Store build results, test reports or artifact blobs in a dedicated ref such as refs/notes/built, so they never clutter commit messages.

useCases.title: Patch cover commentary
useCases.scenario: Keep per-commit explanations as notes, then include them below the '---' line of emailed patches with git format-patch --notes.

useCases.title: Team annotations
useCases.scenario: Different teams keep separate notes refs and combine them with git notes merge, using a strategy such as union or cat_sort_uniq.

interview.question: How do git notes differ from amending a commit message?
interview.answer: Amending creates a new commit with a new hash, which rewrites history. A note is stored as a separate blob in a notes ref, so the original commit stays exactly the same. git log still shows the note under a 'Notes:' heading, which is why notes work for annotating commits that are already published.
interview.followUp: How are notes stored internally? The notes ref points to a commit whose tree has files named after the annotated object IDs, split into two-hex-digit directories for speed; each file is the note blob.

interview.question: What happens if you run 'git notes add' on a commit that already has a note?
interview.answer: With -m or -F it stops with an error, so nothing is overwritten by accident. Use -f to replace the note, or use append to add text to it. If you run add with no message, it opens the existing note in your editor, the same way edit does.
interview.followUp: How do you delete a note, and what happens with an empty message? Use git notes remove (add --ignore-missing to skip objects that have no note). Saving an empty message has the same effect, because empty notes are removed unless you pass --allow-empty.

interview.question: How do you resolve conflicts when merging two notes refs?
interview.answer: git notes merge <notes-ref> uses the manual strategy by default. It checks out the conflicting notes into .git/NOTES_MERGE_WORKTREE so you can fix them by hand. You then run git notes merge --commit to finish or --abort to cancel. You can also pick ours, theirs, union or cat_sort_uniq with -s or the notes.mergeStrategy setting.
interview.followUp: Can you set a different strategy for each notes ref? Yes: notes.<name>.mergeStrategy applies to merges into refs/notes/<name> and takes priority over the general notes.mergeStrategy setting.

keyPoints: If the notes ref does not exist yet, you don't need to create it. Git creates it automatically when you store your first note.
Running 'git notes' with no subcommand runs 'list'. Without an object, list prints every pair of note blob and annotated object.
Use append when you want to add to a note instead of replacing it. Each new message goes after the existing text with a separator between them. If there is no note yet, append creates one.
Notes have their own history: every change commits to the notes ref, so you can review it with git log -p on that ref.
git notes merge brings another notes ref into the current one. Besides the default manual mode, you can choose ours, theirs, union or cat_sort_uniq to resolve conflicts automatically.
prune removes notes whose target objects no longer exist or can't be reached. Add -n to preview what would go.
notes.displayRef controls which extra notes refs git log shows. A ref that doesn't exist gives a warning, but a glob that matches nothing is ignored.
gotchas: Notes are not copied to new commits on amend or rebase unless you set notes.rewriteRef (for example to refs/notes/commits). Without it, rewritten commits lose their notes.
-F is not safe for binary files. To attach binary data, store it with git hash-object -w and attach the blob with -C.
Whether whitespace is cleaned up depends on the order of options. For example, a -m that comes after -C turns cleanup back on.
cat_sort_uniq removes all duplicate lines, including duplicates that were already inside the local or remote note before the merge.

git pull.summary: git pull brings changes from another repository, or from a local branch, into the branch you have checked out. It runs a fetch and then integrates the fetched branch by fast-forwarding, rebasing, merging or squashing.
git pull.explanation: git pull runs in two stages. First it calls git fetch with the same arguments, leaving out merge-only options, to download objects and update remote-tracking refs. Next it chooses a branch to integrate. Branches named on the command line win; otherwise Git uses the current branch's configured upstream (branch.<name>.remote and branch.<name>.merge). Last, it integrates that branch. By default it only allows a fast-forward. You can choose another method with --rebase, --no-rebase (merge) or --squash, or set it once with pull.rebase, pull.squash or pull.ff.

parameters.name: <repository>
parameters.description: The repository to pull from. If you leave it out, Git uses the current branch's upstream, or origin.

parameters.name: <refspec>
parameters.description: The ref or refs to fetch and integrate, such as main in `git pull origin main`. If you leave it out, Git uses the configured upstream.

parameters.name: --ff-only
parameters.description: Update only when the local branch has not diverged from the remote. This is the default when no method is chosen.

parameters.name: --rebase[=(true|merges|false|interactive)]
parameters.description: Rebase the current branch onto the upstream after fetching. merges keeps local merge commits, false merges instead, and interactive opens an interactive rebase.

parameters.name: --no-rebase
parameters.description: Short form of --rebase=false. The fetched branch is merged.

parameters.name: --squash
parameters.description: Put the merged result in the working tree and index without committing or recording MERGE_HEAD.

parameters.name: --autostash
parameters.description: Stash local changes before the operation and apply them again when it finishes.

parameters.name: -s <strategy> / -X <option>
parameters.description: Pick the merge strategy, or pass an option to the strategy.

example.title: Pull safely, then rebase if the branches have diverged
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Optional: make rebase the default way to pull in this repo
git config pull.rebase true

# Try a fast-forward first; fall back to a rebase if branches diverged
if ! git pull --ff-only origin main; then
  echo "Branches diverged; rebasing local commits onto origin/main"
  git pull --rebase --autostash origin main
fi

# Same thing in two steps: fetch, then merge
git fetch origin
git merge --ff-only origin/main

git log --oneline -5
example.explanation: The script tries a fast-forward pull first and rebases (stashing any uncommitted work) only when the branches have diverged. It then shows the same update done as a separate fetch and merge.

useCases.title: Daily sync with upstream
useCases.scenario: Before you start work on a tracked feature branch, run a bare `git pull` so the branch matches its upstream without merge commits.

useCases.title: Linear history before pushing
useCases.scenario: Your push was rejected because others pushed first. Run `git pull --rebase` to replay your unpublished commits on top of theirs, then push again.

useCases.title: Merging a contributor's branch
useCases.scenario: A maintainer runs `git pull <URL> <branch>` to fetch a contributor's branch and merge it in one step.

useCases.title: Deepening a shallow clone
useCases.scenario: Run pull with --depth, --deepen or --unshallow to fetch more history into a shallow CI checkout while still updating the branch.

interview.question: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
interview.answer: git fetch only downloads objects and updates remote-tracking refs such as origin/main. Your current branch stays where it is. git pull runs that same fetch and then integrates the chosen remote branch into your current branch. `git pull origin next` is roughly the same as `git fetch origin` followed by `git merge origin/next`.
interview.followUp: Which merge options does pull pass to the fetch step? None. Pull hands fetch the same arguments minus the merge-related options, and uses those options only when it integrates.

interview.question: What happens when you run git pull on a branch that has diverged from its upstream, with no pull settings configured?
interview.answer: Pull's default is fast-forward only, so it fails and leaves your branch as it was. You need to say how to reconcile the branches. Use --rebase to replay your commits on the upstream, --no-rebase to create a merge, or set pull.rebase or pull.ff in your config.
interview.followUp: How do you get out of a pull that ended in conflicts you don't want to resolve? Run `git merge --abort` or `git rebase --abort`, depending on how pull integrated. After a messy pull you can also go back to an earlier state with git reset.

interview.question: Which branch does a bare git pull integrate?
interview.answer: It uses the current branch's upstream, set by branch.<name>.remote and branch.<name>.merge. Without those it falls back to origin and the configured remote.<origin>.fetch refspecs. If branch.<name>.merge is missing, it integrates the first configured refspec. If that refspec is a glob, nothing is integrated.
interview.followUp: Why is listing two branches on the command line different from configuring two fetch refspecs? Branches named on the command line are all merged, which gives an octopus merge. Configured refspecs are all fetched, but only the first is merged.

keyPoints: Unless you configure it otherwise, a plain pull only fast-forwards. If your branch and the remote have diverged, it stops and makes no changes. You then choose rebase or merge explicitly.
With no repository argument, pull uses the current branch's configured upstream. If there is none, it falls back to origin.
Every branch you name on the command line is integrated. Naming two or more remote refs creates an octopus merge.
When pull relies only on a configured globbing fetch refspec and no branch.<name>.merge is set, it fetches but integrates nothing.
When pull merges a single branch, it uses the ort strategy by default. ort is a 3-way merge that also detects renames.
`git pull origin next` gives the same result as running `git fetch origin` and then `git merge origin/next`. The fetched tip is also kept for a while in FETCH_HEAD.
With --autostash, pull will run even when you have uncommitted changes. Git stashes them first and applies them again afterwards.
gotchas: --rebase rewrites your local commits. Do not use it on history that other people already have.
--no-commit cannot stop a fast-forward, because a fast-forward makes no merge commit. If the branch must not move, add --no-ff as well.
With --autostash, the merge can succeed but applying the stash afterwards can still cause conflicts.
If the two histories share no common ancestor, pull refuses to merge them unless you pass --allow-unrelated-histories.

git push.summary: git push copies your local commits to a remote repository and moves that remote's branches, tags or other refs to match. It sends only the objects the remote does not already have.
git push.explanation: Git first picks a destination. That is either the remote you name, the current branch's upstream, or origin. Next it decides which refs to push, checking these sources in order: refspecs or flags like --all/--tags on the command line, then remote.<name>.push, then push.default (simple by default). Each refspec has the form [+]<src>[:<dst>] and links a local object to a remote ref. Git sends the objects the remote is missing and asks it to update those refs. The remote applies safety rules, such as allowing only fast-forwards on branches, unless you force the update or a hook or config rejects it.

parameters.name: <repository>
parameters.description: Where to push. This can be a URL, a configured remote, or a remote group. If you leave it out, Git uses the current branch's upstream, or origin.

parameters.name: <refspec>...
parameters.description: Says which source object updates which remote ref. A leading + forces that one ref. An empty <src> deletes <dst>. Patterns with * and exclusions starting with ^ are allowed.

parameters.name: --force-with-lease[=<refname>[:<expect>]]
parameters.description: Forces the update only if the remote ref still has the value you expect. By default, the expected value is your remote-tracking branch.

parameters.name: -u, --set-upstream
parameters.description: Records an upstream (tracking) reference for every branch that is pushed or already up to date.

parameters.name: --tags / --follow-tags
parameters.description: --tags pushes every tag. --follow-tags also pushes missing annotated tags that point at commits being pushed.

parameters.name: -d, --delete
parameters.description: Deletes the listed refs on the remote.

parameters.name: -n, --dry-run
parameters.description: Runs the whole push except actually sending the updates.

example.title: Publish a branch, then safely rewrite it
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(mktemp -d)"

# A bare repo stands in for the server
git init --bare -q server.git
git clone -q server.git work && cd work
git config user.email dev@example.com
git config user.name Dev

git switch -q -c feature
echo one > a.txt && git add a.txt && git commit -qm "first"

# First push: create remote branch and record upstream
git push -u origin feature

# Preview what would happen
git commit -q --amend -m "first (reworded)"
git push --dry-run --force-with-lease origin feature

# Rewrite history safely: fails if someone else moved the branch
git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes origin feature

# Tag a release and push it with its commit
git tag -a v1.0 -m "v1.0"
git push --follow-tags

# Clean up the remote branch
git push origin --delete feature
example.explanation: The script creates a local bare remote, publishes a branch with an upstream, previews and then performs a lease-protected force push, pushes an annotated tag along with its commit, and finally deletes the remote branch.

useCases.title: Sharing a new feature branch
useCases.scenario: You push a new branch with -u so your teammates can see it and later pull and push commands need no arguments.

useCases.title: Updating a rebased pull request
useCases.scenario: After an interactive rebase, you use --force-with-lease (optionally with --force-if-includes) so you don't overwrite commits a reviewer pushed in the meantime.

useCases.title: Release publishing in CI
useCases.scenario: A pipeline uses --atomic to push a release branch and its tag together, so the remote never ends up with only one of them.

useCases.title: Mirroring a repository
useCases.scenario: --mirror copies every ref under refs/ to a backup server, including forced updates and deletions.

interview.question: What is the difference between --force and --force-with-lease?
interview.answer: --force overwrites the remote ref no matter what it currently points to, so other people's commits can be lost. --force-with-lease only overwrites if the remote ref still has the value you expect. By default that is your remote-tracking branch, but you can give an exact commit with <refname>:<expect>. If someone pushed in the meantime, the push fails and you can fetch and look before trying again.
interview.followUp: Why add --force-if-includes? A background fetch can quietly update your remote-tracking ref, which makes a plain lease pass anyway. --force-if-includes also checks that the remote tip appears in your local branch's reflog, meaning you actually integrated it.

interview.question: Your push is rejected as non-fast-forward. Why, and how do you fix it without losing work?
interview.answer: A branch update is only accepted if the remote's current tip is an ancestor of the commit you push. When someone else has pushed commits you don't have, your push would discard them. Fetch and merge (git pull), or use git pull --rebase to replay your work on top of theirs, then push the result, which is now a fast-forward.
