interview.followUp: When is a plain --force push acceptable? Only when you really mean to replace history, for example after amending a commit you already pushed, and you're sure nobody has fetched or built on the old commit.

interview.question: What does a bare git push do with no arguments?
interview.answer: It pushes to the current branch's remote, or origin if none is set. Because no refspec was given, it checks remote.<name>.push and then push.default. With the default simple mode, it pushes the current branch to a remote branch with the same name, and it errors if you're pushing back to your pull remote and the upstream has a different name.
interview.followUp: How can you avoid passing -u on every new branch? Set push.autoSetupRemote=true, which turns on --set-upstream automatically the first time you push a branch that has no upstream.

keyPoints: --atomic asks the server to update all the refs together: either every ref changes or none does. If the server doesn't support atomic pushes, the whole push fails.
--follow-tags pushes only the annotated tags that point at the commits you're pushing. That keeps release tags with their commits without uploading every local tag.
-u links each pushed branch to its remote branch. After that, plain git pull and git status know which remote branch to compare against.
To remove refs on the remote, use --delete or a refspec with an empty source, such as origin :dev. Both do the same thing.
Tags are treated differently from branches: an existing tag on the remote can't be moved by a normal push. Branch updates must be fast-forwards and must point at commits.
The local pre-push hook runs by default and can stop a push. --no-verify skips it.
The default push.default mode, simple, pushes the current branch to a remote branch with the same name.
gotchas: --force-with-lease with no explicit expected value compares against your remote-tracking refs. If something runs git fetch in the background (an IDE or a cron job, for example), those refs get updated and the protection is lost.
--force turns off the ancestry check, the other push rules and any lease checks, so commits on the remote can be lost.

--force applies to every ref in the push, not just the current branch. With push.default=matching or several remote.<name>.push entries, it can overwrite other branches. To force a single ref, put + in front of its refspec instead.
You can't combine --atomic with a remote group. Git refuses because each remote gets its own separate push.

git rebase.summary: git rebase takes the commits that are unique to a branch and replays them on a different base commit, creating new commits. It can also rewrite a branch in place by reordering, editing, squashing or dropping commits in interactive mode.
git rebase.explanation: First, rebase lists the commits on your branch that are not already in <upstream>. Commits whose changes are already upstream are left out. Next, it detaches HEAD at the new base, which is <upstream> or the --onto target. It then replays each listed commit in order, much like running cherry-pick on each one. Finally, it moves the branch ref to the last replayed commit. If you don't give an upstream, it uses the branch's configured upstream and assumes --fork-point. The default backend is merge, which uses the ort strategy. The older apply backend, based on git-am, is still available with --apply.
git rebase.syntax:
git rebase [-i | --interactive] [<options>] [--exec <cmd>] [--onto <newbase> | --keep-base] [<upstream> [<branch>]]
git rebase [-i | --interactive] [<options>] [--exec <cmd>] [--onto <newbase>] --root [<branch>]
git rebase (--continue|--skip|--abort|--quit|--edit-todo|--show-current-patch)

parameters.name: <upstream>
parameters.description: The branch or commit to compare against. Any valid commit works. If omitted, the branch's configured upstream is used.

parameters.name: <branch>
parameters.description: The branch to rebase. Defaults to HEAD. If you give it, rebase checks it out first.

parameters.name: --onto <newbase>
parameters.description: Where the new commits will be created, if different from <upstream>. 'A...B' is shorthand for the merge base of A and B.

parameters.name: --keep-base
parameters.description: Replays the commits onto the merge base of <upstream> and <branch>, so the branch's base stays the same. Implies --reapply-cherry-picks and --no-fork-point.

parameters.name: -i, --interactive
parameters.description: Opens the todo list of commits in an editor so you can change it before the rebase runs.

parameters.name: --continue | --skip | --abort | --quit
parameters.description: Control a rebase that has stopped. --continue resumes after you resolve conflicts, --skip drops the current patch, --abort restores the original branch, and --quit stops without resetting HEAD.

parameters.name: --autostash
parameters.description: Stashes uncommitted changes before the rebase and reapplies them afterwards.

git rebase.returns: On success, <branch> is the current branch and points at the rewritten commits. If a conflict, an 'edit' step or a failed exec stops the rebase, it pauses and waits for --continue, --skip or --abort.

example.title: Update a feature branch and tidy fixup commits
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Bring the latest main into this repo
git fetch origin

# Work on the feature branch
git switch feature

# Record a fix aimed at an earlier commit
git commit --fixup=HEAD~2 -am ""

# Replay feature onto origin/main, squash fixups,
# and run the tests after every rewritten commit
git rebase -i --autosquash --autostash \
  --exec "npm test" origin/main

# If it stops on a conflict:
#   git status            # see the conflicted files
#   git add <file>        # mark each one resolved
#   git rebase --continue # or --skip / --abort

# Compare the old and new history
git range-diff @{1}...HEAD

# Publish the rewritten branch safely
git push --force-with-lease
example.explanation: The script moves a feature branch onto the updated origin/main, folds a fixup commit into its target, runs the tests at each step, and compares the result with the old tip from the reflog before force-pushing.

useCases.title: Keep a topic branch current
useCases.scenario: Your PR branch has fallen behind main. Rebasing it onto origin/main gives a linear history with no merge commit when it is merged.

useCases.title: Clean up commits before review
useCases.scenario: Use an interactive rebase to reword unclear messages, squash work-in-progress commits and drop debugging commits before you open a pull request.

useCases.title: Move a branch to a different base
useCases.scenario: A feature was started on 'next' but now needs to ship from 'master'. 'git rebase --onto master next topic' moves only the feature's own commits.

useCases.title: Remove a range of bad commits
useCases.scenario: To cut two broken commits out of the middle of a branch, rebase the commits after them onto the commit just before them with --onto.

interview.question: What does git rebase actually do to commits, and how is that different from git merge?
interview.answer: Rebase finds your branch's commits that are missing from the upstream, then replays them one by one on the new base, like a series of cherry-picks. The results are new commits with new IDs, and the branch ref is moved to them. A merge keeps the existing commits and adds a merge commit. Rebase rewrites history to make it linear, which is why the docs warn against rebasing branches that others build on.
interview.followUp: Why can an unchanged rebase still create new commits? With -f/--force-rebase (implied by options like --committer-date-is-author-date), rebase replays every commit instead of fast-forwarding over the ones that are unchanged, so every commit gets a new ID.

interview.question: Explain 'git rebase --onto A B C'.
interview.answer: First, C is checked out. The commits in B..C, meaning those reachable from C but not from B, are chosen for replay. They are then replayed on top of A. Here B decides which commits move and A decides where they land. This lets you detach a topic from an intermediate branch, or delete a range with something like 'git rebase --onto X~5 X~3 X'.
interview.followUp: How is --keep-base different from --fork-point? Both use a merge base, but --keep-base uses it as the place where new commits are created, while --fork-point uses the reflog to decide which commits get rebased.

interview.question: You resolved a conflict during a rebase, but the result looks wrong. How do you investigate and recover?
interview.answer: While the rebase is paused, 'git rebase --show-current-patch' shows the commit being applied (it is the same as git show REBASE_HEAD). Remember that 'ours' is the upstream side here, not your branch. If things go badly, --abort resets HEAD to the original branch. After a finished rebase, the old tip is still in the branch reflog at @{1}.
interview.followUp: How can you avoid resolving the same conflicts again on later rebases? Turn on git rerere so that recorded resolutions are reused, and use --no-rerere-autoupdate to check the reused resolution before it is staged.

keyPoints: If a conflict happens, the rebase pauses at the commit that caused it. Resolve the conflict, git add the files, then run --continue. You can also use --abort to go back to where you started, or --skip to drop that commit.

--onto separates two things: <upstream> decides which commits get moved, and --onto decides where they land. For example, 'git rebase --onto master next topic' moves topic's own commits off next and onto master.
--keep-base lets you clean up a feature branch without moving it forward onto a newer upstream.
In the interactive todo list, you can change 'pick' to edit, reword, squash, fixup, drop or break, or add exec lines. Lines run from top to bottom.
With --autosquash, commits made with 'git commit --fixup' or '--squash' are moved next to their target commit and squashed into it automatically. Setting rebase.autoSquash turns this on by default.
--exec <cmd> adds a command, such as a test run, after each commit that is created. If the command fails, the rebase stops so you can fix that commit.
By default, merge commits are dropped and the history becomes linear. Use -r/--rebase-merges to recreate the branch-and-merge structure instead.
--update-refs also moves any other branches that point into the rebased range, which helps with stacked branches. Branches that are checked out in a worktree are not updated.
gotchas: During a rebase, 'ours' means the upstream plus the commits replayed so far, and 'theirs' means your branch. That is the opposite of a merge, which matters for -Xours and -Xtheirs.
Rebasing a branch that others have already built on forces everyone downstream to repair their history by hand.
--autostash makes it possible to rebase with uncommitted changes, but reapplying the stash at the end can still produce conflicts.
ORIG_HEAD may no longer point at the old tip if commands like git reset ran during the rebase. Use the branch reflog (@{1}) to get back to the old tip.

git reflog.summary: git reflog shows and manages reference logs. These are local records of every position a branch tip, HEAD or another ref has pointed to, so you can find and restore earlier states.
git reflog.explanation: Each time a ref like HEAD or a branch moves (commit, reset, rebase, checkout and so on), Git adds an entry with the old and new object IDs and a reason. Running git reflog with no subcommand defaults to show for HEAD. It lists those entries newest first, labelled ref@{n}. Those selectors, and date forms like ref@{yesterday}, work in any command that takes a revision. Other subcommands list, check, write, delete, drop or expire entries.
git reflog.syntax:
git reflog [show] [<log-options>] [<ref>]
git reflog list
git reflog exists <ref>
git reflog write <ref> <old-oid> <new-oid> <message>
git reflog delete [--rewrite] [--updateref] [--dry-run | -n] [--verbose] <ref>@{<specifier>}...
git reflog drop [--all [--single-worktree] | <refs>...]
git reflog expire [--expire=<time>] [--expire-unreachable=<time>] [--rewrite] [--updateref] [--stale-fix] [--dry-run | -n] [--verbose] [--all [--single-worktree] | <refs>...]

parameters.name: <ref>
parameters.description: The reference whose reflog to show, check or change. For show, it defaults to HEAD.

parameters.name: <ref>@{<specifier>}
parameters.description: An exact reflog entry for delete to remove, e.g. master@{2}.

parameters.name: --expire=<time>
parameters.description: Used by expire: prunes entries older than this time. The default comes from gc.reflogExpire (90 days); all and never are accepted.

parameters.name: --expire-unreachable=<time>
parameters.description: Used by expire: prunes entries older than this time that the branch's current tip cannot reach. The default comes from gc.reflogExpireUnreachable (30 days).

parameters.name: --all
parameters.description: For expire or drop: work on the reflogs of all refs (for drop, across all worktrees).

parameters.name: --single-worktree
parameters.description: When used with --all, only handles reflogs from the current worktree.

parameters.name: --updateref
parameters.description: If the top entry was pruned, sets the ref to the new top entry (ref@{0}). Ignored for symbolic refs.

parameters.name: --rewrite
parameters.description: When an entry's predecessor is pruned, changes the entry's old SHA-1 to the new SHA-1 of the entry now before it.

parameters.name: --stale-fix
parameters.description: Prunes entries that point to broken commits, meaning commits that are unreachable and depend on missing objects.

parameters.name: -n, --dry-run
parameters.description: Shows what would be pruned without pruning anything.

parameters.name: --verbose
parameters.description: Prints extra information.

git reflog.returns: show prints one line per reflog entry (abbreviated hash, selector and reason). exists signals its answer with the exit code: 0 if the reflog exists, non-zero if not.

example.title: Recover commits lost to a hard reset
example.code:
# Oops: threw away the last two commits
git reset --hard HEAD~2

# Inspect where HEAD has been
git reflog -n 5
# e.g.
# 1a2b3c4 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~2
# 9f8e7d6 HEAD@{1}: commit: add feature B

# Check that the pre-reset state is the one you want
git log --oneline -3 HEAD@{1}

# Restore it
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}

# Optional: preview pruning without changing anything
git reflog expire --expire-unreachable=now --dry-run --all

# Script-friendly existence check
git reflog exists refs/heads/main && echo "main has a reflog"
example.explanation: The reflog still holds the commit HEAD pointed to before the reset, so HEAD@{1} lets you inspect that state and return to it.

useCases.title: Undo a botched rebase or amend
useCases.scenario: Once a rebase finishes you dislike the result. Find the branch's pre-rebase entry with git reflog <branch>, then git reset --hard to that selector.

useCases.title: Retrieve a dropped commit
useCases.scenario: A commit was left behind after reset or checkout, and no branch points to it anymore. Find its hash in the HEAD reflog, then cherry-pick it or create a branch on it.

useCases.title: Retrace recent navigation
useCases.scenario: Scan the HEAD reflog to see which branches and commits you checked out earlier in the day.

useCases.title: Housekeeping and privacy cleanup
useCases.scenario: Before running gc, use expire or drop to remove reflog entries that still keep sensitive or bulky commits alive.

interview.question: What is the reflog and how is it different from git log?
interview.answer: git log walks the commit graph through parent links, and that history is shared between repositories. The reflog instead records the successive values a ref such as HEAD or a branch has held in your own repository. git reflog show is really git log -g, which walks those entries instead of commit ancestry.
interview.followUp: Why can't you use ranges like A..B with git log -g? Because -g walks reflog entries, not ancestry, so commit exclusions (^commit, A..B, A...B) aren't allowed.

interview.question: How would you recover work after git reset --hard?
interview.answer: Run git reflog to find the entry from before the reset, usually HEAD@{1}. Check it with git log or git show, then run git reset --hard HEAD@{1} or create a branch there. This works because the reflog still references the old commit.
interview.followUp: What if the branch itself was deleted? Deleting a branch also deletes its reflog, but HEAD's reflog may still list the commits. If not, git fsck can find dangling commits as long as they haven't been pruned.

interview.question: How long do reflog entries last, and what removes them?
interview.answer: git reflog expire removes them, normally when git gc runs it for you. Entries the current tip can still reach expire after gc.reflogExpire (90 days by default). Unreachable entries expire after gc.reflogExpireUnreachable (30 days by default).
interview.followUp: Why does the unreachable limit default to a shorter time? Those entries usually come from amends or rebases, so they're no longer part of the project and can go sooner.

keyPoints: With no subcommand, git reflog behaves like git log -g --abbrev-commit --pretty=oneline, so it also accepts git log options such as -n or --date.
The HEAD reflog records more than commits: it also logs every branch switch, which makes it the best place to retrace what you checked out.
git reflog list prints every ref that has a reflog. It is a quick way to find out which refs you can inspect.
git reflog exists answers through its exit code, which makes it easy to use in shell scripts and conditionals.
git reflog write adds a new most-recent entry by hand. The ref must be fully qualified (e.g. refs/heads/main) and both object IDs must be full hashes of objects that exist.
drop removes a ref's entire reflog. delete and expire only remove some of its entries.
By default, entries the current tip can still reach are kept for 90 days. Unreachable entries, such as commits left behind by an amend or a rebase, are pruned after just 30 days.
gotchas: Reflogs are local only. They record what moved in your own repository, so a clone or a teammate's repo has a different reflog, and push never sends it.
delete and expire change history in ways you can't undo, and you normally don't need to run them yourself because git gc handles pruning. Run them with --dry-run first.
--stale-fix is expensive: it walks every reachable object, which costs as much as a full git prune.
--updateref has no effect on symbolic refs such as HEAD.

git remote.summary: git remote manages the named remote repositories your local repository tracks. You use it to list, add, rename, remove and inspect remotes and their URLs and tracked branches.
git remote.explanation: A remote is a short name, like origin, saved in the repository config. It mainly lives in remote.<name>.url and a remote.<name>.fetch refspec. Running git remote with no arguments lists the configured names. Subcommands change that config. add creates an entry, and git fetch <name> then fills in remote-tracking branches under refs/remotes/<name>/. rename and remove update or delete those refs together with the config. set-url, set-branches and set-head change the URL, the fetch refspec and the default branch. show, prune and update contact the remote to report on it, clean up stale refs or fetch.
git remote.syntax:
git remote [-v | --verbose]
git remote add [-t <branch>] [-m <master>] [-f] [--[no-]tags] [--mirror=(fetch|push)] <name> <URL>
git remote rename [--[no-]progress] <old> <new>
git remote remove <name>
git remote set-head <name> (-a | --auto | -d | --delete | <branch>)
git remote set-branches [--add] <name> <branch>...
git remote get-url [--push] [--all] <name>
git remote set-url [--push] <name> <newurl> [<oldurl>]
git remote [-v | --verbose] show [-n] <name>...
git remote prune [-n | --dry-run] <name>...
git remote [-v | --verbose] update [-p | --prune] [(<group> | <remote>)...]

parameters.name: -v, --verbose
parameters.description: Shows each remote's URL after its name. For promisor remotes it also shows the configured filters. It must come before the subcommand.

parameters.name: <name>
parameters.description: The short name of a remote, such as origin.

parameters.name: <URL>
parameters.description: Where the remote repository lives. Used by add, and by set-url --delete as a regex.

parameters.name: -t <branch>
parameters.description: Used with add. Tracks only the named branch or branches instead of the default glob refspec.

parameters.name: -m <master>
parameters.description: Used with add. Points refs/remotes/<name>/HEAD at the given branch on the remote.

parameters.name: -f
parameters.description: Used with add. Runs git fetch <name> right after the remote is set up.

parameters.name: --[no-]tags
parameters.description: Used with add. Makes fetch import every tag, or no tags at all.

parameters.name: --mirror=(fetch|push)
parameters.description: Used with add. Creates a fetch mirror (mirrors refs/ directly) or a push mirror (push always behaves as if --mirror were given).

parameters.name: --push / --add / --delete / --all
parameters.description: Modifiers for get-url and set-url. They choose push URLs instead of fetch URLs, add or delete URLs, or list every URL.

parameters.name: -n, --dry-run
parameters.description: With show, uses cached info instead of querying the remote. With prune, only reports what would be pruned.

git remote.returns: Exit status 0 on success. If add, rename or remove cannot find the remote, the status is 2. If the remote already exists, it is 3. Any other error gives some other non-zero value.

example.title: Add an upstream remote, inspect it, and clean up
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Add the original project as 'upstream' and fetch it immediately
git remote add -f upstream https://example.com/project/repo.git

# List remotes with their URLs
git remote -v

# Switch origin to SSH
git remote set-url origin git@example.com:me/repo.git
git remote get-url --all origin

# Point upstream/HEAD at whatever the remote's default branch is
git remote set-head upstream --auto

# Preview, then delete stale remote-tracking branches
git remote prune --dry-run upstream
git remote prune upstream

# Fetch all remotes and prune in one go
git remote update --prune
example.explanation: This script shows a typical fork workflow: add an upstream remote, change origin's URL, set upstream's default branch, and remove stale refs.

useCases.title: Contributing to a fork
useCases.scenario: Clone your fork as origin and add the original project as upstream. You can then fetch upstream changes and push your work to origin.

useCases.title: Moving hosting or switching protocol
useCases.scenario: After a repository moves, or when you switch from HTTPS to SSH, update the stored address with set-url. Your branches and tracking setup stay as they are.

useCases.title: Tracking only a few branches of a large repo
useCases.scenario: Use add -t or set-branches to limit the fetch refspec to the branches you need. This avoids downloading every branch.

useCases.title: Cleaning up after merged PRs
useCases.scenario: Run prune, or update --prune, to remove remote-tracking branches whose branches were deleted on the server.

interview.question: What happens under the hood when you run git remote add origin <URL>?
interview.answer: Git writes a remote section to the repository config: remote.origin.url and a default fetch refspec covering every branch under refs/remotes/origin/. Nothing is downloaded unless you pass -f. A later git fetch origin creates and updates the origin/<branch> remote-tracking refs.
interview.followUp: How would you add a remote that fetches only main and dev? Use git remote add -t main -t dev <name> <URL>. Each -t creates a refspec for that branch only, instead of the default glob.

interview.question: How do git remote prune and git fetch --prune differ?
interview.answer: Both remove remote-tracking refs whose branches no longer exist on the remote. prune does not fetch any new objects or refs, while fetch --prune also downloads updates. prune --dry-run shows what it would delete without deleting it.
interview.followUp: Can pruning delete more than remote-tracking branches? Yes. Depending on global and per-remote config, it can also delete local tags that were never pushed to that remote.

interview.question: Can one remote fetch from one repository and push to another?
interview.answer: You can set a separate push URL with set-url --push, but the docs require both URLs to point to the same repository. Fetching right after a push should show what you just pushed. To fetch from upstream and push somewhere else, define two separate remotes.
interview.followUp: What does git remote set-url --delete do if the pattern matches every fetch URL? Git reports an error, because removing all non-push URLs is not allowed.

keyPoints: Renaming a remote also renames its remote-tracking branches and config entries, so you don't have to fix refs by hand.
rm is an alias for remove. Removing a remote deletes its remote-tracking branches as well as its config entries.
A remote can have more than one URL. get-url prints only the first one unless you pass --all.
prune works like fetch --prune but downloads nothing. With --dry-run it only reports what it would remove.
When you add a remote, fetch brings in only the tags on fetched branches unless you pass --tags or --no-tags.
You can pass -t several times to track only selected branches. set-branches changes that list later.
set-head sets refs/remotes/<name>/HEAD, which lets you type just the remote name, such as origin, wherever you would type origin/<branch>.
Scripts can check for exit status 3 to detect an add that failed because a remote with that name already exists.
gotchas: The push URL and fetch URL must point to the same repository. If you want to fetch from upstream and push to a fork, set up two remotes instead.
Only use --mirror=fetch in bare repositories. In a repository with a working tree, a fetch can overwrite your local commits.
set-head with an explicit branch, or with --auto, fails if that remote-tracking ref hasn't been fetched yet.
Depending on your config, prune may also delete local tags that were never pushed to that remote.

git rerere.summary: git rerere ("reuse recorded resolution") remembers how you resolved a merge conflict. When the same conflict shows up again, Git applies your earlier fix for you.
git rerere.explanation: When a merge fails, rerere saves a snapshot of the conflicted file (a "preimage") with the conflict markers still in it. After you fix the file, it saves the fixed version too. If the same conflict appears later, rerere runs a three-way merge using three versions: the old conflicted file, your old fix, and the new conflicted file. If that merge is clean, the result goes into your working tree. merge, commit and rebase run rerere for you once it is turned on, and its subcommands let you inspect or reset what it has stored.
git rerere.syntax: git rerere [clear | forget <pathspec>… | diff | status | remaining | gc]

parameters.name: clear
parameters.description: Throws away rerere's working data for the current merge, for when you abandon a resolution.

parameters.name: forget <pathspec>
parameters.description: Deletes the stored resolutions for the current conflicts in the paths you name.

parameters.name: diff
parameters.description: Shows diffs of your resolution so far. Any extra arguments go to the system diff program.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: Lists the conflicted paths whose resolution rerere will record.

parameters.name: remaining
parameters.description: Lists the conflicted paths that rerere did not resolve automatically.

parameters.name: gc
parameters.description: Deletes old conflict records that rerere no longer needs.

example.title: Do a test merge, throw it away, and get the conflict fixed automatically later
example.code:
# Turn rerere on once
git config --global rerere.enabled true

# Test merge on the topic branch
git switch topic
git merge master          # conflict; rerere saves the preimage
git rerere status         # paths rerere is tracking
# ...edit the files to fix the conflict...
git rerere diff           # see your fix so far
git add -A && git commit  # rerere saves your fix
git reset --hard HEAD^    # undo the test merge

# Later: the real merge
git switch master
git merge topic           # the saved fix is applied to the working tree
git rerere remaining      # anything rerere could not fix
git diff                  # check the result
git add -A && git commit
example.explanation: The fix you make during the throwaway test merge is saved, then applied again in the real merge, so you only need to review it and stage it.

useCases.title: Long-lived topic branches
useCases.scenario: You often do test merges of master into a feature branch and throw them away to keep the history clean, then let the final merge reuse your earlier fixes.

useCases.title: Rebasing repeatedly
useCases.scenario: You keep a branch rebased on top of an upstream that moves often, and you don't want to fix the same conflicting hunks on every rebase.

useCases.title: Rebuilding an integration branch
useCases.scenario: You merge many topic branches into a test branch. If one topic breaks the tests, you redo the merges without it, and the conflicts you already fixed are resolved again automatically.

interview.question: What does git rerere do, and how do you turn it on?
interview.answer: It records a conflicted merge result together with your manual fix, and later applies that fix when the same conflict comes back. You enable it with the rerere.enabled setting. After that, merge, commit and rebase call it for you.
interview.followUp: Does it run during git am or git rebase --abort? Yes: --skip and --abort in git am and git rebase automatically run 'git rerere clear', which throws away the data for the abandoned resolution.

interview.question: After rerere reuses a fix, can you just run commit?
interview.answer: No. rerere writes the result only to the working tree and does not touch the index, so the file still counts as conflicted. You should review it with git diff (or git diff -c), then stage it with git add.
interview.followUp: How can you make rerere stage the result too? Pass --rerere-autoupdate to commands like merge or am to allow it. --no-rerere-autoupdate keeps a manual check step so you can catch bad merges.

interview.question: How does rerere apply an old fix when the code around the conflict has changed?
interview.answer: It does a three-way merge between three versions: the old conflicted file, your old fix, and the new conflicted file. If that merge is clean, the result is written to the working tree. Otherwise you resolve the conflict by hand as usual.
interview.followUp: How do you get rid of a wrong fix that rerere saved? Run 'git rerere forget <pathspec>' while the conflict is active, then resolve it again; the new fix will be recorded in its place.

keyPoints: Once rerere is enabled you don't need to run it yourself, because the merge and commit commands call it for you.
rerere decides what to do by itself: if a conflict is new it saves your fix, and if it has seen the conflict before it reuses the saved fix.
A saved fix can still apply when the surrounding code has changed, because rerere merges three versions: the old conflict, your old fix and the new conflict.
Rebase uses the same saved fixes. A rebase that hits the conflict you already fixed in a test merge gets that fix applied again.
If you saved a wrong fix, 'forget' removes it for the conflicted paths you name, so you can fix and record them again.
'gc' cleans up old records. By default it keeps unresolved records for 15 days and resolved ones for 60 days. The settings gc.rerereUnresolved and gc.rerereResolved change these limits.
While you resolve a conflict, 'git rerere diff' shows what you have changed compared with the original conflicted file.
gotchas: rerere does nothing until you turn it on with the rerere.enabled setting.
A reused fix changes only the working tree. The file still counts as conflicted, so you must check it and run git add yourself.

rerere finds conflicts by looking for conflict markers. If a file already has lines that look like markers, rerere may fail to record the fix. You can work around this with the conflict-marker-size setting in gitattributes.
Some conflicts can't be tracked at all, such as conflicting submodules. 'remaining' lists them, and you have to resolve them by hand.

git reset.summary: git reset either moves the current branch tip (HEAD) to another commit, or changes what is staged for chosen paths. You use it to undo commits, merges and pulls, or to unstage files.
git reset.explanation: When you give it a commit, reset moves the branch that HEAD points to onto that commit. Before doing so it saves the old tip in ORIG_HEAD. The mode decides how much else changes. --soft moves only the branch. --mixed, the default, also resets the index. --hard also overwrites the working tree. --merge and --keep update the working tree but refuse to run when local edits could be lost. When you give it paths or -p, HEAD stays where it is. Only the index entries for those paths are copied from the given tree-ish, which defaults to HEAD.
git reset.syntax:
git reset [--soft | --mixed [-N] | --hard | --merge | --keep] [-q] [<commit>]
git reset [-q] [<tree-ish>] [--] <pathspec>...
git reset [-q] [--pathspec-from-file=<file> [--pathspec-file-nul]] [<tree-ish>]
git reset (--patch | -p) [<tree-ish>] [--] [<pathspec>...]

parameters.name: <commit>
parameters.description: Commit the current branch is moved to. Defaults to HEAD.

parameters.name: --soft | --mixed | --hard | --merge | --keep
parameters.description: Sets how much of the index and working tree is updated. The default is --mixed.

parameters.name: -N
parameters.description: Only with --mixed. Paths that the reset removes from the index are marked as intent-to-add.

parameters.name: <tree-ish> <pathspec>...
parameters.description: Copies the staged version of the matching paths from the given tree. HEAD and the working tree are left alone.

parameters.name: -p, --patch
parameters.description: Lets you choose hunks interactively to unstage, comparing the index with the tree-ish.

parameters.name: -q, --quiet
parameters.description: Prints errors only.

parameters.name: --[no-]refresh
parameters.description: Refreshes the index after a mixed reset. This is on by default.

parameters.name: --pathspec-from-file=<file>, --pathspec-file-nul
parameters.description: Reads pathspecs from a file, or from stdin if the file is '-'. With --pathspec-file-nul, entries are separated by NUL.

parameters.name: --[no-]recurse-submodules
parameters.description: Also resets the working trees of active submodules.

parameters.name: -U<n>, --inter-hunk-context=<n>
parameters.description: Diff context settings for patch mode.

example.title: Comparing soft, mixed and hard resets in a throwaway repo
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(mktemp -d)" && git init -q demo && cd demo
git config user.email you@example.com && git config user.name You

echo one > a.txt && git add a.txt && git commit -qm "first"
echo two >> a.txt && git commit -qam "second"

# Undo the commit but keep its changes staged
git reset --soft HEAD^
git status --short        # M  a.txt  (staged)

# Unstage, keeping edits on disk (default --mixed)
git reset
git status --short        #  M a.txt  (unstaged)

# Throw away the edits entirely
git reset --hard
cat a.txt                 # one

# Recover the dropped commit via the reflog
git reset --hard 'HEAD@{2}'
git log --oneline
example.explanation: The script undoes one commit at three depths, first keeping the change staged, then unstaged, then discarding it, and finally gets the dropped commit back from the reflog.

useCases.title: Fix the last commit
useCases.scenario: You forgot a file or made a typo in the message. Run `git reset --soft HEAD^`, make the fix, then commit again with `git commit -a -c ORIG_HEAD`.

useCases.title: Move commits to a topic branch
useCases.scenario: You committed to master too early. Create topic/wip at the current HEAD, run `git reset --hard HEAD~3` on master, then switch to topic/wip.

useCases.title: Split a commit
useCases.scenario: Run `git reset -N HEAD^` to remove the commit while keeping its changes, including new files. Then use `git add -p` and commit several times.

useCases.title: Unstage one file before committing
useCases.scenario: Run `git reset -- frotz.c` so that file stays out of the commit while the rest of the staged changes go in.

interview.question: What is the difference between git reset --soft, --mixed and --hard?
interview.answer: All three move the current branch to the target commit. --soft stops there, so your staged and unstaged changes stay as they are. --mixed, the default, also makes the index match the target, so nothing is staged afterwards. --hard also overwrites the working tree, so any uncommitted tracked changes are lost.
interview.followUp: How would you get back commits you lost with --hard? Find the old tip in ORIG_HEAD or in the reflog (for example HEAD@{1}) and run `git reset --hard` to that commit.

interview.question: When should you use git reset rather than git revert?
interview.answer: Reset rewrites the branch by moving its tip, so it suits local commits nobody else has. The docs warn against resetting away commits you have already given to others. Revert adds a new commit that cancels the old one, so it is safe on shared branches.
interview.followUp: What happens if you reset a branch you already pushed? Pushing again needs a force push, and anyone who built on the old commits has to recover, much like after an upstream rebase.

interview.question: What does git reset <path> do, and how is it related to git add?
interview.answer: It copies the given paths from the tree-ish (HEAD by default) into the index. It does not move HEAD or change the files on disk. That makes it the opposite of `git add <path>`, and the same as `git restore --staged <path>`.
interview.followUp: Why can't you combine --hard with a path? A path reset only touches the index. To change the files on disk for specific paths, you use git restore (or checkout) instead.

keyPoints: The default mode, --mixed, unstages everything but keeps all your edits on disk. A bare `git reset` is therefore a quick way to empty the staging area.
--soft leaves both staged and unstaged work alone. That makes `git reset --soft HEAD~N` followed by `git commit` an easy way to squash the last N commits into one.
The previous branch tip is saved in ORIG_HEAD. So you can undo a reset, merge or pull with `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD`, or reuse the old commit message with `git commit -c ORIG_HEAD`.
--keep is the safe way to drop recent commits while keeping uncommitted edits. It refuses to run if those edits touch files that the reset would change.
--merge is designed to back out of a merge that stopped with conflicts. It works on unmerged index entries, for example after `git am -3`.
`git reset -p` is the opposite of `git add -p`. It lets you unstage individual hunks instead of whole files.
The path form never touches the files on disk. If you also want to throw away the edits in the working tree, use git restore.
With --recurse-submodules, the submodules are reset as well. Each one ends up on a detached HEAD at the commit the superproject records.
gotchas: --hard throws away tracked changes. It can also overwrite untracked files that get in the way.
Resetting changes history. Don't use it to remove commits you have already shared, because the people who have them will run into trouble.
If you undo a merge with --hard while you have unrelated local edits, those edits are lost too. Use --merge in that case.
Running --soft while you have unstaged edits is allowed, but it can easily mix up what ends up in the next commit.

git restore.summary: git restore puts selected paths back to the content held in a restore source. It can undo working-tree edits, unstage changes, or bring back a file as it was in an older commit.
git restore.explanation: The command copies content from a source to a location. The location is the working tree (-W/--worktree, used when you give neither flag), the index (-S/--staged), or both. If you don't pass --source, the source is the index when only the working tree is restored and HEAD when --staged is given. --source=<tree> lets you pick any commit, branch or tag instead. Pathspecs choose which files are affected. By default it runs in no-overlay mode, so the result matches the source exactly, and that can mean deleting files.

parameters.name: -s <tree>, --source=<tree>
parameters.description: Tree to take content from. Defaults to HEAD when --staged is given, otherwise the index.

parameters.name: -W, --worktree / -S, --staged
parameters.description: Where to restore: the working tree (the default), the index, or both.

parameters.name: -p, --patch
parameters.description: Choose hunks interactively.

parameters.name: --ours / --theirs
parameters.description: For unmerged paths, take stage #2 or stage #3 from the index.

parameters.name: -m, --merge / --conflict=<style>
parameters.description: Recreate the conflicted merge for unmerged paths, optionally with a specific conflict style.

parameters.name: --overlay / --no-overlay
parameters.description: Whether tracked files missing from the source are removed (no-overlay is the default).

parameters.name: --pathspec-from-file=<file>, --pathspec-file-nul
parameters.description: Read pathspecs from a file or from stdin (-), optionally separated by NUL characters.

parameters.name: <pathspec>...
parameters.description: Limits which paths are affected.

example.title: Unstage, discard and recover files
example.code:
set -e
cd "$(mktemp -d)" && git init -q demo && cd demo
git config user.email you@example.com && git config user.name You
echo v1 > app.txt && git add app.txt && git commit -qm v1
echo v2 > app.txt && git commit -qam v2

# Stage an edit, then unstage it (index <- HEAD)
echo draft > app.txt && git add app.txt
git restore --staged app.txt

# Discard the working-tree edit (worktree <- index)
git restore app.txt

# Bring back the v1 content into both index and worktree
git restore --source=HEAD~1 --staged --worktree app.txt
cat app.txt   # v1
git status --short
example.explanation: The script unstages a change, throws away a working-tree edit, and then pulls an older version of the file into both the index and the working tree.

useCases.title: Unstaging an accidental add
useCases.scenario: You staged too many files. Run git restore --staged <file> to reset the index entry to HEAD while keeping your edits in the working tree.

useCases.title: Recovering an older file version
useCases.scenario: A recent commit broke the Makefile. Restore just that file from master~2 without touching the rest of the code.

useCases.title: Redoing a conflict resolution
useCases.scenario: You got a manual merge resolution wrong. Run git restore --merge (or --conflict=zdiff3) on the file to get the conflict markers back and start over.

useCases.title: Partially discarding edits
useCases.scenario: Use git restore -p to drop only the debugging hunks and keep the rest of your changes.

interview.question: What is the difference between git restore <file> and git restore --staged <file>?
interview.answer: Without flags, only the working tree is written, and it is filled from the index, so you lose unstaged edits. With --staged, only the index is written, and the default source becomes HEAD. That unstages the file but leaves its working-tree content alone.
interview.followUp: How do you discard both staged and unstaged changes to one file? Use git restore --source=HEAD --staged --worktree <file>, or the short form git restore -s@ -SW <file>.

interview.question: How does git restore relate to git checkout and git reset for file-level operations?
interview.answer: The docs say git restore --staged <path> does the same as git reset on that path. Restoring the index and working tree from HEAD does the same as git checkout on that path. git restore handles only files, never branches, so it separates out the file-restoring part of checkout.
interview.followUp: Why can't you use --ours with --source? Stages #2 and #3 exist only in the index while a merge is unresolved, and a tree-ish passed to --source has no such stages.

interview.question: Why can git restore --source=<commit> <dir> delete files?
interview.answer: No-overlay mode is the default. In that mode, tracked files that are missing from the source tree are removed so that the location matches the source exactly. Pass --overlay if you want files that aren't in the source to stay.
interview.followUp: Why quote '*.c' when running git restore? With quotes, Git matches the pattern against index entries, so files you deleted from the working tree are restored too. If the shell expanded the glob, those files would be missed.

keyPoints: You usually name the source by a commit, a branch or a tag, for example --source master~2 to take a file from two commits back.
Writing A...B as the source means the merge base of A and B, provided there is only one. You may leave out one side, and it then defaults to HEAD.
--patch lets you choose, hunk by hunk, which differences between the source and the target get restored. It works the same way as the interactive mode of git add.
During a conflict, --ours and --theirs fill the working-tree file from stage #2 or stage #3 of the index.
--merge rebuilds the conflict markers in a file you had already edited. --conflict=<style> does the same but lets you pick merge, diff3 or zdiff3.
--ignore-unmerged stops the command from aborting when there are conflicted entries. Those paths are simply skipped.
Quote glob patterns such as '*.c' so Git matches them against the index rather than the shell expanding them. This way, deleted files are matched too.
gotchas: --ours, --theirs and --merge work only when restoring from the index. They can't be combined with --source.
No-overlay mode is the default, so tracked files that don't exist in the source are deleted. Use --overlay if you want to keep them.
--recurse-submodules resets the submodule to the commit the superproject recorded and throws away local changes in it.
-U with no number is not an error. Git silently treats it as -p.

git rev-parse.summary: git rev-parse is a low-level plumbing command. It turns revision expressions such as HEAD~2 or v1.0^{commit} into object names, and it can also report details about the repository, such as its top-level path, whether you are inside a work tree, and the current branch.
git rev-parse.explanation: git rev-parse takes a list of arguments and works out which ones are flags, which are revisions meant for git rev-list, and which are something else. It prints each result on its own line. Revisions are resolved with the extended SHA-1 syntax, which covers refs, reflog suffixes like @{n}, ancestry operators like ^ and ~, peeling like ^{type}, and paths like rev:path. Other options switch it into helper roles. It can report repository facts such as paths and booleans, quote arguments for the shell (--sq-quote), or parse script options (--parseopt). Most modes must run inside a repository.

parameters.name: <arg>…
parameters.description: The flags and parameters to parse. Revisions use the extended SHA-1 syntax, for example HEAD, main~3, v1.0^{commit}, or @{u}.

parameters.name: --verify
parameters.description: Requires exactly one argument that resolves to an object name. It prints that name, or fails.

parameters.name: -q / --quiet
parameters.description: Used with --verify. If the name is invalid, it exits with a non-zero status and prints no error message.

parameters.name: --short[=<length>]
parameters.description: Works like --verify but prints a unique abbreviated object name, with a minimum length of 4.

parameters.name: --abbrev-ref[=(strict|loose)]
parameters.description: Prints a short ref name that is not ambiguous, such as the current branch name for HEAD.

parameters.name: --symbolic-full-name
parameters.description: Prints refs as full refnames, such as refs/heads/main, and leaves out any input that is not a ref.

parameters.name: --show-toplevel / --show-prefix / --show-cdup
parameters.description: Report where you are in the working tree: the path of its root, your current directory relative to the root, and the relative path back up to the root.

parameters.name: --git-dir / --absolute-git-dir / --git-path <path>
parameters.description: Find the repository directory, or a file inside it, while respecting relocation variables and worktrees.

parameters.name: --is-inside-work-tree / --is-bare-repository / --is-shallow-repository
parameters.description: Each prints true or false for its check.

parameters.name: --parseopt / --sq-quote
parameters.description: Special operation modes for parsing options in shell scripts and for quoting arguments for the shell. They must come first.

git rev-parse.returns: Writes its results to standard output, usually one line per item: object names, ref names, paths, or true/false. On failure it exits with a non-zero status. In --parseopt mode a usage error exits with code 129.

example.title: Gather repo context safely in a shell script
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Bail out early if not inside a work tree
if [ "$(git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree 2>/dev/null)" != "true" ]; then
  echo "not in a git work tree" >&2
  exit 1
fi

root=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)
branch=$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)
sha=$(git rev-parse --verify HEAD)
short=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)

# Validate a user-supplied revision as a commit, quietly
rev="${1:-main}"
if commit=$(git rev-parse --quiet --verify --end-of-options "${rev}^{commit}"); then
  echo "$rev -> $commit"
else
  echo "'$rev' is not a commit" >&2
fi

# Upstream of the current branch, as a full ref (may be unset)
upstream=$(git rev-parse --symbolic-full-name @{u} 2>/dev/null || echo none)

echo "root=$root branch=$branch sha=$sha short=$short upstream=$upstream"
example.explanation: This script first checks that it is running inside a work tree. It then reads the repository root, the current branch, and the HEAD hash, checks that a revision given by the user names a commit, and looks up the branch's upstream.

useCases.title: Stamping builds with a commit ID
useCases.scenario: A CI job or release script runs rev-parse --short HEAD and embeds the result in an artifact name or version string.

useCases.title: Validating input in Git hooks and tools
useCases.scenario: A hook gets a revision argument and checks it with --verify --end-of-options "$REV^{commit}" before running any destructive step.

useCases.title: Making scripts location-independent
useCases.scenario: A helper script can be started from any subdirectory. It changes into the --show-toplevel path and keeps the user's relative file arguments valid by passing them through --prefix.

useCases.title: Writing Git-style option parsing in shell
useCases.scenario: A custom git-foo shell command describes its options in a spec and passes it to --parseopt. This gives it -h usage output and --no-* negation like built-in Git commands have.

interview.question: In a script, how do you reliably get the commit hash that a user-provided revision points to?
interview.answer: Run git rev-parse --verify --end-of-options "$REV^{commit}". --verify accepts exactly one argument and fails unless it resolves to an object. The ^{commit} suffix peels the object until it reaches a commit, so the command also fails if the name does not point to a commit. Add -q if you want only a non-zero exit status instead of an error message.
interview.followUp: Why can git rev-parse v1.0 and git rev-parse v1.0^{commit} print different hashes? For an annotated tag, the plain name resolves to the tag object itself, and peeling with ^{commit} (or ^0) follows it to the commit the tag points at.

interview.question: How would you get the current branch name and its upstream with rev-parse?
interview.answer: git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD prints a short branch name such as main instead of a hash. For the upstream, git rev-parse --symbolic-full-name @{u} prints the remote-tracking ref, for example refs/remotes/origin/main. @{u} is resolved from the branch's configured remote and merge settings.
interview.followUp: When does @{push} differ from @{upstream}? It differs in a triangular workflow, where you pull from one remote and push to another, such as when remote.pushdefault points to a fork. In a non-triangular setup the two are the same.

interview.question: Why use git rev-parse --git-path instead of building paths like .git/hooks or .git/HEAD yourself?
interview.answer: --git-path resolves a path inside $GIT_DIR while taking relocation variables such as $GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY and $GIT_INDEX_FILE into account. Hard-coded .git/... paths fail when .git is a gitfile, when GIT_DIR is set, or inside linked worktrees. For the same reason, --git-dir or --absolute-git-dir is the reliable way to find the repository directory itself.
interview.followUp: What is the difference between --sq and --sq-quote? --sq still interprets the input as rev-parse arguments and then prints the result as one shell-quoted line. --sq-quote is a separate mode that only quotes its arguments and can run outside a repository.

keyPoints: Its original job is to split a mixed command line into flags, revision arguments for rev-list, and everything else. The filtering options --revs-only, --no-revs, --flags and --no-flags control which of these groups get printed.

--verify is the safe way to resolve one name to an object ID. Pass exactly one argument; anything else is an error. Adding a peel such as ^{commit} also makes sure the object exists and has the type you expect.
--short gives an abbreviated hash that is still unique. If you don't pass a length, it uses core.abbrev.
--abbrev-ref HEAD is the usual way to print the name of the current branch rather than its commit hash.
Scripts can find out where they are running. --show-toplevel gives the absolute path of the work tree root, and --show-prefix gives the current directory's path relative to that root.
The --is-* options print true or false. Use them in scripts to check the current environment, for example whether you are inside a work tree or whether the repository is bare or shallow.

Use --git-path when you need the location of a file inside the repository directory. It takes relocation variables and linked worktrees into account, so it is safer than building $GIT_DIR/... paths yourself.
--disambiguate=<prefix> lists every object whose name starts with a short hex prefix, which shows why a short hash is ambiguous. The prefix has a minimum length.
gotchas: If the name comes from user input, put --end-of-options before it. Otherwise an input like --all would be read as an option instead of a revision.
--parseopt and --sq-quote are operation modes and only work when placed before every other option.
Date and count reflog suffixes such as main@{yesterday} or main@{1} read the local reflog. They fail if the ref has no reflog, for example right after a fresh clone.
Most modes need a repository and stop with a fatal error outside one. Only a few, such as --parseopt and --sq-quote, are documented as working anywhere.

git revert.summary: git revert undoes the effect of one or more existing commits by adding new commits that apply the opposite changes. It does not rewrite history, so it is the safe way to undo work that has already been shared.
git revert.explanation: For each commit you name, Git works out the patch that commit introduced and applies the reverse of it to the current HEAD. This works like a reverse cherry-pick. By default, each reversal is saved as its own new commit, with a message that names the commit being undone. When you name several commits, Git works through them one at a time and keeps its progress in a sequencer state. If a step hits a conflict, it stops so you can fix the conflict and then resume with --continue, or use --skip, --abort or --quit. The original commits stay in history, so branches that others have already pulled are not broken.

parameters.name: <commit>...
parameters.description: The commits to undo. You can use any revision syntax (see gitrevisions), including ranges.

parameters.name: -e, --edit / --no-edit
parameters.description: Opens, or skips, the editor for the revert commit message. The editor opens by default when you run the command in a terminal.

parameters.name: -m, --mainline <parent-number>
parameters.description: Required when reverting a merge commit. It picks which parent counts as the mainline, and the merge is undone relative to that parent.

parameters.name: -n, --no-commit
parameters.description: Applies the reversed changes to the working tree and the index, but does not create a commit.

parameters.name: --cleanup=<mode>
parameters.description: Sets how the commit message is cleaned up, as in git-commit. With scissors, a scissors line is appended to MERGE_MSG if there is a conflict.

parameters.name: -S[<keyid>], --gpg-sign[=<keyid>] / --no-gpg-sign
parameters.description: GPG-signs the resulting commits. --no-gpg-sign overrides the commit.gpgSign setting or an earlier --gpg-sign.

parameters.name: -s, --signoff
parameters.description: Adds a Signed-off-by trailer to the commit message.

parameters.name: --strategy=<strategy>, -X<option>
parameters.description: Chooses the merge strategy, and passes options to that strategy.

parameters.name: --[no-]rerere-autoupdate
parameters.description: Controls whether resolutions reused by rerere are also written to the index.

parameters.name: --reference
parameters.description: Refers to the reverted commit in the message using the --pretty=reference format, instead of its full object name.

parameters.name: --continue / --skip / --quit / --abort
parameters.description: Controls a revert that is in progress: resume it, skip the current commit, forget the sequencer state, or cancel and go back to where you started.

example.title: Undo a bad commit, then undo a range in one commit
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(mktemp -d)" && git init -q demo && cd demo
git config user.email dev@example.com
git config user.name Dev

echo v1 > app.txt && git add app.txt && git commit -qm "Add app"
echo bug >> app.txt && git commit -qam "Introduce bug"
echo a > a.txt && git add a.txt && git commit -qm "Add a"
echo b > b.txt && git add b.txt && git commit -qm "Add b"

# Undo the buggy commit (HEAD~2) with a new commit, no editor
git revert --no-edit HEAD~2
cat app.txt   # -> v1

# Undo 'Add a' and 'Add b' together as a single commit
git revert --no-commit HEAD~2..HEAD~0~1 2>/dev/null || git revert --no-commit HEAD~3 HEAD~2
git commit -qm "Revert a and b: feature postponed"

git log --oneline
example.explanation: The script builds a throwaway repository, removes a buggy commit with one revert, and then undoes two earlier commits together by using --no-commit followed by a single commit with a message that explains the reason.

useCases.title: Hotfix on a shared branch
useCases.scenario: A commit that broke production has already been pushed to main. Reverting it removes the change without force-pushing or rewriting the history that teammates have pulled.

useCases.title: Backing out a merged feature
useCases.scenario: A merged feature branch has to come out before a release. Running git revert -m 1 on the merge commit removes the feature's changes while main stays the mainline.

useCases.title: Squashed rollback of several commits
useCases.scenario: Several related commits need to be undone together. Using --no-commit on each one, then committing once, gives a single rollback commit with a clear reason.

interview.question: How is git revert different from git reset?
interview.answer: git revert adds new commits that undo earlier changes, so the existing history stays as it is. git reset moves the branch pointer, and with --hard it can also throw away uncommitted work. Because revert keeps history intact, it is the right choice for commits that have already been pushed or shared.
interview.followUp: When is reset still the better choice? When the commits exist only in your local repository and you want them gone from history entirely. No one else depends on them, so rewriting history is safe.

interview.question: What happens when you try to revert a merge commit?
interview.answer: Git refuses unless you pass -m <parent-number>, because a merge has more than one parent and Git cannot tell which side is the mainline. With -m 1, Git undoes the merge relative to the first parent, which is usually the branch you merged into.
interview.followUp: If you later fix the feature branch and merge it again, why are some changes missing? The revert told Git you never want that merge's changes, so commits that were already merged are not brought back in. Revert the revert first, then merge.

interview.question: How would you undo several commits but end up with a single commit?
interview.answer: Run git revert -n (--no-commit) with the commits or a range. This applies all the reversed changes to the working tree and index without committing. Then make one commit and explain the reason in its message.
interview.followUp: What do you do if one of the commits in a multi-commit revert conflicts? Resolve the conflict and run git revert --continue. You can also use --skip to drop that commit, or --abort to return to where you started.

keyPoints: Before a normal revert, your working tree must have no changes compared with HEAD.
You can pass a range of commits, but Git does not walk the history by default. See the --no-walk option of git rev-list for how ranges are handled.
With --no-commit, Git applies the reversed changes but does not commit them. This lets you combine several reverts into one commit, and your index does not need to match HEAD.
To revert a merge commit, you must use -m to say which parent is the mainline. Parents are numbered from 1.
If a multi-commit revert stops on a conflict, fix the conflict and run --continue. To cancel, run --abort, which returns you to the state before the sequence started.
The message editor opens automatically in a terminal. Use --no-edit to skip it in scripts.
Setting revert.reference to true makes --reference the default, so revert messages name the commit in a shorter, readable form.
gotchas: Once you revert a merge, later merges of the same branch will not bring back the changes from commits that were already merged. You may have to revert the revert first.
The docs point to reset --hard and restore --source for other kinds of undo, but both of these throw away uncommitted work.
The automatic message only says what was reverted. You should add why. Reverting a revert again and again also produces long, nested subject lines.

git rm.summary: git rm removes tracked files from the index, or from both the index and the working tree. Committing afterwards records the deletion.
git rm.explanation: git rm uses pathspecs to find tracked paths, then removes them from the index (the staging area). By default it also deletes them from disk. Before it does anything, it runs a safety check: each file must match the branch tip and must have no staged changes, which protects work you haven't committed yet. -f skips that check. --cached removes the entry from the index only and leaves the file on disk, so the file becomes untracked after the commit. The deletion is staged like any other change and becomes permanent with git commit.

parameters.name: <pathspec>…
parameters.description: Files to remove. A directory name removes everything under it, but only when -r is given.

parameters.name: -f, --force
parameters.description: Skips the up-to-date safety check.

parameters.name: -n, --dry-run
parameters.description: Lists what would be removed without removing anything.

parameters.name: -r
parameters.description: Allows recursive removal when you give a leading directory name.

parameters.name: --cached
parameters.description: Unstages and removes paths from the index only. Working tree files are left alone.

parameters.name: --ignore-unmatch
parameters.description: Exits with status 0 even if no files matched.

parameters.name: --sparse
parameters.description: Allows updating index entries outside the sparse-checkout cone.

parameters.name: -q, --quiet
parameters.description: Turns off the one-line rm message printed for each removed file.

parameters.name: --pathspec-from-file=<file>
parameters.description: Reads pathspecs from a file instead of the arguments. Use - to read from standard input.

parameters.name: --pathspec-file-nul
parameters.description: Works only with --pathspec-from-file. Pathspecs are separated by NUL, and every other character is taken literally.
Separates options from file names, so a file name can't be mistaken for an option.

example.title: Untrack a committed file and clean up a folder
example.code:
# Stop tracking a secrets file but keep it locally
echo '.env' >> .gitignore
git rm --cached .env

# Preview, then recursively remove an old directory
git rm -r -n legacy/
git rm -r legacy/

# Let Git (not the shell) expand the glob, matching subdirectories too
git rm 'docs/*.txt'

git commit -m "Untrack .env, drop legacy/ and docs text files"
example.explanation: This shows the three most common uses: --cached for untracking, -n and -r for a safe recursive delete, and a quoted pathspec so Git expands the glob itself.

useCases.title: Fixing a tracked file that should be ignored
useCases.scenario: A build artifact or .env file was committed by mistake. Add it to .gitignore and run git rm --cached so it leaves the repository but stays on your disk.

useCases.title: Deleting obsolete code
useCases.scenario: Delete a retired module directory and stage the deletion in one step with git rm -r, ready to commit.

useCases.title: Removing a submodule
useCases.scenario: Drop a vendored submodule from the superproject. git rm removes its work tree and its .gitmodules entry, and stages both.

useCases.title: Scripted cleanup
useCases.scenario: In CI, feed a generated list of paths through --pathspec-from-file=- with --ignore-unmatch so the cleanup doesn't fail when a path is already gone.

interview.question: What is the difference between git rm and git rm --cached?
interview.answer: Plain git rm removes the path from the index and also deletes it from the working tree. With --cached, only the index entry is removed and the file on disk stays as it is, so after you commit it shows up as untracked. --cached is the standard way to untrack something you are about to add to .gitignore.
interview.followUp: What check does --cached apply? The staged content must match either the branch tip or the file on disk. Otherwise you need -f.

interview.question: Why might git rm refuse to delete a file, and how do you override it?
interview.answer: git rm runs an up-to-date check. The file must match the tip of the branch, and it can't have staged changes. If either condition fails, the command refuses so that it doesn't destroy uncommitted work. Passing -f/--force skips the check.
interview.followUp: Why is git rm 'src/*.js' different from git rm src/*.js? In the quoted form, Git expands the pattern and matches across directory boundaries, including subdirectories. In the unquoted form, the shell expands it and matches only files directly in src/.

interview.question: You deleted several tracked files with a plain rm. How do you stage those deletions?
interview.answer: git rm has no option that stages only files already missing from disk. Running git add -u, or committing with git commit -a, records those removals along with any other changes to tracked files. To stage only the deletions while other edits are in progress, pipe git diff --name-only --diff-filter=D -z into xargs -0 git rm --cached.
interview.followUp: How do you import a vendor code drop so that additions, modifications and deletions are all recorded? Remove all tracked files, unpack the new tree into the working directory, then run git add -A.

keyPoints: Removing a whole directory takes -r. Without it, giving a directory name is not enough.
Use --cached to stop tracking a file but keep your local copy. It is the usual fix for a file committed before it was added to .gitignore.
Run -n first to preview which index entries a pattern would hit before you delete anything.
Untracked files are never touched, even when a pattern matches them on disk.
--ignore-unmatch makes the command safe in scripts, where a pattern that matches nothing would otherwise fail.
With --pathspec-file-nul, a large or awkward list of paths (for example, names with newlines) can come from a file or stdin without any escaping.
When removing a submodule, ignored files inside it don't block the removal. Its .gitmodules entry is also removed and staged.
In a sparse checkout, --sparse is needed to change index entries outside the cone.
gotchas: git rm refuses to remove a file whose content has staged changes or no longer matches the branch tip. You must decide whether to use -f, which discards those changes.
Git's own globbing crosses '/' boundaries. A quoted 'd*' therefore also matches a sibling directory like d2, while 'd/*' does not.
You can't delete a file from disk while keeping it staged. To do that, use a plain shell rm.
git rm has no flag to stage only the files you already deleted with a plain rm. Use git add -u, git commit -a, or a diff --diff-filter=D pipeline instead.

git shortlog.summary: git shortlog condenses commit history into a list grouped by contributor, with each person's commit subjects under their name. It is meant for release notes and contributor statistics.
git shortlog.explanation: git shortlog walks history like git log and accepts the same options for choosing commits, such as revision ranges, paths, dates and --no-merges. Instead of printing every commit in full, it puts commits into buckets and prints each bucket's header followed by its commit subjects. By default the buckets are authors, sorted alphabetically. You can bucket by committer, by a trailer such as Reviewed-by, or by any git log format string. You can also replace the subjects with counts. It can read git log output from a pipe instead of a repository, and it applies .mailmap so that one person's different identities are merged into one.
git shortlog.syntax:
git shortlog [<options>] [<revision-range>] [[--] <path>…]
git log --pretty=short | git shortlog [<options>]

parameters.name: -n, --numbered
parameters.description: Sorts groups by how many commits they have instead of alphabetically.

parameters.name: -s, --summary
parameters.description: Prints only a commit count for each group and leaves out the subjects.

parameters.name: -e, --email
parameters.description: Adds each author's email address to the output.

parameters.name: --format[=<format>]
parameters.description: Describes each commit with a git log pretty-format string instead of its subject.

parameters.name: --date=<format>
parameters.description: Sets how dates are formatted. Most useful together with --group=format:<format>.

parameters.name: --group=<type>
parameters.description: Sets what commits are grouped by. The default is author, and you can pass it more than once.

parameters.name: -c, --committer
parameters.description: Short form of --group=committer.

parameters.name: -w[<width>[,<indent1>[,<indent2>]]]
parameters.description: Wraps and indents the output lines. A width of 0 indents the lines without wrapping them.

parameters.name: <revision-range>
parameters.description: Limits the summary to commits in this range, for example origin..HEAD. Defaults to HEAD.

parameters.name: [--] <path>...
parameters.description: Limits the summary to commits that explain how the matching files came to be.

git shortlog.returns: Text on standard output: one header per group (with a commit count) followed by indented commit descriptions, or only counts and names when -s is used.

example.title: Contributor stats and release notes
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Ranked contributor counts with emails for the whole history
git shortlog -sne HEAD

# Release notes: commit subjects per author between two tags, skipping merges
git shortlog --no-merges v1.0..v2.0

# Who has been reviewing? Count Reviewed-by trailers
git shortlog -ns --group=trailer:reviewed-by HEAD

# Credit authors and co-authors together
git shortlog -ns --group=author --group=trailer:co-authored-by HEAD

# Commits per year, grouped by a date format
git shortlog -s --date=format:%Y --group=format:%ad HEAD

# Summarize piped log output from a topic branch
git log main..feature | git shortlog
example.explanation: Each command passes an explicit revision (or reads from a pipe) so it behaves the same in scripts and in a terminal, and together they show counting, release notes, trailer grouping, multi-grouping and date grouping.

useCases.title: Writing release announcements
useCases.scenario: A maintainer runs shortlog over the range between the previous and new tags. This produces a by-author list of changes to paste into the announcement.

useCases.title: Recognizing code reviewers
useCases.scenario: A team that adds Reviewed-by trailers groups history by that trailer to see who does the most reviewing.

useCases.title: Checking what a topic branch contains
useCases.scenario: Before merging, a developer pipes the log of commits not yet on main into shortlog to see a summary of the branch's changes and who wrote them.

useCases.title: Activity over time
useCases.scenario: Grouping by a formatted author date gives a count of commits per year or per month for project health reports.

interview.question: How would you get a ranked list of everyone who contributed to a repository, with commit counts and email addresses?
interview.answer: Run `git shortlog -sne HEAD`. -s replaces the commit subjects with a count, -n sorts by that count instead of by name, and -e adds email addresses. Including HEAD explicitly avoids the stdin behavior when running in a script.
interview.followUp: The same person appears twice under different emails. How do you merge them? Add a .mailmap file that maps the old identities to one canonical name and email; shortlog applies the mailmap when it groups commits.

interview.question: Why might `git shortlog` print nothing in a CI pipeline when it works fine in your terminal?
interview.answer: When no revisions are given and stdin is not a terminal, or there is no current branch (as with a detached HEAD in many CI checkouts), shortlog summarizes log text read from stdin instead of the repository. In CI stdin is usually empty or redirected, so there is nothing to summarize. Passing a revision such as HEAD or a tag range fixes it.
interview.followUp: How can you deliberately use the stdin mode? Pipe git log output into it, for example `git log main..feature | git shortlog`; outside a repository it then looks for .mailmap in the current directory.

interview.question: How can shortlog credit co-authors as well as commit authors?
interview.answer: Pass --group more than once, for example `--group=author --group=trailer:co-authored-by`. Each commit then counts under its author and under each distinct Co-authored-by value. The trailer name is matched without regard to case, and trailer values that look like 'Name <email>' are parsed as identities and passed through the mailmap.
interview.followUp: Why can the counts add up to more than the total number of commits? A single commit is counted once in every group it matches, such as its author and each of its co-authors, so totals across groups overlap.

keyPoints: -n changes the order so that the most active contributors come first. Without it, groups are listed alphabetically by name.
-s turns the output into a compact table of commit counts. Combined with -n and -e (-sne), it gives a ranked list of contributors.
Besides authors, you can group commits by committer, by a commit-message trailer (matched without regard to case), or by any git log format string.
If you pass --group more than once, a commit counts toward every matching group. Within one commit, each distinct value is counted only once.
shortlog removes the "[PATCH]" prefix from commit subjects, which keeps the output clean for projects that apply emailed patches.
With -w and no values, lines wrap at 76 columns. The first line of each entry is indented 6 spaces and continuation lines 9 spaces.
A revision range such as v1.0..v2.0 limits the summary to the commits between two releases, which is how you build per-release notes.
gotchas: In CI jobs, hooks or other scripts where stdin is not a terminal, running plain `git shortlog` reads from stdin instead of the repository and may print nothing. Pass an explicit revision such as HEAD.
When grouping by trailer, commits without that trailer are left out of the totals entirely. This makes the totals unreliable as a count of all work.
A commit with several trailers of the same kind, such as multiple Signed-off-by lines, can be counted in several groups. Totals across groups can therefore be larger than the number of commits.
When you pipe log text into shortlog outside a repository, it looks for .mailmap only in the current directory. Run it in the wrong directory and identities will not be merged.

git show.summary: git show prints one or more Git objects in a readable form: a commit, an annotated tag, a tree, or a blob. With no argument it shows HEAD, the latest commit on the current branch.
git show.explanation: You pass git show any object names (revisions). Git resolves each one and chooses the output by object type. A commit shows its log message and a patch. A merge commit shows a dense combined diff by default. A tag shows the tag message and then the object it points to. A tree shows a list of names, and a blob shows its raw contents. Display options come from the git log and git diff machinery. Use --pretty or --format to control the header, and use -s, --stat, --name-only or --diff-merges to control the diff part.

parameters.name: <object>...
parameters.description: One or more objects to show. Defaults to HEAD. Any form from gitrevisions works, such as hashes, branches, tags, HEAD~2, or <rev>:<path>.

parameters.name: --pretty[=<format>] / --format=<format>
parameters.description: Sets the commit header layout. It can be oneline, short, medium (the default), full, fuller, reference, email, raw, or a custom format:/tformat: string.

parameters.name: --abbrev-commit / --oneline
parameters.description: Shows a short unique hash prefix instead of the full hash. --oneline is the same as --pretty=oneline --abbrev-commit.

parameters.name: -s / --no-patch
parameters.description: Hides the diff output and keeps only the commit or tag information.

parameters.name: --diff-merges=<format>
parameters.description: Sets how merge commits are diffed. Options are off, on, first-parent, separate, combined, dense-combined, and remerge.

parameters.name: --stat / --name-only / --name-status
parameters.description: Shows a summary of the changed files instead of the full patch.

parameters.name: --show-signature
parameters.description: Checks the commit's GPG signature and prints the result.
