git show.returns: The rendered objects are written to stdout: commit headers and diffs, tag messages, tree entry names, or raw blob contents.

example.title: Inspecting commits, tags and old file versions
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Latest commit with full patch
git show

# Only the subject and author of the previous commit, no diff
git show -s --format='%h %an: %s' HEAD~1

# Files changed by a commit, with diffstat
git show --stat HEAD

# Annotated tag message plus the commit it points to, names only
git show --name-status v1.0.0

# Contents of a file as it was two commits ago (blob output)
git show HEAD~2:README.md > README.old.md

# How conflicts were resolved in a merge commit
git show --remerge-diff HEAD

# Verify the signature of the tip commit
git show --show-signature -s HEAD
example.explanation: These commands show git show used on commits, a tag, and a blob, with options that trim, summarize, or verify the output.

useCases.title: Reviewing a single commit
useCases.scenario: After git bisect or git log finds a suspicious commit, run git show <hash> to read its message and exact changes before you report or revert it.

useCases.title: Recovering an old file version
useCases.scenario: Write a file's content from an earlier revision to disk with git show <rev>:<path>, without checking out that revision or touching the working tree.

useCases.title: Scripting release notes
useCases.scenario: In a CI step, use git show -s --format=... on a tag to pull the commit subject, author, and date into a changelog.

useCases.title: Auditing merge resolutions
useCases.scenario: Use --remerge-diff or --diff-merges=first-parent to see what a merge commit actually introduced, or how its conflicts were resolved.

interview.question: How does git show decide what to print, and what does it show when you give no arguments?
interview.answer: It looks at the type of each object you name. A commit shows its log message and diff. A tag shows its message and the object it references. A tree shows its entry names, and a blob shows its contents. With no arguments, the object defaults to HEAD.
interview.followUp: What does `git show v1.0.0^{tree}` print? It peels the tag down to the root tree of the tagged commit and lists that tree's entry names, with no commit header or diff.

interview.question: How would you print just the subject line of a commit, with no diff, in a script?
interview.answer: Use git show -s --format=%s <rev>. The -s flag (--no-patch) turns off the diff output, and --format chooses which commit fields to print. Prefer tformat:, or a bare %-string, which is treated as tformat:, so each entry ends with a newline.
interview.followUp: Why does --format=%s end with a newline when --format=format:%s might not? A bare string containing % is treated as tformat:, which adds a terminator after each entry. format: only puts separators between entries.

interview.question: What does git show print for a merge commit by default, and how can you change it?
interview.answer: By default it prints a dense combined diff (--cc). This shows only the hunks where the merge result differs from every parent. You can change it with --diff-merges, for example first-parent, separate, combined, remerge, or off, or with shortcuts like --dd or --remerge-diff.
interview.followUp: When is --remerge-diff more useful than --cc? When you want to see how a person resolved conflicts. It re-runs the merge into a temporary tree, which may contain conflict markers, and diffs that against the committed result.

keyPoints: For a tree object, git show lists only the entry names, the same output as ls-tree with name-only. For more detail about a tree, use ls-tree directly.
For a blob, git show prints the file contents with no headers. This lets you redirect an old version of a file straight into a new file.
When you show an annotated tag, you see the tag's own message first and then the object it points to. For a tag that points to a commit, that means the commit and its diff.
git show uses the git log options for formatting, so placeholders like %h, %an, %s and %ad work in --format.
Add -s (or --no-patch) when you want only the metadata without the diff. This also cancels a --patch or --stat set earlier, for example in an alias.
--remerge-diff redoes a two-parent merge in a temporary tree and diffs that result against the real merge commit. This shows how the conflicts were resolved by hand.
--show-signature runs gpg verification on a signed commit and prints the result next to the normal output.
gotchas: The man page lists only the most common options. Many other options come from git log and git diff, so check those pages as well.
Passing -m alone prints nothing for merges. You must also pass -p, or use --diff-merges=on.
format: puts a separator between entries, so the last line may have no trailing newline. tformat: adds a newline after each entry, which suits scripts better.
If re-encoding the commit message fails, Git prints the original bytes without any warning. Invalid sequences can end up in your output.

git sparse-checkout.summary: git sparse-checkout limits your working tree to a chosen subset of tracked files. You can also use it to change that subset later or to bring back the full checkout.
git sparse-checkout.explanation: Git keeps your chosen directories or patterns in $GIT_DIR/info/sparse-checkout. Whenever Git updates the working tree, it uses that file to set or clear the skip-worktree bit on each index entry. Files with the bit set are left out of the working tree, and Git does not treat them as missing. In cone mode, which is the default, you list directories and Git turns them into recursive and parent patterns that it can match quickly with hashing. The set and add subcommands write the file and then update the working tree to match.
git sparse-checkout.syntax: git sparse-checkout (init | list | set | add | reapply | disable | check-rules | clean) [<options>]

parameters.name: set <dir>...
parameters.description: Turns on the required config settings, replaces the sparsity definition with the given directories or patterns, and updates the working tree to match.

parameters.name: add <dir>...
parameters.description: Adds more directories (cone mode) or patterns (non-cone mode) to the current definition.

parameters.name: list
parameters.description: Shows the directories or patterns in the sparse-checkout file.

parameters.name: reapply
parameters.description: Applies the current rules to the working tree again. It also accepts --[no-]cone and --[no-]sparse-index, so you can switch modes without listing your paths again.

parameters.name: disable
parameters.description: Turns off core.sparseCheckout and checks out every file again.

parameters.name: check-rules
parameters.description: Reads paths from stdin and prints the ones that match the sparsity rules. Options: --rules-file <file> to test other rules, and -z for NUL-terminated input and output.

parameters.name: clean
parameters.description: Deletes leftover files that are outside the sparse definition. It only works in cone mode and needs -f/--force unless clean.requireForce is false. Also accepts --dry-run and --verbose.

parameters.name: init
parameters.description: Deprecated. Works like set with no paths and may be removed in the future.

parameters.name: --stdin
parameters.description: For set or add: read directories or patterns from standard input, one per line, instead of from the arguments.

parameters.name: --[no-]cone
parameters.description: Choose directory-based cone mode (the default) or gitignore-style pattern (non-cone) mode.

parameters.name: --[no-]sparse-index
parameters.description: Turn the experimental sparse index on or off. It is off by default.

git sparse-checkout.returns: Most subcommands change config, the sparse-checkout file and the working tree. list prints the directories that are included (cone mode), and check-rules prints the input paths that match the rules.

example.title: Narrow a repo to two directories, inspect, extend, and restore
example.code:
set -e
rm -rf demo && mkdir demo && cd demo && git init -q
mkdir -p MY/DIR1 MY/other SUB/DIR2 docs
for f in README MY/a MY/DIR1/b MY/other/c SUB/DIR2/d docs/e; do echo x > "$f"; done
git add . && git -c user.name=me -c user.email=me@x commit -qm init

# Keep only MY/DIR1 and SUB/DIR2 (cone mode is the default)
git sparse-checkout set MY/DIR1 SUB/DIR2
git sparse-checkout list          # MY/DIR1, SUB/DIR2
find . -path ./.git -prune -o -type f -print | sort

# Which of these paths would be included?
printf 'docs/e\nMY/DIR1/b\n' | git sparse-checkout check-rules

# Grow the cone, then go back to a full checkout
git sparse-checkout add docs
git sparse-checkout disable
ls MY/other                       # c is back
example.explanation: The script builds a small repository, limits it to two directory cones, checks paths against the rules, adds a third directory, and then restores the full working tree.

useCases.title: Monorepo team focus
useCases.scenario: A developer on one service in a large monorepo checks out only that service's directory and the shared libraries it needs, so status and checkout stay fast.

useCases.title: CI jobs on a subset
useCases.scenario: A CI pipeline that builds or tests one component uses set --stdin to read the directories it needs from a generated list, so it only puts those files on disk.

useCases.title: Recovering after a conflicted merge
useCases.scenario: After a rebase writes conflicted files outside the cone, the engineer resolves them and runs reapply, then clean -f, to make the tree sparse again.

useCases.title: Validating sparsity rules in tooling
useCases.scenario: A script runs check-rules with --rules-file on a list of changed paths to see whether a proposed sparse definition would include them.

interview.question: How does Git implement a sparse checkout internally?
interview.answer: Each index entry has a skip-worktree bit. When Git updates the working tree, it sets or clears that bit according to the rules in $GIT_DIR/info/sparse-checkout. Files with the bit set are left out of the working tree, and Git treats their absence as expected rather than as a deletion. They are still tracked, so commits contain the full tree.
interview.followUp: Why does git sparse-checkout list show only directories in cone mode when the file contains many patterns? Answer: In cone mode Git writes the expanded recursive and parent patterns to the file, but list shows only the directories that define the recursive patterns.

interview.question: What is the difference between cone mode and non-cone mode, and which should you use?
interview.answer: In cone mode you list directories, and Git includes everything below them plus the files directly inside their parent directories. Because the rules are this limited, Git can match them quickly with hashing. Non-cone mode accepts any gitignore-style pattern, which costs O(N*M) pattern matches, does not work with --sparse-index, and is deprecated. Use cone mode, which is the default.
interview.followUp: What happens if a hand-edited sparse-checkout file no longer fits the cone pattern format? Answer: Git prints a warning and falls back to non-cone matching, whatever core.sparseCheckoutCone is set to.

interview.question: After a rebase with conflicts, files outside your sparse cone appear in the working tree. How do you clean this up?
interview.answer: Resolve the conflicts and commit or undo any changes to those files, then run git sparse-checkout reapply to apply the rules again. If directories outside the cone still contain leftover files, run git sparse-checkout clean, which only deletes with -f/--force. Run it with --dry-run or --verbose first to see what it would remove.
interview.followUp: Why might clean still leave a directory in place? Answer: Merge conflicts or modified files outside the definition can keep files that would otherwise be removed. --verbose lists the files in each directory being considered, which helps explain why one is still there.

keyPoints: In cone mode you get everything at any depth under each listed directory. You also get the files that sit directly inside each of its parent directories, including the repository root.
Even when you list no directories, files at the top level of the repository stay in the working tree.
Sparsity is set per worktree. The set subcommand turns on worktree-specific config so that other linked worktrees keep their own settings.
Other commands respect the sparse definition. Switching branches leaves files outside it alone, and commit -a does not record those missing files as deleted.
add extends an existing definition. It is not a way to start one, so run set first.
A merge or rebase can bring files outside your cone back into the working tree, for example to show a conflict. Once you have resolved it, run reapply to make the tree sparse again.
A sparse index stores directory entries in place of the files beneath them. This can make commands like status and add much faster.
Changing the sparse rules never initializes or removes a submodule's checkout, because removing one could lose unpushed or untracked work.
gotchas: Non-cone (pattern) mode is officially deprecated. It scales poorly and makes it easy to pass shell-expanded globs by mistake, so use cone mode.
Narrowing the selection with set can silently delete ignored files, such as build output, in directories that drop out of the cone.
If a directory outside the cone holds untracked files that are not ignored, Git leaves the directory in place and prints a warning.
Older Git versions and external tools may not understand a sparse index. To rewrite the index as a normal one, run init --no-sparse-index.

git stash.summary: git stash saves your uncommitted changes to the working tree and index, then resets them to match HEAD so your directory is clean. You can bring the saved changes back later, either on the same commit or on a different one.
git stash.explanation: Running git stash with no subcommand is the same as running git stash push. It records your work as a special commit and then rolls the tracked files back to HEAD. That commit has two parents. The first is the HEAD commit. The second is a commit holding the state of the index. The stash commit's own tree holds the state of the working tree. The newest entry is stored at refs/stash, and older entries live in that ref's reflog. You refer to entries as stash@{n}, or just n. Use list and show to inspect entries, apply or pop to restore them, and drop or clear to delete them.

parameters.name: -m, --message <message>
parameters.description: An optional description stored with the entry. Without it, the entry is labelled "WIP on <branch>".

parameters.name: -u, --include-untracked
parameters.description: push/save: also stashes untracked files and then removes them. show: includes untracked files in the diff.

parameters.name: -a, --all
parameters.description: Like -u, but also stashes and removes ignored files.

parameters.name: -k, --[no-]keep-index
parameters.description: Leaves your staged changes in place in the index after stashing.

parameters.name: -S, --staged
parameters.description: Stashes only the changes that are currently staged.

parameters.name: -p, --patch
parameters.description: Lets you pick, hunk by hunk, which changes to stash. Implies --keep-index.

parameters.name: --index
parameters.description: apply/pop: tries to restore the staged changes to the index as well as restoring the working tree.

parameters.name: <pathspec>...
parameters.description: push only: stashes and rolls back only the files that match.

parameters.name: <stash>
parameters.description: The entry to use with apply, pop, drop, show, branch or export. Defaults to stash@{0}.

git stash.returns: Exits with status 0 on success. If apply, pop or branch hits conflicts, it exits with status 1 and keeps the entry. Any other failure gives a different non-zero status.

example.title: Shelve work, hotfix, then resume
example.code:
# mid-feature, untracked files included
git stash push -u -m "feature: half-done parser"
git stash list

# make the urgent fix on a clean tree
git switch main
# ...edit...
git commit -am "Fix crash on empty input"

# go back and restore work (index too)
git switch feature
if ! git stash pop --index; then
  echo "Conflicts: resolve, then run: git stash drop"
fi

# preview another entry as a patch
git stash show -p stash@{1}
example.explanation: This stashes tracked and untracked changes under a label, makes a fix on another branch, then pops the work back with the staged changes restored, and warns you if the pop hit conflicts.

useCases.title: Pulling into a dirty tree
useCases.scenario: git pull won't run because your local edits conflict with incoming changes. Stash them, pull, then pop them back.

useCases.title: Testing a partial commit
useCases.scenario: Stage part of your changes and run git stash push --keep-index. Now you can build and test exactly what you are about to commit, then pop the rest.

useCases.title: Parking an unrelated fix
useCases.scenario: Stage a small unrelated change, run stash push --staged, and pop it later on a separate fixup branch.

useCases.title: Stash no longer applies cleanly
useCases.scenario: Use git stash branch <name> to restore the stash on a new branch that starts from its original base commit.

interview.question: What is the difference between git stash pop and git stash apply?
interview.answer: Both restore a stash entry on top of your current working tree. pop also removes the entry from the list, but apply keeps it. apply also accepts any commit that looks like it was made by stash push or stash create. If pop hits conflicts, it does not drop the entry, so you have to run git stash drop yourself once you've resolved them.
interview.followUp: Why would you choose apply in a script? Because the entry survives whatever happens, so you can apply the same stash to several branches, and you only drop it once you know it applied cleanly.

interview.question: How is a stash entry stored internally?
interview.answer: A stash is a commit whose tree holds the state of the working directory. Its first parent is the HEAD commit at the time you stashed. Its second parent is a commit holding the state of the index, and that commit is itself a child of HEAD. The newest stash is stored at refs/stash, and older stashes are entries in that ref's reflog.
interview.followUp: Where do untracked files go when you use -u? They are stored in an extra commit attached to the stash. The page doesn't describe that layout in detail, but stash show -u or --only-untracked will show you those files.

interview.question: Which changes does a plain git stash leave behind, and how do you change that?
interview.answer: A plain stash only saves tracked files, both modified and staged. Untracked and ignored files stay where they are. Add -u to include untracked files, or -a to also include ignored ones; either way they are removed from the directory afterwards. You can also narrow a stash with a pathspec, --staged or --patch.
interview.followUp: How can you get back a stash you dropped by accident? Run git fsck --unreachable, keep the commit hashes, and pipe them to git log --merges --no-walk --grep=WIP to find likely stash commits. Then apply the one you want, or save it with git stash store.

keyPoints: Entries form a stack. stash@{0} is the newest, and older ones are reached through the reflog of refs/stash. You can also use time-based names like stash@{2.hours.ago}.
By default, untracked files are left out. Add -u to stash them too and remove them from the directory, or -a to also include ignored files.
--keep-index stashes everything but leaves what you have staged in place. This lets you build and test exactly the changes you are about to commit.
--staged stashes only what is in the index. It works like committing those changes, except they go to the stash instead of the current branch.
If you give a pathspec to push, only the matching files are stashed and reset. Every other change stays in your working tree.
--patch lets you choose individual hunks to stash interactively, the same way git add -p works.
export turns stashes into a chain of commits that you can push to and fetch from another repository. On the other side, import adds them back to the stash list.
Scripts can detect a conflicted apply, pop or branch because the command exits with status 1.
gotchas: If pop runs into conflicts, the entry stays in the list. Resolve the conflicts yourself, then run git stash drop.
Entries removed with clear or drop are no longer referenced and can be garbage-collected. The only way to recover them is to search with git fsck --unreachable.
git stash save is deprecated and does not accept pathspecs. All of its non-option arguments are joined together into the message.
If you use the short form without the word 'push', you must put '--' before any paths. This stops a mistyped subcommand from creating a stash by accident.

git status.summary: git status reports the state of your working tree. It lists what is staged for the next commit, what has changed but is not staged, and which files Git is not tracking.
git status.explanation: Git makes three comparisons. It compares HEAD with the index, which gives the changes that a plain commit would record. It compares the index with the working tree, which gives edits you have not staged yet. It also scans for files that are neither tracked nor ignored. The default long output is meant for people and includes hints about what to do next. The short format (-s) shows each path with a two-letter XY code. The --porcelain format looks like the short format, but it is meant for scripts and stays stable. By default, status also refreshes the cached stat information in the index and writes it back, so later commands don't have to repeat that work.

parameters.name: -s, --short
parameters.description: Prints the compact XY-code format.

parameters.name: -b, --branch
parameters.description: Adds the branch name and upstream tracking info to short output.

parameters.name: --show-stash
parameters.description: Shows how many stash entries exist.

parameters.name: --porcelain[=<version>]
parameters.description: Machine-parseable output that stays stable. Defaults to v1.

parameters.name: --long
parameters.description: Human-readable long format. This is the default.

parameters.name: -v, --verbose
parameters.description: Also shows the staged diff. Give it twice to also show the unstaged diff.

parameters.name: -u[<mode>], --untracked-files[=<mode>]
parameters.description: Controls how untracked files are listed. With no mode given, it means all.

parameters.name: --ignore-submodules[=<when>]
parameters.description: Controls which submodule changes are ignored. Defaults to all.

parameters.name: --ignored[=<mode>]
parameters.description: Also lists ignored files.

parameters.name: -z
parameters.description: Ends entries with NUL instead of LF. Implies --porcelain=v1 unless another format is given.

parameters.name: --column[=<options>], --no-column
parameters.description: Shows untracked files in columns.

parameters.name: --ahead-behind, --no-ahead-behind
parameters.description: Turns detailed ahead/behind counts against the upstream on or off. On by default.

example.title: Fail a script if the working tree is dirty
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Human-friendly overview with branch info
git status -sb

# Stable, script-safe check (no lock contention)
changes=$(git --no-optional-locks status --porcelain=v1)
if [ -n "$changes" ]; then
  echo "Working tree is not clean:" >&2
  echo "$changes" >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "Clean - safe to release"
example.explanation: The script prints a short status with branch info, then uses lock-free porcelain output to exit with an error if anything is staged, modified or untracked.

useCases.title: Review before committing
useCases.scenario: Before running git commit, check which files are staged and which edits you still need to git add.

useCases.title: CI clean-tree check
useCases.scenario: After a build or code generation step, have the pipeline run git status --porcelain and fail if any files changed unexpectedly.

useCases.title: Shell prompt or IDE integration
useCases.scenario: Show the branch, ahead/behind counts and dirty state using --porcelain=v2 --branch, and run it with --no-optional-locks so it doesn't block other Git processes.

useCases.title: Resolving merge conflicts
useCases.scenario: Find the unmerged paths (UU, AA and similar codes) that still need resolving before you finish a merge, rebase or cherry-pick.

interview.question: What three sets of paths does git status report?
interview.answer: First, paths that differ between HEAD and the index; these are what a commit would record. Second, paths that differ between the index and the working tree. Third, untracked files that are not ignored. You would have to git add the second and third groups before committing them.
interview.followUp: How do you see the actual content changes and not just file names? Pass -v to include the staged diff, like git diff --cached, and pass -v -v to add the unstaged diff too.

interview.question: In the short format, what do 'M ', ' M' and '??' mean?
interview.answer: The left character X is the index, and the right character Y is the working tree. 'M ' means the change is staged and the working tree matches the index. ' M' means the file was modified but not staged. '??' means the file is untracked.
interview.followUp: What does 'UU' mean? It is an unmerged path where both sides of the merge modified the file, so the conflict still needs to be resolved.

interview.question: Why use --porcelain in scripts instead of the default output?
interview.answer: The long format is meant for people and may change at any time. Porcelain output is guaranteed to stay backward-compatible and ignores user settings such as color.status and status.relativePaths. For filenames with unusual characters, add -z so entries end with NUL and nothing is quoted.
interview.followUp: When would you choose v2 over v1? Choose v2 when you need branch headers (oid, head, upstream, ahead/behind), file modes and object names, or rename scores with the original path.

keyPoints: For scripts, use --porcelain. Its output is designed to stay the same across Git versions, and your personal settings such as colour do not change it.

If you run it from a subdirectory, the human-readable output shows paths relative to where you are, which makes them easy to copy and paste. Porcelain output always shows paths relative to the repository root.

In short format, the two letters XY mean different things depending on the situation. Normally X is the index and Y is the working tree. During an unresolved conflict, they describe the two sides of the merge. '??' marks an untracked file.
With -v you also see the staged diff, just like git diff --cached. Pass -v twice to also see the unstaged diff.
--porcelain=v2 adds header lines such as branch.oid, branch.head and branch.ab, plus file modes and object names for each changed entry.
In large repositories, setting core.untrackedCache=true, optionally together with core.fsmonitor, means status only rescans directories that have changed since the last run.
Add -b to short output to get a '## branch tracking-info' header line, and --show-stash to see how many stash entries you have.
gotchas: Don't parse the default long output in scripts. Its wording and layout can change between releases.
status writes the refreshed index back to disk. If you run it in the background, for example from an editor or a prompt, it can block other Git processes. Use git --no-optional-locks status there.
The mode for -u has to be attached directly to the flag. '-uno' works, but '-u no' does not.
-uno (or status.showUntrackedFiles=no) is the fastest setting, but it hides new files completely, so they are easy to forget to commit.

git submodule.summary: git submodule lets you add, initialize, update, inspect and manage submodules. A submodule is another Git repository nested inside a superproject and pinned to a specific commit.
git submodule.explanation: The superproject records each submodule in two places: a commit pointer (gitlink) in its tree, and a name/path/URL entry in the versioned .gitmodules file. The init subcommand copies URLs from .gitmodules into your local .git/config. The update subcommand then clones any missing submodules, fetches commits that are missing, and moves each submodule's working tree to match what the superproject expects. By default it does this by checking out the recorded commit on a detached HEAD. Other subcommands handle status, URL syncing, branch tracking, unregistering submodules and running a command in every submodule.
git submodule.syntax:
git submodule [--quiet] add [<options>] [--] <repository> [<path>]
git submodule [--quiet] status [--cached] [--recursive] [--] [<path>…]
git submodule [--quiet] init [--] [<path>…]
git submodule [--quiet] deinit [-f|--force] (--all|[--] <path>...)
git submodule [--quiet] update [<options>] [--] [<path>…]
git submodule [--quiet] set-branch [<options>] [--] <path>
git submodule [--quiet] set-url [--] <path> <newurl>
git submodule [--quiet] summary [<options>] [--] [<path>…]
git submodule [--quiet] foreach [--recursive] <command>
git submodule [--quiet] sync [--recursive] [--] [<path>…]
git submodule [--quiet] absorbgitdirs [--] [<path>…]

parameters.name: <repository>
parameters.description: Used by add. This is the origin URL of the new submodule. It can be absolute, or relative (starting with ./ or ../) to the superproject's default remote.

parameters.name: <path>...
parameters.description: Limits the command to the submodules at these paths. It is required for add, where it sets where the clone goes and, by default, the submodule's logical name.

parameters.name: --recursive
parameters.description: Also processes nested submodules. Only valid for foreach, update, status and sync.

parameters.name: --init
parameters.description: Used with update. Initializes any submodules that have not been initialized yet before updating them.

parameters.name: --remote
parameters.description: Used with update. Updates the submodule to its remote-tracking branch instead of the commit recorded in the superproject.

parameters.name: --checkout | --rebase | --merge
parameters.description: Chooses how update applies the target commit: a detached checkout (the default), rebasing the current branch, or merging into it.

parameters.name: -b, --branch=<branch>
parameters.description: Used with add. Sets the branch to track, which is stored as submodule.<name>.branch in .gitmodules for update --remote.

parameters.name: -f, --force
parameters.description: Forces add, deinit or update to go ahead even when it would normally fail.

parameters.name: -j, --jobs=<n>
parameters.description: Used with update. Clones new submodules in parallel. Defaults to submodule.fetchJobs.

parameters.name: --depth=<depth>
parameters.description: Used with add or update. Makes a shallow clone with history truncated to this many revisions.

parameters.name: -q, --quiet
parameters.description: Prints only error messages.

example.title: Add, clone and maintain submodules
example.code:
# Add a library as a submodule and commit it
git submodule add -b main https://example.com/libfoo.git vendor/libfoo
git commit -m "Add libfoo submodule"

# After cloning the superproject elsewhere: init + fetch everything, including nested ones
git submodule update --init --recursive --jobs 4

# Inspect state (- uninitialized, + differs from index)
git submodule status --recursive

# Pull upstream changes from the tracked branch, then record the new pointer
git submodule update --remote vendor/libfoo
git add vendor/libfoo
git commit -m "Bump libfoo"

# Run a command in each submodule
git submodule foreach 'echo $sm_path $(git rev-parse HEAD)'
example.explanation: This walks through the usual cycle: add a submodule, set it up after a fresh clone, check its status, move it to a newer upstream commit and record that change in the superproject.

useCases.title: Vendoring a third-party library
useCases.scenario: Pin an external dependency to an exact commit inside your repo, and move to a newer version only when you choose to.

useCases.title: Setting up a fresh clone in CI
useCases.scenario: Run update --init --recursive with --jobs (and optionally --depth) so a build agent gets every nested repo at the exact commits recorded.

useCases.title: Handling a moved upstream URL
useCases.scenario: After a submodule's hosting location changes in .gitmodules, run sync (or set-url) so existing local clones fetch from the new address.

useCases.title: Bulk maintenance across submodules
useCases.scenario: Use foreach to run commands such as git fetch or git clean in every checked-out submodule at once.

interview.question: Why does a submodule end up on a detached HEAD after git submodule update?
interview.answer: The superproject records a specific commit for each submodule, not a branch. The default update procedure, checkout, checks out that recorded commit on a detached HEAD. If you want to stay on a branch, use --rebase or --merge, or set submodule.<name>.update.
interview.followUp: What is the difference between 'update --merge' and 'update --remote --merge'? The plain version merges the commit recorded in the superproject's gitlink into the submodule's current branch. With --remote, it merges the commit from the submodule's upstream tracking branch instead.

interview.question: What is the difference between git submodule init and git submodule update?
interview.answer: init copies each submodule's URL (and its update setting, if safe) from .gitmodules into .git/config, which marks the submodule as one you want. update then clones missing submodules, fetches missing commits and puts each working tree at the expected commit. You can combine both steps with update --init.
interview.followUp: Why doesn't init copy a custom '!command' update setting from .gitmodules? .gitmodules comes from whoever publishes the repo, so copying an arbitrary command would let a remote repo run code on your machine. Git skips it for security reasons.

interview.question: How do you fully remove a submodule versus just getting rid of your local copy?
interview.answer: git submodule deinit <path> removes the submodule's section from .git/config and its working tree, but leaves the project's history alone. To remove the submodule from the repository for everyone, run git rm <path>, which also removes its .gitmodules entry, and commit the change.
interview.followUp: What happens to the submodule's git directory after deinit? It stays under the superproject's $GIT_DIR/modules, so running git submodule init again can bring the submodule back without re-cloning.

keyPoints: In the output of status, a leading '-' means the submodule is not initialized, '+' means its checked-out commit differs from the one in the superproject's index, and 'U' means it has merge conflicts.
init only registers submodules in your local .git/config, using .gitmodules as a template. Before running update, you can edit those URLs for your own setup.

update --remote takes its target from the submodule's upstream branch. That branch comes from submodule.<name>.branch, or the remote HEAD if none is set, and the command fetches first unless you pass --no-fetch.

foreach runs a shell command in every checked-out submodule and exposes $name, $sm_path, $displaypath, $sha1 and $toplevel. It stops at the first non-zero exit unless you append '|| :' to the command.
sync copies the URLs in .gitmodules into the local config, but only for submodules that already have a URL entry there.
--recursive makes foreach, update, status and sync go into submodules of submodules, to any depth.

absorbgitdirs moves a .git directory that sits inside a submodule into the superproject's $GIT_DIR/modules, then connects it back with a .git file. This fixes repos that were cloned on their own and added later.
gotchas: deinit only removes your local checkout and config. To actually remove a submodule from the project and commit that change, use git rm.
deinit refuses to run without a path. You must name the paths or pass --all explicitly.
Relative URLs are resolved like directories: a sibling repo next to bar.git must be written ../foo.git, not ./foo.git.
update --force with the checkout procedure throws away local changes in the submodule.

git switch.summary: git switch moves you onto a different branch. It can also create a branch, reset one, detach HEAD at a commit, or start an orphan branch as part of the same command.
git switch.explanation: When you run git switch <branch>, Git points HEAD at that branch. It then rewrites the index and working tree so they match the branch's tip, and every commit you make after that goes on top of the branch. You can add flags to create a branch first (-c), reset an existing one (-C), or land on a bare commit with no branch (--detach). Unlike git checkout, switch never restores individual files and only changes branches. If the switch would overwrite your uncommitted work, Git stops unless you tell it to throw that work away or carry it along.
git switch.syntax:
git switch [<options>] [--no-guess] <branch>
git switch [<options>] --detach [<start-point>]
git switch [<options>] (-c|-C) <new-branch> [<start-point>]
git switch [<options>] --orphan <new-branch>

parameters.name: <branch>
parameters.description: The existing branch to move to. Use - for the previous branch, or @{-N} for the Nth-last branch or commit you switched to.

parameters.name: <new-branch>
parameters.description: The name to give the branch created by -c, -C or --orphan.

parameters.name: <start-point>
parameters.description: Where the new branch (or detached HEAD) begins. It defaults to the current HEAD. You can write A...B to mean their single merge base.

parameters.name: -c, --create
parameters.description: Create <new-branch> at <start-point> and then switch to it.

parameters.name: -C, --force-create
parameters.description: Same as -c, but if the branch already exists it is reset to <start-point>.

parameters.name: -d, --detach
parameters.description: Switch to a commit without being on any branch.

parameters.name: --guess / --no-guess
parameters.description: Turns on or off creating a tracking branch automatically from a remote branch with the same name. It is on by default, and the checkout.guess setting can change that.

parameters.name: -f, --discard-changes
parameters.description: Switch even when you have local changes, and throw those changes away.

parameters.name: -m, --merge
parameters.description: Stash conflicting local changes automatically and reapply them after the switch.

parameters.name: --conflict=<style>
parameters.description: Works like --merge but sets how conflict hunks are shown.

parameters.name: -t, --track[=(direct|inherit)] / --no-track
parameters.description: Turns upstream configuration for the new branch on or off. -t implies -c.

parameters.name: --orphan
parameters.description: Create a new branch that has no commits yet.

example.title: Everyday branch hopping
example.code:
# Start a feature branch from main
git switch -c feature/login main

# Carry uncommitted edits to another branch
git switch -m hotfix

# Jump back to the previous branch
git switch -

# Inspect an old commit without a branch
git switch --detach HEAD~3

# Keep experimental work done while detached
git switch -c spike/idea

# Track a remote branch (auto-guessed from origin)
git switch new-topic
example.explanation: These commands show the common ways to use git switch: creating a branch, carrying local edits, jumping back, detaching HEAD, keeping detached work, and tracking a remote branch automatically.

useCases.title: Hotfix interruption
useCases.scenario: You're partway through a feature when an urgent fix comes in. You create a branch with git switch -c hotfix main, fix the bug, and return to the feature with git switch -.

useCases.title: Reviewing a teammate's branch
useCases.scenario: After git fetch, running git switch their-topic creates a local branch that tracks origin/their-topic, so you don't need to type any --track options.

useCases.title: Bisect-style inspection
useCases.scenario: To check whether an old release had a bug, you run git switch --detach v1.2.0 and build or test it without moving any branch.

useCases.title: Separate history for docs
useCases.scenario: git switch --orphan gh-pages starts an empty branch with no shared history, for example to hold generated site files.

interview.question: Why was git switch introduced when git checkout already exists?
interview.answer: git checkout does two unrelated jobs: it changes branches and it restores files, so a slip in its arguments can overwrite your work. git switch only changes branches, and git restore handles files. That split makes it clearer what each command is meant to do and harder to destroy changes by accident.
interview.followUp: What is the git switch equivalent of git checkout -b feature origin/main? Answer: git switch -c feature origin/main. Depending on branch.autoSetupMerge, it may also set up upstream tracking to origin/main.

interview.question: What happens if you run git switch while you have uncommitted changes?
interview.answer: Git switches and keeps your changes as long as none of the files you edited differ between the two branches. If a file does differ, Git refuses and reports that you have local changes. You can then use -m to stash the conflicting edits and reapply them after the switch, or -f/--discard-changes to throw them away.
interview.followUp: After git switch -m reports conflicts, how do you clean up? Answer: the stash entry is kept, so you resolve the conflicts and then run git stash drop. Alternatively, reset the working tree and run git stash pop later.

interview.question: How does git switch -c differ from git switch -C?
interview.answer: -c creates a new branch and fails if that name already exists. -C creates it, or if it already exists, resets it to the start point, which is the same as git branch -f followed by git switch. Both are transactional, so nothing changes if the switch itself fails.
interview.followUp: Why can git switch refuse a branch even though it exists? Answer: another worktree may already have it checked out. You can override that with --ignore-other-worktrees, which lets more than one worktree hold the same branch.

keyPoints: You can switch with uncommitted changes in place. Git only refuses when the switch would destroy some of those changes.
-c works like running git branch and then git switch as one all-or-nothing step. If the switch fails, for example because another worktree is using the branch, no branch is created or reset.
-C is the force version of -c. If the branch name already exists, Git moves that branch to the start point.

If you name a branch that doesn't exist locally but exists on exactly one remote, Git creates a local tracking branch for it automatically. If several remotes have it, the checkout.defaultRemote setting decides which one wins.
git switch - takes you back to the branch you were on before, which is the same as @{-1}.
--detach lets you check out any commit or tag to look around or experiment without moving a branch. If the work turns out useful, you can keep it later with git switch -c.
-m keeps your uncommitted work: Git stashes the edits that conflict, switches, and then applies them again on the new branch.
gotchas: -f is a short alias for --discard-changes, so it silently deletes your uncommitted edits in both the index and the working tree.
With -m, reapplying your changes can still produce conflicts. When that happens the stash entry is kept, and you have to resolve the conflicts and drop the stash yourself.
--orphan clears out all tracked files, so the working tree starts empty on the new branch.
Submodules stay where they are unless you ask for --recurse-submodules, so after a switch they can point at the wrong commits.

git tag.summary: git tag creates, lists, deletes and verifies tags. Tags are names stored under refs/tags/ that mark a specific object, usually a commit such as a release point.
git tag.explanation: When you give it a name, git tag adds a reference under refs/tags/ that points at the target object, which is HEAD unless you name another one. If you pass -a, -s or -u, Git first writes a tag object that holds the tagger, the date, a message and an optional signature, and the ref points at that object. Passing -m, -F or --trailer on its own also gives you an annotated tag. Without any of those flags you get a lightweight tag, which is a ref that points straight at the commit. The -d, -l and -v flags switch the command into delete, list or verify mode. Listing is the default when you pass no arguments.
git tag.syntax:
git tag [-a | -s | -u <key-id>] [-f] [-m <msg> | -F <file>] [-e] [--trailer <token>[(=|:)<value>]] <tagname> [<commit> | <object>]
git tag -d <tagname>...
git tag [-n[<num>]] -l [--contains <commit>] [--no-contains <commit>] [--points-at <object>] [--sort=<key>] [--format=<format>] [--merged <commit>] [--no-merged <commit>] [<pattern>...]
git tag -v [--format=<format>] <tagname>...

parameters.name: <tagname>
parameters.description: The tag to create, delete or describe. It must pass the git check-ref-format rules.

parameters.name: <commit> | <object>
parameters.description: What the new tag points at, usually a commit. Defaults to HEAD.

parameters.name: -a / --annotate
parameters.description: Creates an unsigned annotated tag object.

parameters.name: -s / --sign, -u / --local-user=<key-id>
parameters.description: Creates a signed tag, using either the default signing key or the key you name.

parameters.name: -m <msg> / -F <file>
parameters.description: Supplies the tag message inline or from a file (use - to read from stdin). Either one implies -a.

parameters.name: -f / --force
parameters.description: Replaces an existing tag that has the same name instead of failing.

parameters.name: -d / --delete
parameters.description: Deletes the named tags.

parameters.name: -v / --verify
parameters.description: Verifies the cryptographic signature of the named tags.

parameters.name: -l / --list [<pattern>...]
parameters.description: Lists tags, optionally only those matching shell-wildcard patterns.

parameters.name: -n<num>
parameters.description: Prints up to <num> lines of each tag's annotation when listing.

parameters.name: --sort=<key>
parameters.description: Sorts the listing by a for-each-ref key. Prefix the key with - for descending order.

parameters.name: --contains / --no-contains / --merged / --no-merged / --points-at
parameters.description: Filters the listing by containment, reachability or the object a tag points at.

example.title: Tag a release, inspect and clean up
example.code:
# Annotated release tag on the current commit
git tag -a v1.4.0 -m "Release 1.4.0"

# Lightweight bookmark on an older commit
git tag before-refactor 9fceb02

# List v1.* tags in version order, newest first, with first message line
git tag -n -l 'v1.*' --sort=-version:refname

# Which tags already contain a given fix?
git tag --contains a1b2c3d

# Remove the temporary bookmark
git tag -d before-refactor

# Publish the release tag
git push origin v1.4.0
example.explanation: The script creates an annotated release tag and a lightweight tag, lists and filters tags, deletes the lightweight one, and pushes the release tag.

useCases.title: Marking releases
useCases.scenario: A CI pipeline creates a signed annotated tag such as v2.3.0 on the release commit, so builds and changelogs can refer to an exact, verifiable point in history.

useCases.title: Finding which releases include a fix
useCases.scenario: While triaging a bug, run git tag --contains <fix-sha> to see which shipped versions already include the patch.

useCases.title: Temporary bookmarks
useCases.scenario: Before a risky rebase, a developer drops a lightweight tag on the current commit so they can easily get back to it, then deletes it with -d.

interview.question: What is the difference between a lightweight and an annotated tag, and how does git tag decide which one to create?
interview.answer: An annotated tag is a real tag object holding the tagger, the date, a message and optionally a signature, and the ref points at that object. A lightweight tag is a ref under refs/tags/ that points straight at the target. git tag makes an annotated tag when you pass -a, -s or -u, or when you pass -m, -F or --trailer without those flags. Otherwise it makes a lightweight tag.
interview.followUp: Why might git describe print nothing useful in a repo that only has lightweight tags? Because describe skips lightweight tags by default, which reflects the view that annotated tags are the ones meant for releases.

interview.question: You tagged the wrong commit as v1.0. How do you fix it?
interview.answer: If you haven't pushed it, re-run git tag -f v1.0 <correct-commit> to replace it. If it has already been published, the docs say the sensible choice is a new name such as v1.0.1, because Git deliberately won't change tags other people already have.
interview.followUp: If you do force-move a published tag, what do other people have to do? Each person deletes their local copy with git tag -d v1.0 and fetches it again with git fetch origin tag v1.0, then checks it with git rev-parse.

interview.question: How do you list only the v2 tags, sorted as versions, with their first message line?
interview.answer: Run git tag -n -l 'v2*' --sort=version:refname. -l takes shell-glob patterns, -n with no number prints the first line of each annotation, and version:refname sorts names as version numbers. Adding - in front of the key reverses the order.
interview.followUp: What does -n show for a lightweight tag that has no annotation? It shows the commit message of the tagged commit instead.

keyPoints: An annotated tag stores extra metadata: who created it, when, a message and possibly a signature. A lightweight tag is just a name for an object.
Use annotated tags for releases you publish, and lightweight tags for private or throwaway bookmarks.
Listing patterns are shell globs, and you can pass several. A tag is shown if it matches any one of them.
The version:refname (or v:refname) sort key orders tags like version numbers, so v1.10 comes after v1.9. Plain lexicographic order would put it first.
If you leave out the target, the tag goes on HEAD. To tag an older commit, add its hash or another revision name after the tag name.
Signing works with several backends, not only GPG. The gpg.format setting picks the backend.
When you combine several --contains filters, a tag only has to contain at least one of the listed commits to be shown.
Tag names follow the ref-name rules, so some characters are not allowed.
gotchas: git describe and some other commands that name commits skip lightweight tags by default. A release marked only with a lightweight tag may not show up in their output.
Moving a tag that has already been pushed does not update other people's copies. They keep the old target unless they delete the tag and fetch it again.
If tag creation fails, the message you typed in the editor is kept in TAG_EDITMSG, but the next git tag run can overwrite it.
With tag.gpgSign turned on, a script can end up signing many tags, so use an agent to avoid typing your passphrase over and over.

git worktree.summary: git worktree lets one repository have several working directories, so you can check out more than one branch at once. Its subcommands add, list, lock, unlock, move, remove, prune and repair these linked worktrees.
git worktree.explanation: A repository has one main worktree (none if it is bare) and can have any number of linked worktrees. Running add creates a directory for the new worktree plus a private admin folder under $GIT_DIR/worktrees/<id>. The new directory gets a small .git file that points back to that folder. All worktrees share the same objects, refs and config. Each one keeps its own HEAD, index and pseudo-refs. If you omit <commit-ish>, add uses the last part of the path as the branch name and creates that branch from HEAD if it doesn't exist yet.
git worktree.syntax:
git worktree add [-f] [--detach] [--checkout] [--lock [--reason <string>]] [--orphan] [(-b | -B) <new-branch>] <path> [<commit-ish>]
git worktree list [-v | --porcelain [-z]]
git worktree lock [--reason <string>] <worktree>
git worktree move <worktree> <new-path>
git worktree prune [-n] [-v] [--expire <expire>]
git worktree remove [-f] <worktree>
git worktree repair [<path>...]
git worktree unlock <worktree>

parameters.name: <path>
parameters.description: Directory where add creates the new worktree. If no branch is given, its last component becomes the branch name.

parameters.name: <commit-ish>
parameters.description: What to check out in the new worktree. A bare '-' means @{-1} (the previous branch).

parameters.name: <worktree>
parameters.description: Names an existing worktree by relative or absolute path, or by its last path components if they are unique.

parameters.name: -b / -B <new-branch>
parameters.description: Creates a new branch at <commit-ish> (HEAD by default) for the worktree. -B resets the branch if it already exists.

parameters.name: -f / --force
parameters.description: Overrides safety checks: a branch checked out elsewhere, a missing path, or an unclean worktree. Give it twice for locked worktrees.

parameters.name: -d / --detach
parameters.description: With add, gives the new worktree a detached HEAD instead of a branch.

parameters.name: --orphan
parameters.description: With add, starts the worktree with an empty tree and index on a new unborn branch.

parameters.name: --lock / --reason <string>
parameters.description: Locks the worktree as soon as it is created, optionally recording why.

parameters.name: --porcelain / -z
parameters.description: With list, prints machine-readable output; -z ends each line with NUL instead of a newline.

parameters.name: -n / --dry-run, --expire <time>
parameters.description: With prune, reports what would be removed without removing it, or only prunes missing worktrees older than <time>.

example.title: Hotfix in a temporary worktree without touching your current work
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Create ../hotfix on a new branch based on main
git worktree add -b hotfix ../hotfix main

# Do the fix there; your current checkout stays as it is
(
  cd ../hotfix
  echo "fix" >> CHANGELOG.md
  git commit -am "Hotfix: patch release"
)

# See every worktree in script-friendly form
git worktree list --porcelain

# Clean up when done (fails if ../hotfix has uncommitted changes)
git worktree remove ../hotfix

# Clear admin data for any worktree folders that were deleted by hand
git worktree prune --verbose
example.explanation: The script commits a hotfix on its own branch in a separate directory, lists all worktrees, then removes the temporary one and prunes leftover entries, all without disturbing the original checkout.

useCases.title: Urgent fix in the middle of a refactor
useCases.scenario: Your working tree is full of moved and new files that you don't want to stash. You add a temporary worktree on main, commit the fix there, and remove the worktree when you're done.

useCases.title: Throwaway test checkout
useCases.scenario: Run git worktree add -d to get a detached worktree for trying out a build or experiment. No branch is created and your current branch is left alone.

useCases.title: Reviewing several branches side by side
useCases.scenario: Keep long-lived worktrees for a release branch and a feature branch, so you can build and test both at once without switching back and forth.

useCases.title: Worktree on removable storage
useCases.scenario: Keep a worktree on an external drive and lock it with a reason, so automatic pruning doesn't delete its admin data while the drive is unplugged.

interview.question: What do linked worktrees share with the main worktree, and what does each one keep separately?
interview.answer: Every worktree uses the same object database, the same refs under refs/, and by default the same config file. Each worktree has its own HEAD, index and other pseudo-refs, plus refs under refs/bisect, refs/worktree and refs/rewritten. These per-worktree files live in $GIT_DIR/worktrees/<id>, and $GIT_COMMON_DIR points back to the main .git directory.
interview.followUp: How do you read another worktree's HEAD from the one you're in? Use the special ref paths: main-worktree/HEAD for the main worktree, or worktrees/<name>/HEAD for a linked one. Commands like git rev-parse resolve these correctly.

interview.question: You deleted a linked worktree's folder with rm -rf. What happens, and how do you clean up?
interview.answer: The admin entry under $GIT_DIR/worktrees stays behind, and git worktree list marks it as prunable. Git eventually removes it on its own, depending on gc.worktreePruneExpire. You can also run git worktree prune from any worktree right away, adding -n first to preview what would go.
interview.followUp: What if you moved the folder instead of deleting it? Run git worktree repair from inside the moved worktree, or from any worktree with the new path as an argument, and Git rewrites the gitdir links instead of pruning the entry.

interview.question: How do you give one worktree settings that the others don't get?
interview.answer: Turn on the extension with git config extensions.worktreeConfig true. Then git config --worktree writes to that worktree's own config.worktree file. If core.worktree or core.bare is set in the shared config, move it into the main worktree's config.worktree. Older Git versions can't open repositories that have this extension enabled.
interview.followUp: Why can turning on worktreeConfig break a bare repository setup? Once the extension is on, core.bare=true in the shared config no longer applies only to the main worktree, so it affects every worktree; you have to move it into the main worktree's config.worktree.

keyPoints: Refs are mostly shared between worktrees. Pseudo-refs such as HEAD belong to each worktree, and so do refs under refs/bisect, refs/worktree and refs/rewritten.
Every linked worktree gets its own admin folder under $GIT_DIR/worktrees. The folder is usually named after the worktree's directory, with a number added if that name is taken.
Locking a worktree keeps prune from deleting its admin data. That matters when the worktree sits on removable media or a network share. A lock also blocks move and remove.
Passing --lock to add locks the worktree as part of creating it. That is safer than running lock afterwards.
Scripts should use list --porcelain, preferably with -z, because that format won't change between versions or with user settings.
add --no-checkout creates the worktree without checking files out. That gives you a chance to set things up first, for example sparse-checkout.
To name a worktree in a command, the tail of its path is enough as long as no other worktree's path ends the same way.
gotchas: A branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time. add refuses to check out a branch that another worktree is using unless you pass --force.
remove fails if the worktree has untracked or modified files. You need --force for that, and --force twice if the worktree is locked.
move can't relocate the main worktree or a linked worktree that contains submodules. If you move them by hand, run repair afterwards to fix the links.
Using multiple worktrees with submodules is still experimental. The docs advise against checking out a superproject more than once.

HEAD.summary: Git's main options can select the repository and working tree, change the command directory, control paging, and show the Git program path. These options affect one command invocation.
HEAD.explanation: Git can use command-line options to select the repository and working tree, control output paging, and choose where its programs are installed. The `-C` option changes the directory for one command, while `--git-dir` and `--work-tree` set repository paths directly.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Path to the repository directory, normally `.git`.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Path to the working tree.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Directory containing Git's core programs.

HEAD.returns: `--exec-path` without a path prints the current setting and exits.

example.title: Run a command in another directory
example.code: git -C /path/to/repository status
example.explanation: Run Git as if it started in the given directory.

useCases.title: Use a repository by path
useCases.scenario: Run Git from a script while staying in the script's current directory.

useCases.title: Separate repository and working tree
useCases.scenario: Work with a repository whose `.git` directory is separate from its files.

useCases.title: Control output paging
useCases.scenario: Prevent long output from opening a pager or force paging for terminal output.

useCases.title: Check the Git program path
useCases.scenario: Inspect or configure the directory containing Git's core programs.

interview.question: What are `--git-dir` and `--work-tree` used for?
interview.answer: `--git-dir` tells Git where the repository directory is. `--work-tree` tells Git where the checked-out files are. These paths can be absolute or relative to the current directory.
interview.followUp: What does `git -C path command` do? It runs the command as though Git started in `path`, without changing the caller's directory.

interview.question: How can you control Git's pager?
interview.answer: `-p` or `--paginate` sends terminal output through `less`, or through the configured pager. `-P` or `--no-pager` prevents this.
interview.followUp: Which option wins if both are supplied? The later command-line setting normally determines the final option state.

interview.question: What does `--exec-path` do?
interview.answer: `--exec-path` identifies the directory containing Git's core programs. With a path, it sets that location for the command; without a path, Git prints the current location and exits.
interview.followUp: What environment variable provides another way to control it? `GIT_EXEC_PATH` can control the same setting.

keyPoints: Use `git -C <path>` to run one Git command from another directory.
`--git-dir=<path>` selects the repository directory instead of the default `.git` directory.
`--work-tree=<path>` selects the directory that contains the checked-out files.
`--paginate` uses `less` or the configured `PAGER` when output goes to a terminal.
`--no-pager` keeps Git output out of a pager.
`--exec-path` refers to the directory containing Git's core programs.
gotchas: Using `--git-dir` disables normal repository discovery. Git then treats the supplied location as the repository.
When the current directory is not the working-tree root, also set `--work-tree` to the correct path.

Merge conflict.summary: `git merge` combines another branch with the current branch. It can move the branch pointer directly or create a merge commit, depending on the history and selected options.
Merge conflict.explanation: Git combines another branch into the current branch. If the current branch already leads directly to the other branch, Git can move the branch pointer without creating a commit. Otherwise, Git creates a merge commit unless an option changes this behavior.

parameters.name: <commit>...
parameters.description: Branches, tags, or other commits to merge into the current branch.

Merge conflict.returns: A successful merge updates the current branch, either by moving its pointer or by creating a merge commit. A refused `--ff-only` merge exits with a non-zero status.

example.title: Create a merge commit
example.code:
git switch main
git merge feature/login --no-ff
example.explanation: This switches to `main` and merges `feature/login`. The merge commit is created even if a fast-forward would be possible.

useCases.title: Always create a merge commit
useCases.scenario: Keep a feature branch's history as a visible merge point.

useCases.title: Require fast-forward merges
useCases.scenario: Allow only linear history updates.

useCases.title: Use a three-way merge
useCases.scenario: Combine branches that have diverged.

interview.question: When does `git merge` create a merge commit?
interview.answer: Git uses a fast-forward when the merged branch is already a descendant of the current branch. This only moves the current branch pointer, so no merge commit is made. If that relationship does not exist, Git creates a merge commit by default.
interview.followUp: How can a project require a merge commit? Use `git merge --no-ff`. This creates a merge commit even when a fast-forward could be used.

interview.question: What does `--ff-only` do?
interview.answer: `--ff-only` permits only a fast-forward merge. If the histories have diverged, Git refuses to merge and returns a non-zero status.
interview.followUp: What option forces a merge commit in all cases? `--no-ff`.

interview.question: What is the default merge strategy?
interview.answer: The default `ort` strategy handles a merge of two heads with a three-way merge. It can also handle renames, but it does not use detected copies.
interview.followUp: How can conflicting hunks be resolved in favor of the current branch? Pass `-X ours`; this does not discard all changes from the other tree.

keyPoints: `--ff` is normally the default. Git assumes `--no-ff` for an annotated tag that is outside its natural `refs/tags/` location.
A normal merge fast-forwards only when the other history descends from the current history. Otherwise, Git makes a merge commit.
The default `ort` strategy detects and handles renames during the merge. It does not use detected copies.
gotchas: `--ff-only` refuses the merge when a fast-forward is not possible. It exits with a non-zero status.
The `ours` strategy option resolves conflicting parts in favor of the current branch, but it still keeps non-conflicting changes from the other branch. It is different from the `ours` strategy.

post-merge hook.summary: The post-merge hook runs after a successful Git merge. Use it to restore untracked working-tree data or check external files needed by the project.
post-merge hook.explanation: A post-merge hook is a client-side script that Git runs after a successful merge. It can restore working-tree data that Git does not track, or check for files outside Git that should be copied when the working tree changes.

example.title: A post-merge hook
example.explanation: Save this executable script as .git/hooks/post-merge. Git runs it after a successful merge.

useCases.title: Restore permission data
useCases.scenario: A merge changes files and the project needs local permission settings restored.

useCases.title: Check external files
useCases.scenario: A project depends on files that are kept outside the repository.

useCases.title: Update external project files
useCases.scenario: A merge changes the working tree and local files must be copied into place.

interview.question: When does the post-merge hook run, and what is it useful for?
interview.answer: Git invokes post-merge after a merge command succeeds. It is useful for restoring untracked working-tree data or checking external files.
interview.followUp: Can it reject a completed merge? The documentation describes it as a post-merge action, not as a pre-merge validation hook; use an earlier validation mechanism when rejection is required.

interview.question: What kinds of tasks can a post-merge hook perform?
interview.answer: A hook can restore data that Git cannot track, such as permissions data. It can also check for external files that may need to be copied into the working tree.
interview.followUp: Why is this needed? Git does not manage every property or file used by a project, so the hook can synchronize those external details after a merge.

interview.question: How should a post-merge script be designed?
interview.answer: The hook is run after a successful merge, so its work happens after Git has changed the working tree. A script can then perform project-specific setup or validation.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid unnecessary work? Make the script check whether the external data or files actually need updating before changing them.

keyPoints: Git runs this client-side hook only after a merge completes successfully.
It can restore working-tree information that Git does not track, including permission data.
It can check that required files outside Git control are present.
The hook can help copy external files when a merge changes the working tree.
gotchas: It does not run when the merge fails.

pre-commit hook.summary: The pre-commit hook runs before Git creates a commit. It can inspect the staged snapshot and stop the commit by exiting with a nonzero status.
pre-commit hook.explanation: Git runs the pre-commit hook during git commit, before it creates the commit. The hook receives no parameters. A nonzero exit status stops the commit, but git commit --no-verify can skip it.
pre-commit hook.returns: A zero exit status allows the commit to continue; a nonzero exit status aborts git commit.

example.title: Run tests before a commit
example.explanation: Save this executable file as .git/hooks/pre-commit. A failing test makes Git stop the commit.

useCases.title: Check code quality
useCases.scenario: Run tests or linters before a commit is created.

useCases.title: Check whitespace
useCases.scenario: Reject staged files with formatting problems.

useCases.title: Validate the snapshot
useCases.scenario: Apply project-specific checks to the staged snapshot.

interview.question: When does the pre-commit hook run, and what happens if it fails?
interview.answer: Git invokes pre-commit before it obtains the proposed commit message and creates the commit. The hook has no parameters, and a nonzero exit status aborts git commit.
interview.followUp: Can the hook always enforce a rule? No. git commit --no-verify can bypass it, so important rules should also be enforced on the server.

interview.question: What is a suitable use for pre-commit?
interview.answer: The hook is called by git-commit. It can inspect the snapshot that is about to be committed, such as checking tests or formatting.
interview.followUp: How would you check the commit message instead? Use prepare-commit-msg to edit the message before the editor, or commit-msg to validate the finished message.

interview.question: What checks does Git's default pre-commit hook perform?
interview.answer: The default enabled hook checks for non-ASCII filenames and trailing whitespace. The non-ASCII filename check can be enabled or disabled with hooks.allownonascii.
interview.followUp: Can this hook be used for a central repository policy? Not by itself, because client-side hooks are local and can be bypassed; use a server-side hook for enforcement.

keyPoints: Git runs pre-commit during git commit.
The hook has no command-line parameters and runs before Git gets the proposed message.
Return a nonzero status to stop the commit before Git creates it.
Git's enabled sample hook rejects newly introduced filenames that contain non-ASCII characters.
The enabled sample hook also rejects lines that end with trailing whitespace.
Set hooks.allownonascii to true to disable the sample hook's non-ASCII filename check.
gotchas: A user can skip this hook with git commit --no-verify, so it is not a reliable server-side policy.
When no editor will open, Git sets GIT_EDITOR to a colon for commit hooks.

pre-push hook.summary: The `pre-push` hook runs during `git push` before Git transfers objects. It can inspect proposed reference updates and stop the push by returning a non-zero status.
pre-push hook.explanation: Git runs a pre-push hook during `git push`, after it checks the remote references but before it sends objects. The hook receives the remote name and location as arguments, and receives the references that would change through standard input. A non-zero exit status cancels the push.

parameters.name: remote-name
parameters.description: The remote name used by the push.

parameters.name: remote-location
parameters.description: The remote repository location.

parameters.name: to-be-updated-refs
parameters.description: References that Git plans to update, read from standard input.

pre-push hook.returns: A zero exit status allows the push to continue; a non-zero exit status aborts it.

example.title: Run tests before pushing
example.code:
#!/bin/sh
# .git/hooks/pre-push
set -eu
npm test
example.explanation: Save this executable script as .git/hooks/pre-push. A failed test returns a non-zero status, so Git stops the push.

useCases.title: Pre-push testing
useCases.scenario: Run automated tests before code leaves the local repository.

useCases.title: Validate updates
useCases.scenario: Check branch names, commit rules, or proposed reference changes.

useCases.title: Local policy checks
useCases.scenario: Reject a push that violates local project rules.

interview.question: When does the pre-push hook run, and how can it stop a push?
interview.answer: Git runs `pre-push` during `git push`, after remote references are updated and before objects are transferred. The hook can inspect the proposed reference updates and reject them by returning a non-zero exit status.
interview.followUp: What input does it receive? It gets the remote name and location as arguments, while the references to update arrive on standard input.

interview.question: What data does a pre-push hook receive?
interview.answer: The hook receives the remote name and its location as parameters. Git sends the list of references that would be updated through standard input.
interview.followUp: Why use standard input for the references? A push can update several references, so the hook can validate the complete set before transfer.

interview.question: What is a common use for pre-push?
interview.answer: A pre-push hook is a client-side hook used to validate reference updates before a push. For example, it can run tests or check branch rules and return failure when the proposed push is invalid.
interview.followUp: How can a server enforce policy for every pusher? Use server-side `pre-receive` or `update` hooks, which can reject pushes on the server.

keyPoints: Git runs this hook as part of `git push`, before object transfer finishes.
The remote name and location are command-line arguments. Proposed reference updates are sent through standard input.
Use it to check the complete group of reference updates before Git sends the objects.
Return a non-zero status to cancel the push.
gotchas: The hook runs during a push, before Git transfers objects. Its checks can stop the push by returning a non-zero status.
A failing hook aborts the push.

Signed commits.summary: Git can verify trusted GPG signatures on commits during a merge. Use -S to sign the resulting merge commit.
Signed commits.explanation: Git can check signatures while merging. With --verify-signatures, the merge stops if a commit lacks a trusted GPG signature. The -S option signs the merge commit that Git creates. The check and the new signature are separate actions.

parameters.name: branch
parameters.description: Branch or other commit reference to merge.

Signed commits.returns: The merge proceeds only when the required signatures are valid; otherwise Git reports an error and does not merge.

example.title: Verify and sign a merge
example.code: git merge --verify-signatures -S signed-branch
example.explanation: This checks that every commit being merged has a valid signature and signs the new merge commit.

useCases.title: Reject unsigned commits
useCases.scenario: A repository requires every incoming commit to have a trusted GPG signature.

useCases.title: Sign a merge commit
useCases.scenario: A project wants the merge commit to record the integrator's signature.

useCases.title: Plan a signing policy
useCases.scenario: A team is deciding whether signed commits should be part of its standard workflow.

interview.question: How can Git reject an unsigned commit during a merge?
interview.answer: Use git merge --verify-signatures branch-name. Git checks the commits in the branch and refuses the merge if one lacks a valid trusted GPG signature.
interview.followUp: How do you also sign the merge commit? Add -S, as in git merge --verify-signatures -S branch-name.

interview.question: What is the difference between --verify-signatures and -S?
interview.answer: The --verify-signatures option checks the commits being merged. The -S option signs the merge commit created by the operation.
interview.followUp: Does -S alone check all commits in the source branch? No. Use --verify-signatures for that check.

interview.question: What should a team consider before requiring signed work?
interview.answer: A team should understand GPG and agree on the workflow before requiring signed commits. Otherwise, developers may need to rewrite existing commits with signatures.
interview.followUp: What can happen when a branch contains one unsigned commit? A merge using --verify-signatures is rejected.

keyPoints: Git 1.8.3 and later can check signatures during merge or pull.
Use --verify-signatures to require trusted GPG signatures on commits being merged.
The merge stops when the source branch contains an unsigned or invalid commit.
When all checked commits are valid, Git displays the signatures and continues.
Use -S to sign the merge commit produced by Git.
gotchas: A team should agree on signing before making it part of its normal workflow. Otherwise, unsigned commits may need to be rewritten later.

Staging area.summary: The staging area, which Git also calls the index, is one of Git's four core kinds of data. It holds the exact file snapshot your next commit will record, so you can choose what goes into a commit separately from what is in your working directory.
Staging area.explanation: Each index entry has four fields: a file type (regular, executable, symlink or gitlink), the ID of the blob holding the file's contents, a stage number and a path. Running git add stores the file's current content as a blob and points the entry at it. When you commit, Git turns this flat list of paths into nested tree objects and records that tree in the new commit. That means a commit holds whatever is staged, not whatever is on disk. During a merge conflict, one path can have several entries with stage numbers 1 to 3.

example.title: Stage part of your work and inspect the index
example.code:
set -e
mkdir demo && cd demo && git init -q
echo 'print("hi")' > hello.py
echo 'notes' > TODO.txt

# Stage only hello.py
git add hello.py
git status --short        # A  hello.py / ?? TODO.txt

# Look at the raw index entries: mode, blob id, stage, path
git ls-files --stage

# Edit after staging: the new edit is NOT staged
echo 'print("bye")' >> hello.py
git diff                  # working tree vs index
git diff --cached         # index vs HEAD (what will be committed)

# Commit records only the staged snapshot
git commit -qm 'Add hello.py'
git status --short        # ' M hello.py' and '?? TODO.txt' remain
example.explanation: The script stages one file, lists the index entries, then shows that an edit made after staging stays out of the commit until you run git add on that file again.

useCases.title: Splitting work into focused commits
