useCases.scenario: You fixed a bug and refactored code in the same file. You use git add -p to stage only the bug-fix hunks, commit them, and then stage and commit the refactor separately.

useCases.title: Resolving merge conflicts
useCases.scenario: After a conflicted merge, the index holds several stage entries for each conflicted path. Once you have edited a file to remove the conflict markers, you stage it to mark it as resolved, then you commit.

useCases.title: Reviewing exactly what will be committed
useCases.scenario: Before you commit, git diff --cached shows the difference between HEAD and the index, so you can check that only the intended changes go in.

interview.question: What is the Git index and what does it actually store?
interview.answer: The index, also called the staging area, is a flat list of entries. Each entry has a file type, a blob ID for the contents, a stage number and a path. git add writes the file's contents as a blob and updates the entry, and git commit converts the list into tree objects for the new commit.
interview.followUp: Why is the index a flat list instead of a tree? A flat list of full paths is easy to update one file at a time, and Git only builds the nested trees when it creates a commit.

interview.question: If you run git add on a file, edit it again, and then commit, what gets committed?
interview.answer: The version you staged gets committed. git add records the content at the moment you run it, and git commit with no arguments commits only what is staged. The later edit stays unstaged until you run git add on the file again.
interview.followUp: How would you see both sets of changes? git diff --cached shows staged changes (index vs HEAD), and plain git diff shows unstaged edits (working tree vs index).

interview.question: How does the index represent a merge conflict?
interview.answer: Each entry has a stage number. Normally it is 0, but when a merge conflicts, the same path can have several entries with stages 1, 2 and 3 for the different versions. Running git add on the resolved file replaces them with a single entry.
interview.followUp: What does git add --resolved do differently? It stages only unmerged paths that no longer contain conflict markers, and if any matching path still has markers, it refuses to stage anything.

keyPoints: Unlike a tree object, the index has no nested directories. It is a single flat list of paths, and Git only builds the directory trees at commit time.
The stage number is normally 0. If a merge has a conflict, the same path can appear several times in the index, once for each competing version.
You rarely need to read the raw index. Usually you compare it to HEAD with git status, and you can dump its entries (mode, blob ID, stage, path) with git ls-files --stage.
You don't have to stage a whole file. git add -p shows each hunk of the difference between the index and the working tree and lets you choose which ones to stage.
git add -N (intent-to-add) creates an index entry with no content. The file then shows up in git diff, and git commit -a will pick it up.
Some changes exist only in the index. For example, git add --chmod=+x sets the executable bit on the staged entry and leaves the file on disk unchanged.
gotchas: Staging copies the file's content at that moment. If you edit the file again before committing, the new edits are not included unless you run git add again.
Ignored files are skipped. If a glob matches an ignored file, Git skips it without any message. Use --force to stage it anyway.
git add -u updates and removes entries for files Git already tracks, but it never stages new untracked files.
If you hand-edit a patch with git add -e, the change is applied only to the index. Your working tree can then look as if it undid the staged change.

Upstream branch.summary: An upstream branch links a local branch to a remote-tracking branch. Git uses it as the default for several remote operations, including push, pull, and fetch without arguments.
Upstream branch.explanation: An upstream branch connects a local branch to a remote-tracking branch. Git uses this connection for commands such as git pull and for git push without arguments. The connection is stored in the repository configuration with the remote name and the remote branch reference.

parameters.name: <remote>
parameters.description: The remote name or URL to use for the push.

parameters.name: <branch>
parameters.description: The local branch to push and associate with the upstream.

Upstream branch.returns: The command pushes the branch and records its upstream branch; the documentation does not define a separate return value.

example.title: Push and set an upstream
example.code: git push --set-upstream origin feature/login
example.explanation: Pushes the local branch to the origin remote and records origin/feature/login as its upstream branch.

useCases.title: Publish a branch
useCases.scenario: A new local branch must be published and remembered for later pushes.

useCases.title: Set tracking information
useCases.scenario: A local branch should track a specific remote branch.

useCases.title: Use default remote targets
useCases.scenario: Commands without explicit remote arguments should use a known branch.

interview.question: What is an upstream branch?
interview.answer: An upstream branch is a remote branch associated with a local branch. Git uses it as the default for operations such as pull, fetch, and, in many cases, push without arguments. The association stores a remote name and a remote branch reference in the repository configuration.
interview.followUp: How do you create the association explicitly? Run git push --set-upstream <remote> <branch>; this pushes the branch and records its upstream.

interview.question: How do you set an upstream branch?
interview.answer: Use git push --set-upstream origin <branch> to push the branch and set its upstream. After that, git push can usually run without naming the remote and branch.
interview.followUp: What can set an upstream automatically? Cloning sets one for the default branch, and push.autoSetupRemote can set one on a first push.

interview.question: What does push.default=simple require?
interview.answer: With push.default=simple, git push without arguments uses the upstream branch only when its name matches the current branch. If no suitable upstream exists, the command can fail.
interview.followUp: Can the push destination differ from the pull destination? Yes. branch.<name>.pushRemote can select a different remote for pushing.

keyPoints: A local branch may be linked to one remote branch as its upstream.
The upstream branch supplies the default target for pull or fetch when those commands have no arguments.
Git stores the upstream remote and branch reference in .git/config.
Use git push --set-upstream to create the upstream association explicitly.
Cloning normally creates an upstream for the local copy of the default branch.
gotchas: With the default simple mode, a push without arguments expects the upstream branch to have the same name as the current local branch.
A push without arguments can fail when the current branch has no upstream, depending on push.default.

Working tree.summary: The working tree is the directory of real, checked-out files that you edit. It usually starts from the tree of the HEAD commit and also holds any local changes you have not committed yet.
Working tree.explanation: Git keeps history as compressed objects inside the repository, but you work on ordinary files on disk. When you check out a branch or commit, Git writes that commit's tree into your working directory and records it in the index. After that, you can edit files freely. Git finds your changes by comparing the files on disk with the index and with HEAD. When the files match the commit HEAD points to, the working tree is clean. Once you make edits that are not committed, it is dirty. A non-bare repository has one main working tree. git worktree can attach more working trees, and each one has its own HEAD and index.

example.title: Watching the working tree go from clean to dirty and back
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
git init -q demo && cd demo
git config user.email you@example.com
git config user.name You

echo 'hello' > greet.txt
git add greet.txt
git commit -qm 'initial'
git status --short   # nothing printed: working tree is clean

echo 'world' >> greet.txt   # edit a file on disk
git status --short          # ' M greet.txt' -> working tree differs from index
git diff                    # shows working tree vs index

git restore greet.txt       # copy the index version back into the working tree
git status --short          # clean again

git rev-parse --show-toplevel   # prints the root of the working tree
example.explanation: The script edits a committed file, uses git status and git diff to show that the working tree is now dirty, and then runs git restore to make it clean again.

useCases.title: Checking state before risky commands
useCases.scenario: Before you rebase, switch branches, or reset, run git status to find out whether the working tree has uncommitted edits. If it does, commit or stash them first so nothing gets overwritten.

useCases.title: Working on two branches at once
useCases.scenario: An urgent fix comes in while you are halfway through a refactor. Use git worktree add to create a second working tree on another branch, so you do not have to disturb the files you are already editing.

useCases.title: Running commands from a subdirectory in scripts
useCases.scenario: A build script runs from somewhere deep in the project. It can use git rev-parse --show-toplevel or :/ pathspecs so its paths are resolved from the root of the working tree.

interview.question: How do the working tree, the index and HEAD differ?
interview.answer: HEAD names the commit you are on, usually through the current branch. The index is a stored snapshot that will become the next commit. The working tree holds the editable files on disk. It normally matches HEAD's tree plus any uncommitted edits you have made.
interview.followUp: What do git diff, git diff --cached and git diff HEAD each compare? git diff compares the working tree with the index. git diff --cached compares the index with HEAD. git diff HEAD compares the working tree directly with HEAD.

interview.question: What makes a working tree clean or dirty, and how do you check?
interview.answer: A working tree is clean when its contents match the revision referenced by the current head. It is dirty when it has modifications that have not been committed to the current branch. git status shows this by listing staged changes, unstaged changes and untracked files.
interview.followUp: Why can git status look clean even though untracked build files exist? Files that match .gitignore patterns are ignored, so git status does not list them. You can see them with git status --ignored.

interview.question: Can a repository have zero working trees, or more than one?
interview.answer: Yes, both. A bare repository has no working tree, and a normal repository has one main working tree. git worktree add can attach more linked worktrees, each with its own HEAD and index, while they all share the same object database and refs.
interview.followUp: Why does Git refuse to check out the same branch in two worktrees by default? If two working trees had the same branch checked out, a commit in one would move that branch under the other and leave it out of sync. git worktree add only allows it with --force.

keyPoints: The glossary defines the working tree as the set of files that are actually checked out, as opposed to objects stored in the repository database.
The index sits between your files on disk and the next commit. It stores a snapshot of the working tree, and during a merge it can hold more than one version of a file.
A bare repository has no working tree. It holds only the files Git uses to manage the repository, which is why servers usually host bare repositories.
The :/ pathspec magic (top) matches paths from the root of the working tree, even when you run a command from inside a subdirectory.
A working tree's top level can contain a plain .git file (a gitfile) that points to the real repository directory instead of a .git folder. Linked worktrees and submodules use this.
gotchas: By default, checking out files from the index or a tree-ish only adds or updates files. In no-overlay mode, Git also deletes tracked files that are missing from the source, so you can lose files you did not expect to.
When an attr: pathspec is matched against a tree object, Git still reads the attributes from the working tree, not from that tree object. Results can change if your local .gitattributes differs.

Changes you have made but not committed make the working tree dirty. Some operations refuse to run or need --force when the tree is dirty. For example, git worktree remove only works on clean worktrees unless you force it.
